topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Percentage and decimal equivalents
topic.description: Solve problems requiring knowledge of percentage and decimal equivalents of 1/2, 1/4, 1/5, 2/5, 4/5 and fractions with denominators that are multiples of 10 or 25
evidence: State that 1/5 = 20% = 0.2 and use this to find 20% of 60
Convert 3/4 to 75% and to 0.75
A shop offers 25% off a £40 item — what is the sale price?
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} knows that 1/4 = 25% = 0.25, can they use that to work out 25% of £80 — and also find 4/5 of 60 sweets?

pedagogy.summary: Children need fluent, usable knowledge that 1/2, 1/4, 3/4, 1/5, 2/5, 4/5 and tenths/hundredths have partner percentage and decimal forms, and — crucially — must DEPLOY those equivalences to solve problems (25% off £40; 20% of 60). The skill is procedural: recognise which landmark equivalent applies, convert to the handiest form, and compute. Good teaching anchors the equivalents to a hundred-grid or bar so 'per cent = per hundred' stays concrete, and builds a benchmark toolkit (50% = half, 10% = ÷10, 1% = ÷100, 25% = ÷4) that children combine to reach any of the target percentages rather than memorising isolated facts.
bestPractices: Teach percentages of amounts via landmark benchmarks — 50% (halve), 10% (divide by 10), 1% (divide by 100), 25% (quarter) — and combine them (e.g. 20% = double 10%), so the child reasons rather than recalls a rule.
Ground every equivalent on a hundred-grid or bar model: 1/5 shaded is 20 of 100 squares = 20% = 0.2, keeping 'per cent means per hundred' visible.
Rehearse the recall set (1/2, 1/4, 3/4, 1/5, 2/5, 4/5 and /10, /25 denominators) as a connected web, deriving 2/5 and 4/5 from 1/5 rather than as separate facts.
Always require the child to interpret the answer in context — '25% off £40' means find the DISCOUNT (£10) then the SALE PRICE (£30), not just compute 25% of 40.
Move between all three forms in problems so the child chooses the easiest tool: 1/5 of 60 is fastest as 60 ÷ 5, while 20% of 60 might be found as double-10%.
keyRepresentations: Hundred-grid (10×10) with a fraction shaded, read simultaneously as fraction, hundredths-decimal and percentage
Bar model / percentage bar marked at 0, 25, 50, 75, 100% aligned with the whole amount
Double number line: amount on top, percentage on the bottom, for scaling to any percentage
Benchmark toolkit table: 50% = ÷2, 25% = ÷4, 10% = ÷10, 1% = ÷100 with worked combinations
commonMisconceptions: Base-neglect: treats a percentage as a fixed amount independent of the whole — '25% off means £25 off' or '20% of 60 is 20'.
Denominator-as-decimal / faulty equivalent: converts 1/5 to 0.5 (copies the 5) or thinks 1/5 = 15%.
Rote 'divide by 100' with no meaning: divides by 100 and stops, or divides by the wrong number (e.g. by 20 for 20%).
Solves '25% off' by finding 25% and forgetting to subtract, giving the discount as the sale price.

learn.summary: Children build fluent, usable knowledge that landmark fractions (1/2, 1/4, 3/4, 1/5, 2/5, 4/5 and tenths/hundredths) have partner percentage and decimal forms, and — crucially — deploy those equivalences to solve problems (25% off £40; 20% of 60). The core is procedural: recognise which landmark applies, convert to the handiest form, and compute. Ground every equivalent on a hundred-grid or bar so 'per cent = per hundred' stays concrete, and build a benchmark toolkit (50% = halve, 10% = ÷10, 1% = ÷100, 25% = ÷4) that children combine to reach any whole-number target percentage rather than memorising isolated facts. Always require interpreting the answer in context (discount vs sale price).

activities.title: Live percentage bar over a settable amount
feedback: If the learner expects £10 for 25% of both £40 and £80, pause on the two bars side by side: the same 25% shades a different amount because the whole differs.
If the learner reports £10 as the sale price, prompt: 'that's how much comes off — what does the coat cost now?' and show discount-then-remaining on the bar (£40 − £10 = £30).
When they build 20% from two 10% blocks, highlight that 10% of 60 = 6 so 20% = 12, connecting the combination to the arithmetic.
activities.rationale: Acting on a model where the whole is settable is intended to make base-dependence felt and to let learners rehearse benchmark combinations with immediate feedback; the settable whole is meant to make base-neglect hard to sustain. The live recompute and sale-price readout are optional, proposed interaction examples that make the discount-vs-remaining distinction concrete; their comparative efficacy over other formats is not established.
sourceClaims: Base-neglect — treating a percentage as an absolute quantity rather than a proportion of the whole — is a documented, persistent student error in percentage problems.
Percentages of amounts are best taught via benchmark percentages (50%, 10%, 1%, 25%) that students combine, grounded on hundred-grid and bar models.
learnerActions: Set the whole amount to £40 on a percentage bar and move a marker to 25%; read off the shaded amount (£10) and a separate sale-price readout (£30), so discount and remaining stay distinct.
Build 20% of 60 by stacking two 10% benchmark blocks (10% of 60 = 6, so 20% = 12), watching the arithmetic appear as you combine them.
Keep the marker at 25% but change the whole from £40 to £80 and observe the pounds answer change from £10 to £20 — the same percentage, a different amount.
Try each target percentage two ways where possible (e.g. 1/5 of 60 as 60 ÷ 5, and 20% of 60 as double 10%) and compare.
activities.intendedInsight: A percentage is a proportion of the whole, not a fixed amount: changing the whole changes the pounds answer. Benchmark percentages (50%, 10%, 1%, 25%) can be combined to reach any whole-number target percentage, and the discount is a different quantity from the sale price.

activities.title: Hundred-grid reference for landmark equivalents
feedback: If a learner writes 1/5 = 0.5, point to the grid: five equal parts of 100 is 20 each, so 1/5 = 20 hundredths = 0.2, not 0.5.
If a learner writes 1/5 = 15%, recount the shaded squares to confirm 20 of 100 = 20%.
Reinforce that 2/5 is just two of the 1/5 blocks (40 squares) rather than a new fact to memorise.
activities.rationale: A hundred-grid keeps 'per cent = per hundred' visible and consolidates the landmark equivalents and conversions. This is a reference/consolidation scaffold: a tap-to-reveal grid cannot by itself vary the whole or compute a percentage of a chosen amount, so it supports but does not replace the problem-solving work.
sourceClaims: Percentages of amounts are best taught via benchmark percentages (50%, 10%, 1%, 25%) that students combine, grounded on hundred-grid and bar models.
learnerActions: Shade 1/5 of a 10×10 hundred-grid and count the squares (20 of 100), then read it simultaneously as 1/5 = 20 hundredths = 0.2 = 20%.
Shade 1/4 to reveal 25 squares = 25% = 0.25, and 3/4 to reveal 75 squares = 75% = 0.75.
Contrast 1/5 (20 squares) with 1/2 (50 squares) to check against the 'copy the denominator digit' habit (1/5 is not 0.5 or 15%).
Derive 2/5 and 4/5 from 1/5 by counting 40 and 80 squares, building the recall set as a connected web rather than separate facts.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Per cent means per hundred': the fraction, hundredths-decimal and percentage are three readings of the same shaded quantity on a hundred-grid, and related fractions (2/5, 4/5) derive from 1/5.

activities.title: Fluency and context-step rehearsal
feedback: If a learner selects £10 as the sale price, confirm the discount is right but ask what remains: £40 − £10 = £30.
If a learner selects £25, revisit per-cent-means-per-hundred: 25% of £40 is a quarter of 40 = £10, not £25.

If a learner writes 60 ÷ 100 or 60 ÷ 20 and presents it as 20% of 60, connect the divisor to the fraction: 1% = ÷100 (so 60 ÷ 100 = 0.6 is one per cent), then 20% = 20 of those = 12; or 20% = 1/5 = ÷5, not ÷20.
If a learner can only reach an answer one way, prompt a benchmark route (e.g. 10% then double) to build flexibility.
activities.rationale: The evidence statements (20% of 60; convert 3/4; sale price of a 25%-off £40 item) can be rehearsed as scored items, efficiently practising the recall set and catching the forgot-to-subtract and rote-divisor errors. Recognition/matching items rehearse and check fluency but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a method, so pair them with the model and explanation work.
learnerActions: Match the three equivalent forms: 1/5 ↔ 20% ↔ 0.2 and 3/4 ↔ 75% ↔ 0.75.
Complete fill-in-the-blank computations such as '20% of 60 = __' and '1/5 of 60 = __'.
Answer a contextual item: a shop offers 25% off a £40 item — what is the sale price? Watch for the trap of £10 (that is the discount, not the price) and £25 (base-neglect, '25% off = £25').
Explain, for at least one item, a second route to the same answer (e.g. 20% of 60 via 10% of 60 doubled).
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent recall of the equivalents must combine with the context subtract-step: finding the discount is not the same as finding the sale price.

constraints: Always require interpreting the answer in context: '25% off £40' means find the discount (£10) then the sale price (£30), not just compute 25% of 40.
Teach percentages of amounts via combinable benchmarks (50% halve, 10% ÷10, 1% ÷100, 25% ÷4), e.g. 20% = double 10%, so children reason rather than recall an isolated rule.
Ground every equivalent on a hundred-grid or bar so 'per cent means per hundred' stays visible; connect the divisor to the fraction (20% = 1/5 = ÷5), not to the percentage number.
Address base-neglect directly by varying the whole: 25% of £40 vs 25% of £80 gives different pounds for the same percentage.

A static/tap-to-reveal hundred-grid is a reference scaffold for the recall set; it does not let the learner vary the whole or compute a percentage of a chosen amount, so it is not sufficient on its own for the problem-solving evidence.
Matching and multiple-choice items check recognition and fluency but do not elicit independent construction of a method; use them alongside tasks where the learner builds and explains a calculation.
A shopping role-play can motivate the context, but the calculation and model-manipulation must be where the doing happens, not just talked about.

Distinguish the forgot-to-subtract error (calculation correct, interpretation incomplete — scaffold the re-read, do not reteach percentages) from genuine misconceptions (base-neglect or faulty equivalents — reteach the meaning).

probeDeeper: You found the £10 — so what does the coat cost now? Why?
How did you know 1/5 is the same as 20%? Show me on the grid.
If the coat had been £80 instead of £40, would the 25%-off amount be the same? Why not?
Quick one: what's 20% of 60 a different way — can you get it from 10% of 60?
assess.correctAnswer: 25% of £40 = £10 (a quarter of 40), so the sale price is £40 − £10 = £30. 1/5 = 20% = 0.2, and 1/5 of 60 = 60 ÷ 5 = 12 (equivalently 20% of 60 = 12).

errorPatterns.pattern: Base-neglect: 'it's 25% off so that's £25 off' or '20% of 60 is 20' — treats the percentage as a fixed amount not tied to the whole.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to per-cent-means-per-hundred on a bar: 25% of £40 vs 25% of £80 side by side so the same percent gives different pounds; rebuild the calculation as a quarter of the actual amount.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes £25 (or a sale price of £15) for the coat, or gives 20 for 1/5 of 60; the number equals the percentage figure regardless of the amount.

errorPatterns.pattern: Faulty equivalent: converts 1/5 to 0.5 (copies the denominator digit) or thinks 1/5 = 15%, then computes with the wrong value.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild 1/5 on a hundred-grid: five equal parts of 100 is 20 each, so 1/5 = 20 hundredths = 0.2 = 20%; contrast with 1/2 to break the copy-the-digit habit.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States 1/5 = 0.5 or 1/5 = 15%, or finds 1/5 of 60 as 30 (used 0.5); the conversion itself is wrong before any arithmetic.

errorPatterns.pattern: Forgets the context subtract-step: finds 25% of £40 = £10 correctly but gives £10 as the sale price.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach percentages — the calculation is right. Prompt re-reading: 'that's how much comes off; what does the coat cost now?' Model discount-then-remaining on a bar. Scaffold, don't re-teach.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct discount (£10) written as the final answer; child computed the percentage but didn't interpret 'off'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rote 'divide by 100' with no meaning: divides by 100 and stops, or divides 60 by 20 taking the '20' as the divisor.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor the benchmark meaning: 1% = ÷100 (so 60 ÷ 100 = 0.6 is ONE per cent), then 20% = 20 of those = 12; or 20% = 1/5 = ÷5. Connect the divisor to the fraction, not the percentage number.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 60 ÷ 100 or 60 ÷ 20 = 3 and presents it as 20% of 60; procedure applied without tracking what the numbers mean.

responseLevels.gap: Treats the percentage as a fixed amount (£25 off, 20% of 60 = 20) and/or converts 1/5 wrongly (0.5, 15%); cannot connect the fraction, percentage and decimal forms to a calculation.
responseLevels.full: Computes the sale price (£10 off → £30) with the subtract-step, states 1/5 = 20% = 0.2, uses it to get 1/5 of 60 = 12, and can reach the same result a second way (e.g. via 10%), showing flexible, meaning-based use of the equivalents.
responseLevels.partial: Recalls the equivalents and can compute 25% of £40 = £10 and 1/5 of 60 = 12, but stumbles on interpreting the context (gives the discount as the sale price) or can only do it one way without deriving via benchmarks — knows the parts but doesn't reliably assemble them in a problem.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A coat costs £40 and there is 25% off. Work out the sale price and show your method. Then tell me the percentage and the decimal that are equal to 1/5, and use that to find 1/5 of 60.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the method, not asking about it, exposes the two things that separate real fluency from surface performance: whether the child SUBTRACTS to reach the sale price (vs stopping at the £10 discount) and whether they use a correct equivalent for 1/5 (vs 0.5/15% or dividing by the wrong number). Requiring both a discount problem and a fresh conversion-and-use in one task means a child can't pass on a single memorised fact.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Understanding Percentages
topic.description: Understand the per cent symbol (%); know that per cent means ‘number of parts per hundred’; write percentages as a fraction with denominator 100 and as a decimal
evidence: Write 35% as 35/100 and as 0.35
Shade 40% of a 10×10 grid and write the fraction 40/100
Explain that 100% means the whole, 50% means half
topic.assessmentPrompt: If a shop advertises 50% off, can {{name}} explain that this means half price — and write 50% as both a fraction and a decimal?

pedagogy.summary: A percentage is a proportion expressed as parts per hundred: 40% means 40 out of every 100, so it is naturally 40/100 and 0.40, and 100% is the whole while 50% is half of it. The decisive idea — and the one children most often miss — is that a percentage is an OPERATOR ON A BASE, not a plain number: 50% is not 'fifty', it is half of whatever the whole is, so 50% of 20 is 10 while 50% of 200 is 100. Because a percentage is inherently 'out of 100', its size relative to the whole is fixed but its actual amount depends entirely on the base. Teach it on the hundred square (40 of 100 shaded) tied to the fraction n/100, the decimal, and a 0%–100% number line, and confront base-neglect head-on.
bestPractices: Anchor 'per cent = parts per hundred' on a 10×10 hundred square: shade 40 squares to show 40%, and read off 40/100 and 0.40 from the same picture.

Foreground the base from the outset: a percentage is a proportion OF a whole, so always ask '% of what?'; show that 50% of a small set and 50% of a large set are the same proportion but different amounts.
Link the three forms explicitly — 40% = 40/100 = 0.40 — and simplify where natural (40/100 = 2/5) so percentage sits inside the fraction–decimal web.
Establish landmarks: 100% = the whole, 50% = a half, 25% = a quarter, 10% = a tenth, 1% = a hundredth; and seed that percentages can exceed 100%.
Confront base-neglect with deliberate comparisons (10% of 500 = 50 versus 90% of 60 = 48) so children see a smaller percentage of a bigger base can be the larger amount.
keyRepresentations: 10×10 hundred square shaded to the percentage
Four-way link: percentage + fraction n/100 + decimal + 0%–100% number line
Bar model of a whole partitioned to show a percentage of it
Landmark strip (0%, 10%, 25%, 50%, 100%) against fractions/decimals
Two different-sized wholes each showing '50%' to expose the role of the base
commonMisconceptions: Base-neglect: treating a percentage as a fixed number independent of the whole ('50% is always 50 / a lot').
Reading a percentage as a fraction with the number as denominator ('24% means 1/24', '40% means 1/40').
Percentage–decimal placeholder error: writing 9% as 0.9 instead of 0.09.
Believing 100% is the maximum — that you cannot have more than 100%.
Thinking a bigger percentage always means a bigger amount, regardless of the base.

learn.summary: A percentage is a proportion expressed as parts per hundred: 40% means 40 out of every 100, so it equals 40/100 and 0.40, with 100% as the whole and 50% as half of it. The decisive idea — and the one children most often miss — is that when we find a percentage OF an amount, the percentage acts on a base rather than standing for a fixed amount: 50% is not 'fifty' (it equals 50/100 = 0.5), it is half of whatever the whole is, so 50% of 20 is 10 while 50% of 200 is 100. Teach percentage on the hundred square (40 of 100 shaded) tied to the fraction n/100, the decimal, and a 0%–100% number line, establish landmarks (100%, 50%, 25%, 10%, 1%) and that percentages can exceed 100%, keep asking '% of what?', and confront base-neglect directly through deliberate comparisons.

activities.title: Same percentage, different whole: resize the base
feedback: If a learner says 50% is 'always 50' or 'always a lot', show 50% of 20 and 50% of 200 side by side: the square is half-shaded in both, but one amount is 10 and the other is 100 — same proportion, different amount.
Confirm the three forms read from one picture: 40 shaded of 100 is 40/100 and 0.40; where natural, 40/100 simplifies to 2/5.
If they treat the square as fixed, point out the square always shows 'out of 100' (the proportion) while the amount tracks the size of the whole.
activities.rationale: Letting the base vary while the percentage is held constant makes base-dependence something the learner observes directly, rather than being told; linking shading, fraction, decimal and number line welds percentage into the fraction–decimal web. A live, controllable base is one concrete way to make this visible; a fixed picture cannot be varied, though it can still illustrate 'parts per hundred'.
sourceClaims: A percentage represents part of a quantity and functions as an operator on a base, not a plain number; base-neglect — not attending to the whole from which the percentage is taken — is a robust, documented misconception (e.g. treating 32% of one amount as identical to 32% of another). The essential teaching principle is to establish which whole the percentage is calculated from.

'Per cent' means number of parts per hundred and a percentage can be an operator on a quantity; percentages have fraction and decimal equivalents; proportion is independent of the size of the number, so 10% of 500 (=50) can exceed 90% of 60 (=48); a documented error is writing 9% as 0.9; percentages can exceed 100%.

Pupils should understand the per cent symbol and that per cent relates to 'number of parts per hundred', and write percentages as a fraction with denominator 100 and as a decimal (Year 5 statutory content).
learnerActions: Set a percentage (e.g. 50%) and shade that proportion of a 10×10 hundred square.
With the whole set to 20, read off the actual amount (50% of 20 = 10); then change the whole to 200 and read the new amount (50% of 200 = 100).
Describe what stays the same (the proportion / the shaded half of the square) and what changes (the actual amount) as the base changes.
Alongside the shading, write the percentage as a fraction n/100 and as a decimal, and locate it on a 0%–100% number line.
activities.intendedInsight: A percentage fixes the PROPORTION of a whole, not a fixed number; the actual amount depends entirely on the base, so you must always ask '% of what?'.

activities.title: Bigger percentage, smaller amount: compare across different bases
feedback: 10% of 500 = 50; 80% of 60 = 48, so 10% of 500 is the larger amount even though 10% < 80%.
If a learner assumes the bigger percentage must win, point back to the base: 10% of a large whole can beat 80% of a small whole.
A twin-panel or two-bar display of the two amounts makes the 50-versus-48 comparison visible side by side.
activities.rationale: A deliberately contrasting pair where the smaller percentage yields the larger amount directly challenges the belief that 'bigger percentage = bigger amount'. The numbers (50 vs 48) are chosen so the gap is small and surprising.
sourceClaims: 'Per cent' means number of parts per hundred and a percentage can be an operator on a quantity; percentages have fraction and decimal equivalents; proportion is independent of the size of the number, so 10% of 500 (=50) can exceed 90% of 60 (=48); a documented error is writing 9% as 0.9; percentages can exceed 100%.
learnerActions: Work out 10% of 500 and 80% of 60, showing each amount.
State which is the larger AMOUNT and explain how you know without guessing.
Reflect on why the 'smaller' percentage (10%) gave the bigger amount (50 beats 48).
activities.intendedInsight: A bigger percentage does not guarantee a bigger amount, because the amount also depends on the size of the base being taken.

activities.title: Writing and checking the three forms
feedback: 9% = 9/100 = 0.09, not 0.9: nine hundredths needs a zero in the tenths place; similarly 5% = 0.05. Read 0.09 aloud as 'nine hundredths' to check.
40% means 40 out of 100 = 40/100, NOT 1/40: per cent is parts per HUNDRED, so 100 is the denominator. The '24% means one twenty-fourth' error has the same cause.
Check the landmarks against the hundred square: 25% is a quarter (25 of 100 = 1/4 = 0.25), 10% is a tenth (10 of 100 = 1/10 = 0.1), 1% is a hundredth (1 of 100 = 1/100 = 0.01).
100% is not a maximum: 150% means one and a half wholes (150 parts per hundred).
activities.rationale: These conversions are cleanly checkable and the common errors (1/n denominator, missing decimal placeholder, '100% is the maximum') are diagnostic. Landmark percentages give familiar anchors across the three forms. Single-digit cases are included deliberately because 40% → 0.40 can hide the placeholder error that 5% → 0.5 exposes.
sourceClaims: In national Key Stage 2 test analysis, percentages caused particular difficulty; a common error in finding 24% of 525 was to calculate 24% as one twenty-fourth — evidence of connecting percentages to fractions but not understanding what a percentage is or how it acts on a quantity.

'Per cent' means number of parts per hundred and a percentage can be an operator on a quantity; percentages have fraction and decimal equivalents; proportion is independent of the size of the number, so 10% of 500 (=50) can exceed 90% of 60 (=48); a documented error is writing 9% as 0.9; percentages can exceed 100%.

Pupils should understand the per cent symbol and that per cent relates to 'number of parts per hundred', and write percentages as a fraction with denominator 100 and as a decimal (Year 5 statutory content).
learnerActions: Complete links such as 40% = __/100 = 0.__ and 35% = 35/100 = 0.35.
Shade 40 of 100 squares to match 40%, and simplify 40/100 to 2/5 where asked.

Place landmark percentages on a 0%–100% strip and match them to their fraction and decimal: 100% = the whole = 1, 50% = a half = 0.5, 25% = a quarter = 0.25, 10% = a tenth = 0.1, 1% = a hundredth = 0.01.
Convert single-digit percentages carefully: write 9% as a decimal and as a fraction, and 5% as a decimal.
Decide whether a percentage can exceed 100% and say what 150% would mean.
activities.intendedInsight: Percentage, fraction (over 100) and decimal are three names for the same proportion; 'per cent' means parts per hundred, key landmarks (100%, 50%, 25%, 10%, 1%) link to familiar fractions and decimals, 100% is the whole, and percentages can exceed 100%.

activities.title: Predict, count, reconcile: '50% is always 50?'
feedback: A base-neglecter predicts 'same, both 50%'; the count (5 vs 50) contradicts this — same proportion, different amount because the wholes differ.
Jo is wrong: 50% means half of whatever the whole is (fifty parts per hundred), so 50% of 20 is 10 and 50% of 200 is 100.
For the sale claim, 50% off £40 saves £20 while 50% off £1000 saves £500 — the saving tracks the price, so the £50 claim fails.
If a learner cannot say '50% of what?', return to two different-sized wholes and reteach that a percentage is always OF a whole.
activities.rationale: A predict-then-check task with a stated reason makes the misconception observable and gives a moment of contradiction to resolve. A character's wrong claim can surface the misconception for discussion; the resolution is strengthened by actually computing and comparing the amounts.
sourceClaims: A percentage represents part of a quantity and functions as an operator on a base, not a plain number; base-neglect — not attending to the whole from which the percentage is taken — is a robust, documented misconception (e.g. treating 32% of one amount as identical to 32% of another). The essential teaching principle is to establish which whole the percentage is calculated from.
learnerActions: PREDICT first: Ann eats 50% of a plate of 10 grapes; Ben eats 50% of a plate of 100 grapes. Since both ate 50%, do they eat the same NUMBER of grapes? Give your reason before working it out.
Then count: Ann eats 5, Ben eats 50.
Reconcile the result with your prediction — same proportion, different amount.
Respond to the claim 'Jo says 50% is always 50': is Jo right, and what does 50% really mean?
Discuss or argue the case 'a 50%-off sale always saves £50' and explain why the saving depends on the original price.
activities.intendedInsight: Stating a reason before calculating exposes base-neglect; reconciling prediction with the count cements that 50% is a proportion of a base, not a fixed number.

constraints: Always tie the percentage to a named whole: ask '% of what?' every time an amount is computed, so the base stays visible.

A fixed/static hundred square annotated with 40% = 40/100 = 0.40 is a useful reference and can illustrate 'parts per hundred', but it cannot itself vary the base; base-dependence is best experienced by changing the whole or by comparing two different-sized wholes.

Recognition-only responses (e.g. choosing 'Jo is right/wrong') check understanding but do not by themselves require the learner to construct and justify the amount; include tasks where the learner computes and explains.
Include single-digit percentages (5%, 9%) as well as 40% so the decimal placeholder error cannot hide behind cases like 40% → 0.40.
Simplify fractions (40/100 = 2/5) only where it is natural and does not obscure the 'out of 100' meaning that defines percentage.

Establish landmark percentages (100%, 50%, 25%, 10%, 1%) alongside their fraction and decimal equivalents, and seed deliberately that percentages can exceed 100% so '100% is the maximum' does not take hold.

Any base-comparison example used with learners must be arithmetically correct and must actually demonstrate the intended point (e.g. 10% of 500 = 50 truly exceeds 80% of 60 = 48); do not reuse the source row's '90% of 60 = 48' figure, which is wrong (90% of 60 = 54).

Two of the four cited sources were flagged in the source row as verified:false (the KS2 'Misconceptions with the Key Objectives' analysis and the DfE National Curriculum programmes of study); treat the claims drawn from them — including the 24%-as-one-twenty-fourth error pattern and the Year 5 statutory conversion requirement — as unconfirmed.

The source row and the NCETM sourceClaim state the base-comparison as '90% of 60 (=48)', but 90% of 60 = 54, not 48. With the correct value (54) the smaller percentage would NOT exceed it (50 < 54), defeating the intended point. Learner-facing content has therefore been corrected to 80% of 60 = 48 so that 10% of 500 = 50 genuinely beats the larger-percentage amount while 10% < 80%. The verbatim source quote retaining '90%...(=48)' is kept only as the cited claim and must not be used as the computed example.

The original row rated 3D as 'poor' with 'adds no conceptual value' and framed a fixed image/dialogue as unable to 'deliver' the insight. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements; the live-base, twin-panel, two-bar, and tap-to-reveal elements are retained as optional concrete mechanisms, not mandatory ones.

assess.poeTask: Ask the child to PREDICT before working: 'Ann eats 50% of a plate of 10 grapes; Ben eats 50% of a plate of 100 grapes. Since both ate 50%, do they eat the same NUMBER of grapes? Why?' The stated reason is the diagnostic part — a base-neglecter predicts 'same, both 50%'. Then count: Ann eats 5, Ben eats 50. Have the child reconcile this with their prediction (same proportion, different amount).
probeDeeper: Is 50% of this small square the same AMOUNT as 50% of that big square? Is it the same PROPORTION? Why?
Can you have more than 100% of something? What would 150% mean?
You wrote 40% = 40/100. Can you write that fraction more simply?
Which is more: 10% of 500, or 90% of 60? How do you know without guessing?
assess.correctAnswer: Shade 40 of the 100 squares; 40% = 40/100 (= 2/5) = 0.40. Jo is wrong: 50% means half of whatever the whole is (fifty parts per hundred), so 50% of 20 is 10 and 50% of 200 is 100 — the amount depends on the base. 100% is the whole; 50% is half of it.

errorPatterns.pattern: Base-neglect: treats a percentage as a fixed number — 'Jo's right, 50% is 50 / 50% is just a lot' — ignoring the whole it is taken from.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show 50% of two different-sized wholes (20 and 200) on hundred squares so the amounts differ though the proportion is the same; establish '% is always OF a whole'. Reteach the meaning of per cent.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Agrees with Jo, or gives a single amount for 50% regardless of the base; cannot say '50% of what?'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the percentage as a fraction with the number as denominator — '40% means 1/40' (the classic '24% = one twenty-fourth').
errorPatterns.nextMove: On the hundred square, 40% is 40 of 100 squares = 40/100; per cent is parts per HUNDRED, so 100 is the denominator. Reteach 'out of 100'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 40% as 1/40 instead of 40/100; connects percentage to fractions but with the wrong denominator.

errorPatterns.pattern: Percentage–decimal placeholder error: writes a single-digit percentage such as 9% as 0.9 instead of 0.09.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Read 0.09 as 'nine hundredths'; 9% = 9/100 sits in the hundredths place, needing a zero in tenths. Reteach decimal notation for hundredths.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On single-digit percentages, drops the placeholder (9% → 0.9); 40% → 0.40 may look fine but 5% → 0.5.

responseLevels.gap: Treats a percentage as a fixed number (agrees '50% is always 50') or as 1/n; cannot shade the grid to match or write the fraction/decimal.
responseLevels.full: Explains a percentage as parts per hundred of a base, so 50% depends on the whole (10 of 20, 100 of 200); shades 40 of 100, writes 40/100 = 0.40 = 2/5; knows 100% is the whole and >100% is possible; judges base-dependent comparisons and transfers to new cases.
responseLevels.partial: Writes 40% = 40/100 = 0.40 and knows 100% is the whole and 50% is half, but still treats the amount as fixed regardless of the base, or converts without articulating that a percentage is parts per hundred OF a whole.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Shade 40% of this 10×10 grid, and write 40% as a fraction and as a decimal. Then tell me: Jo says '50% is always 50'. Is Jo right? Explain what 50% really means.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The grid + fraction + decimal checks the 'parts per hundred' meaning; the Jo question is the hinge — a child who understands percentage as a proportion of a base rejects '50% is always 50' and ties the amount to the whole, while a base-neglecter agrees or treats 50% as a fixed number. Reasoning correctly and incorrectly give opposite verdicts on Jo, which is hard to fake.

sources.claim: A percentage represents part of a quantity and functions as an operator on a base, not a plain number; base-neglect — not attending to the whole from which the percentage is taken — is a robust, documented misconception (e.g. treating 32% of one amount as identical to 32% of another). The essential teaching principle is to establish which whole the percentage is calculated from.
sources.source: Bassan Cincinatus & Sheffet (2016), 'With percentages the 100 is always in the denominator', IJRES 2(1), 143–155 (peer-reviewed; fetched in full)

sources.claim: 'Per cent' means number of parts per hundred and a percentage can be an operator on a quantity; percentages have fraction and decimal equivalents; proportion is independent of the size of the number, so 10% of 500 (=50) can exceed 90% of 60 (=48); a documented error is writing 9% as 0.9; percentages can exceed 100%.
sources.source: NCETM Mathematics Guidance, Spine 3: Fractions, Segment 3.10 'Linking fractions, decimals and percentages' (Year 6 Teacher Guide)

sources.claim: In national Key Stage 2 test analysis, percentages caused particular difficulty; a common error in finding 24% of 525 was to calculate 24% as one twenty-fourth — evidence of connecting percentages to fractions but not understanding what a percentage is or how it acts on a quantity.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Percentages (age 9+)
topic.description: Know and use the vocabulary of ratio and proportion — ratio, proportion, percentage, scale, equivalent, unequal, relative size, part-to-part, part-to-whole, and out of — and understand the difference between ratio (comparing parts to parts) and proportion (comparing a part to the whole)
evidence: Explain the difference between a 'ratio' and a 'proportion' using a concrete example like mixing paint
Use 'per cent' correctly and convert between fractions, decimals, and percentages in context
Define 'scale factor' and use it to describe how a shape has been enlarged or reduced
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is sharing something 3 ways and 2 ways, can they explain the difference between a ratio (like 3:2) and a proportion (like 3 out of 5) — showing they know what each word means?

pedagogy.summary: This is the vocabulary foundation for the whole ratio-and-proportion strand: children must use ratio, proportion, percentage, scale, equivalent, relative size, part-to-part, part-to-whole and 'out of' precisely, and grasp the central distinction that a RATIO compares part to part (3 red : 2 blue) while a PROPORTION compares a part to the whole (3 out of 5 are red = 3/5). Because these words are used loosely in everyday speech and are often taught as an inseparable phrase ('ratio and proportion'), the teaching goal is to differentiate them through repeated use in concrete contexts — mixing paint or squash, recipes, sharing — rather than through memorised definitions. Language precision here prevents the classic error of reading a part-to-part ratio as if it were a part-to-whole fraction.
bestPractices: Introduce terms through a concrete mixing/sharing context (e.g. squash: '1 part concentrate to 4 parts water') and the 'for every' phrasing before any notation — 'for every 1 concentrate there are 4 water' makes part-to-part audible.

Contrast ratio and proportion side by side on the SAME situation: 'the ratio of concentrate to water is 1:4' vs 'the proportion that is concentrate is 1 out of 5' — so children hear part-to-part against part-to-whole.

Attach each term to a representation: ratio → two coloured bars side by side; proportion/percentage → one bar (the whole) with a shaded part; scale → an enlargement pair. Language and picture reinforce each other.
Use 'out of' deliberately as the bridge to fractions and percentages: 3 out of 5 = 3/5 = 60%, all describing the same proportion.
Elicit and require the vocabulary in pupils' own explanations (talk moves) rather than accepting a right numeric answer with vague words — the objective IS the language.
Draw scale/equivalent language from enlargement examples ('every length is 3 times as big — a scale factor of 3') so 'scale' and 'equivalent' are grounded in action.
keyRepresentations: Two side-by-side coloured bars (part-to-part) contrasted with one part-shaded whole bar (part-to-whole / proportion)
'For every ___ there are ___' sentence frame linking language to the ratio
Squash/paint mixing jugs or coloured counters (concrete part-to-part)
A double-headed 'same proportion' triple: fraction 3/5 = 60% = 3 out of 5
An enlargement pair of shapes labelled with the scale factor
commonMisconceptions: Uses 'ratio' and 'proportion' interchangeably, as if they mean the same thing
Reads a part-to-part ratio as a part-to-whole fraction: hearing 'red to blue is 2:3' and saying '2/3 are red' (should be 2/5)
Treats 'proportion' only as everyday 'a large proportion' (a vague amount) rather than a comparison of part to whole
Confuses 'scale' / 'scale factor' with a difference (adds a fixed amount) rather than a multiplicative enlargement

learn.summary: Language foundation for ratio and proportion (ages 9–11): children must use ratio, proportion, percentage, scale, equivalent, relative size, part-to-part, part-to-whole and 'out of' precisely, and grasp the central distinction that a RATIO compares part to part (3 red : 2 blue) while a PROPORTION compares a part to the whole (3 out of 5 are red = 3/5 = 60%). Because these words are used loosely in everyday speech and are often taught as the inseparable phrase 'ratio and proportion', the objective is to differentiate them through repeated use in concrete mixing/sharing/recipe contexts rather than through memorised definitions. The payoff is preventing the classic error of reading a part-to-part ratio as if it were a part-to-whole fraction.

activities.title: Squash-mixing bench: one mixture, two descriptions
feedback: If a child writes the proportion as '1 out of 4', point to the single whole-bar: it visibly shows five parts in the whole, not four, so the 4 cannot be the whole — count all parts first (1 + 4 = 5), then name the proportion as 1 out of 5.

If a child gives the same numbers for both (e.g. 1:4 for the ratio AND '1 out of 4' for the proportion), have them re-describe each from its own picture using the matching word: the twin-bar for ratio, the whole-bar for proportion.
When both frames are correct, prompt the 'say it another way' link: 1 out of 5 = 1/5 = 20%, all naming the same proportion.

When the recipe is scaled to 2 concentrate and 8 water, work it through: the ratio 2:8 is equivalent to 1:4, and to find the proportion count the whole first (2 + 8 = 10), so the proportion that is concentrate is 2 out of 10 = 1 out of 5 — unchanged from the 1:4 mixture even though the numbers grew.
activities.rationale: A LANGUAGE objective is met when the child manipulates a situation and NAMES what changes; showing part-to-part and part-to-whole pictures simultaneously lets the learner attach each term to a distinct representation and makes the wrong denominator visibly contradicted rather than corrected by a rule. The live twin-bar/whole-bar pairing and the completion frames are offered as a concrete mechanism for this language work, not as the only possible medium.
sourceClaims: Ratio compares part to part while proportion compares a part to the whole; the 'for every' phrasing and simple pictures (rectangles/counters) are recommended for first teaching, and proportion is related to fractions.
learnerActions: Build a mixture by adding whole 'parts' of concentrate and water into a jug (for example 1 part concentrate to 4 parts water).

As each part is added, read two pictures that update together: a twin-bar showing concentrate beside water (part to part) and a single stacked bar showing the whole mixture with the concentrate shaded (part to whole).
Complete two sentence frames about the SAME mixture: 'the RATIO of concentrate to water is __ : __' and 'the PROPORTION that is concentrate is __ out of __'.
Then 'say it another way': express the proportion as a fraction, a percentage and an 'out of' phrase (for 1 part in 5: 1/5 = 20%).
Change the recipe and say whether the ratio and the proportion change.
activities.intendedInsight: The same mixture is described two different ways depending on which picture you read: for 1 concentrate to 4 water, the 1 sits against the 4 in the twin-bar (ratio 1:4) and against the whole of 5 parts in the single bar (proportion 1 out of 5). Ratio compares part to part; proportion compares part to whole; the whole = the sum of the parts.

activities.title: 'For every' spoken frame before notation
feedback: If the child jumps straight to '1 out of 5' when asked 'for every', redirect: 'for every' compares the two amounts to each other (1 to 4), not to the whole.
If the child says 'for every 1 there are 5', count the water parts only (4) — the whole (5) is a separate idea named by proportion, not by the 'for every' comparison.
activities.rationale: Grounding language in 'for every' speech before notation is explicitly recommended for first teaching and keeps part-to-part distinct from part-to-whole from the start.
sourceClaims: Ratio compares part to part while proportion compares a part to the whole; the 'for every' phrasing and simple pictures (rectangles/counters) are recommended for first teaching, and proportion is related to fractions.

At upper KS2 percentages, decimals and fractions are taught as different ways of expressing proportions; pupils meet ratio informally via 'for every' and unequal sharing, and 'scale factor' describes multiplicative enlargement.
learnerActions: Describe a mixture aloud using 'for every' before any colon notation: 'for every 1 concentrate there are 4 water'.
Then translate the spoken frame into the ratio 1:4.
State separately how much of the WHOLE drink is concentrate: 1 out of 5.
Repeat with coloured counters or paint instead of squash to hear the same structure in a new context.
activities.intendedInsight: 'For every ___ there are ___' makes part-to-part audible before symbols are introduced, so the ratio notation is read as a comparison of parts rather than copied as a rule.

activities.title: In-role recipe talk that requires precise words
feedback: If the child swaps the terms, the partner asks which comparison they mean and points back to the two amounts (part to part) versus the whole (part to whole).
Accept a correct numeric answer only when it is paired with the matching word; the goal is the language, not just the number.
activities.rationale: A responsive partner can require precise term use and gently challenge everyday blurred usage; this targets the language objective through genuine use rather than recited definitions. Offered as one route; a human conversation partner serves the same purpose.
learnerActions: Describe recipes and drink orders to an in-role partner (for example a smoothie-bar owner), using 'ratio' and 'proportion' correctly.
When the partner challenges a loose statement — 'you said proportion; did you mean part to part or part to whole?' — re-say it with the matching word.
Explain a part-to-part comparison and a part-to-whole comparison for the same order.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct USE of the vocabulary in unscripted dialogue is the actual objective; being asked to clarify loose usage forces the part-to-part vs part-to-whole reference to become explicit.

activities.title: Sort and complete: ratio vs proportion across contexts
feedback: If a child reads 'red to blue is 2:3' as '2/3 are red', count the whole: 2 + 3 = 5 parts, so 2 out of 5 are red — the 3 is the other part, not the whole.
If a statement is miscategorised, ask: does it compare two parts to each other (ratio) or a part to the whole (proportion)?
activities.rationale: A scored sorting and fill-in set can check whether the child selects the right term and distinguishes part-to-part from part-to-whole across contexts; it checks recognition and discrimination but does not by itself require the child to generate descriptions unprompted, so pair it with the spoken/building tasks.
sourceClaims: Ratio compares part to part while proportion compares a part to the whole; the 'for every' phrasing and simple pictures (rectangles/counters) are recommended for first teaching, and proportion is related to fractions.
learnerActions: Sort statements about mixtures, recipes and beads into 'this is a ratio' vs 'this is a proportion'.
Fill in sentence frames: 'the ratio of red to blue is __ : __' and 'the proportion that is red is __ out of __'.
For a described situation such as 'red to blue is 2:3', state what proportion are red (2 out of 5) and explain why '2/3 are red' is wrong.
activities.intendedInsight: Across varied contexts the same structural distinction holds: the ratio uses the part counts; the proportion uses the whole (sum of the parts).

activities.title: Labelled mixing glossary (reference scaffold)
feedback: Reveals the correct label on tap; because it does not require the child to produce or choose the word, use it as a glossary alongside, not instead of, tasks that demand use.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal labelled example is a useful reference, but a LANGUAGE objective is met by using the words, which a reveal-only artefact does not require; hence it is a support, not the main activity.
learnerActions: On a worked mixing example, tap the concentrate to reveal 'part', tap the jug to reveal 'whole', and tap the pair to reveal 'ratio 1:4 / proportion 1 out of 5'.
Use it to look up which word names which comparison while doing the building or talking tasks.
activities.intendedInsight: Each term is anchored to a concrete feature of the mixture: parts, the whole, and the two comparisons built from them.

activities.title: Scale factor from an enlargement pair
feedback: If a child says the shape got '2 cm bigger' on each side, check a second length that was a different length on the original shape (e.g. a 1 cm side and a 2 cm side enlarged by 3 become 3 cm and 6 cm, adding 2 cm and 4 cm): the added amount differs between those sides while the multiplier stays the same — scale factor is the multiplier. (If every side starts the same length, as in a square, the added amounts will match, so compare sides of different original lengths.)
Confirm by checking that each length of the new shape equals the matching original length times the scale factor.
activities.rationale: Grounding 'scale' and 'equivalent' in an enlargement action connects the words to a multiplicative relationship, addressing the common confusion of scale with additive difference.
sourceClaims: At upper KS2 percentages, decimals and fractions are taught as different ways of expressing proportions; pupils meet ratio informally via 'for every' and unequal sharing, and 'scale factor' describes multiplicative enlargement.
learnerActions: Compare an original shape with its enlargement and find how many times bigger every length is ('every length is 3 times as big').
State the scale factor as that multiplier ('a scale factor of 3') and check it is multiplicative, not an added amount.
Describe a reduction the same way (for example a scale factor of 1/2).
activities.intendedInsight: 'Scale'/'scale factor' names a multiplicative enlargement or reduction — every length is multiplied by the same number — not a fixed amount added on.

constraints: The objective is linguistic and relational: require the vocabulary in the child's own explanations rather than accepting a correct number with vague words.
Introduce terms through a concrete mixing/sharing context and 'for every' speech before any colon notation.

Reveal-only labelled examples and sort/fill-in tasks are scaffolds: they support recognition and reference but do not by themselves require the child to generate correct descriptions unprompted; pair them with building and spoken tasks.
Keep ratio and proportion contrasted on the SAME situation so the part-to-part vs part-to-whole difference is heard and seen, not memorised.
The whole used for a proportion is the SUM of the parts (1 concentrate + 4 water = 5), so the proportion that is concentrate is 1 out of 5, not 1 out of 4.

Scaling the amounts (e.g. 1:4 to 2:8) leaves the ratio equivalent (2:8 = 1:4) and the proportion unchanged once the whole is recomputed (2+8=10, so 2 out of 10 = 1 out of 5); use this to test real command of the language.
'Scale factor' is multiplicative (every length times the same number), not an added difference.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row's '3D adds nothing' judgement about this being spatial-only has been removed as a universal claim; a spatial model is simply not the proposed route here, which is a narrow design choice, not an established law.

Independent re-audit confirmed the scaled-mixture feedback is now correct: for 2:8 the whole is 2+8=10 and the proportion of concentrate is 2 out of 10 = 1 out of 5 (unchanged), derived rather than carried as a fixed denominator; no residual '1 out of 10' error remains.

Self-audit of central numbers: 1 concentrate to 4 water gives ratio 1:4 and proportion 1 out of 5 = 1/5 = 20% (concentrate); water is 4 out of 5 = 4/5 = 80%. 'red to blue is 2:3' gives 2 out of 5 red, not 2/3. Scale factor 3 and reduction 1/2 are multiplicative. All consistent.
Coverage note: the vocabulary terms 'relative size' and 'unequal' from the stated objective are only lightly exercised; consider an explicit task if full vocabulary coverage is required.

probeDeeper: 'Say the same thing as a fraction and as a percentage' — checks the 'out of'/proportion link to 3/5, 60% style equivalence.

Counterexample: 'If I made it 2 cups concentrate to 8 cups water, would the ratio change? Would the proportion that is concentrate change?' — a child with the language sees ratio 2:8 = 1:4 and proportion still 1 out of 5 (unchanged); a child without it thinks bigger numbers mean a different drink.
'Point to what the ratio compares, and what the proportion compares' — forces the part-to-part vs part-to-whole reference to be made explicit.
'A recipe says the ratio of sugar to flour is 2:3 — what proportion of the mixture is sugar?' checks transfer of the whole = 2+3 = 5 idea to a new context.
assess.correctAnswer: The RATIO of concentrate to water is 1:4 (or 'for every 1 concentrate there are 4 water') — a part-to-part comparison; and the PROPORTION of the drink that is concentrate is 1 out of 5 (1/5, 20%) — a part-to-whole comparison. The two numbers (4 vs 5) differ because ratio compares part to part and proportion compares part to whole.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here's a jug of orange squash made with 1 cup of concentrate and 4 cups of water. Tell me about this drink using the words 'ratio' and 'proportion' — describe how much concentrate there is compared with the water, and how much of the whole drink is concentrate.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The context forces the child to USE both words about the same situation, so the part-to-part vs part-to-whole distinction shows itself in whether they say 1:4 for the ratio but 1 out of 5 for the proportion. topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Calculating Percentages
topic.description: Solve problems involving the calculation of percentages of amounts (e.g. 15% of 360) and the use of percentages for comparison
evidence: Calculate 15% of 360 by finding 10% and 5% and combining
Compare two discounts given as percentages of different original prices

topic.assessmentPrompt: If a jumper originally costs £40 and is 15% off, can {{name}} work out how much the discount is and what the sale price would be?

pedagogy.summary: This is the procedural workhorse of percentages: finding a percentage of an amount (15% of 360) and using percentages to COMPARE quantities. At this age the reliable, meaning-preserving method is to build any percentage from friendly known facts — 10% (divide by 10), 5% (half of 10%), 1% (divide by 100) — and combine them (15% = 10% + 5%), which keeps the calculation grounded in 'parts per hundred' rather than a memorised rule. The second, subtler skill is comparison: a percentage is always relative to its base, so comparing two percentages of DIFFERENT amounts requires calculating the actual amounts, not just comparing the percentages. Teaching should anchor percentages to a 100-grid or bar, drill the 10%/5%/1% building blocks, and force explicit attention to 'percent of WHAT' whenever comparing.
bestPractices: Build percentages from benchmark facts: 10% (÷10), 1% (÷100), 5% (half of 10%), 25% (÷4), 50% (÷2), then combine (15% = 10% + 5%; 35% = 25% + 10%).
Anchor to a 100-square or a bar split into ten 10% chunks so 'parts per hundred' stays visible and 10% of 360 = 36 is seen, not just computed.

Make 'percent of what?' explicit in every comparison problem: a bigger percentage of a smaller amount can be less than a smaller percentage of a bigger amount — always compute the actual amounts to compare.
Connect the three forms fluently — 15% = 15/100 = 0.15 — and check the decimal is placed correctly (15% = 0.15, not 1.5), since misplacing it is a common source of tenfold errors.
Use bar models for percentage-of-amount: the whole bar is 100%, partition and shade to read off the required percentage.
Progress from friendly percentages (multiples of 5) to any percentage, and to a single-multiplier method (×0.15) once the benchmark method is secure.
keyRepresentations: 100-square (each cell = 1%) and a bar split into ten 10% chunks
Benchmark fact ladder: 10%, 5%, 1%, 25%, 50% and how to combine them
Percentage bar model (whole = 100%, shade the required part)
The equivalence triple 15% = 15/100 = 0.15
Two labelled bars of different totals for comparison (percent of WHICH base)

Cannot assemble a percentage from benchmarks, or takes 5% as 10% ÷ 5 instead of 10% ÷ 2
Treats a percentage as a fixed absolute amount rather than a proportion of the given whole

learn.summary: Year 6 pupils learn to find a percentage of an amount (e.g. 15% of 360) by building from benchmark facts — 10% (÷10), 5% (half of 10%), 1% (÷100) — and combining them (15% = 10% + 5%), keeping the calculation grounded in 'parts per hundred'. The subtler skill is comparison: because a percentage is always relative to its base, comparing two percentages of DIFFERENT amounts requires computing the actual amounts, not just comparing the percentages. Anchoring to a 100-grid or bar, drilling the benchmark building blocks, and forcing explicit attention to 'percent of WHAT' when comparing are the core moves.

activities.title: Build a percentage from benchmark chunks
feedback: If 10% of 360 is given as 3.6 or 360, return to 'parts per hundred': 10% means one of ten equal chunks, i.e. ÷10, so 10% of 360 = 36. Rebuild the triple 10% = 10/100 = 0.1.
If 5% is computed as 360÷5 = 72, point out that dividing the whole by 5 gives a fifth, which is 20%, not 5%. 5% is HALF of 10%, so 5% of 360 = 36 ÷ 2 = 18.
If the pupil cannot combine, show that 15% = 10% + 5%, so £36 + £18 = £54.

A running total shown as chunks snap together is one way to let the pupil watch £36 + £18 = £54 build up rather than only computing it (an optional illustration of the mechanism, not a required tool).
activities.rationale: Building percentages from benchmarks keeps the meaning (proportion of a hundred) in view and is treated here as the reliable, meaning-preserving method at this age; the equivalence triple and decimal-placement work directly target the documented percent-to-decimal conversion errors. An interactive bar with a live running total is a proposed way to make the build-and-combine action concrete; efficacy of the specific interaction is not established by the sources, which also note that benchmark-then-combine can be inefficient relative to a single multiplier.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils solve problems involving the calculation of percentages (e.g. of measures, such as 15% of 360) and the use of percentages for comparison.

Documented common student errors include converting a percent to a decimal incorrectly (e.g. treating 6% as 0.6) and using inefficient benchmark-then-combine methods; the underlying idea is percentage as a proportion, and translating fluently between percents, decimals and fractions is a key difficulty.
learnerActions: Treat a bar as the whole amount (e.g. £360 = 100%) and partition it into ten equal 10% chunks.
Find 15% of £360 by taking one 10% chunk (£36) and half of another (5% = £18), then combining them to read £54.
Say aloud how each benchmark is found: 10% = ÷10, 1% = ÷100, 5% = half of 10%, 25% = ÷4, 50% = ÷2, and combine (e.g. 35% = 25% + 10%).
Record the matching equivalence each time: 15% = 15/100 = 0.15, and check the decimal point is in the right place (0.15, not 1.5).
Progress from friendly multiples of 5 to any percentage, and later to a single multiplier (×0.15) once the benchmark method is secure.
activities.intendedInsight: Finding a percentage of an amount is assembling friendly known pieces, not recalling an opaque rule; 'parts per hundred' stays visible on the bar.

activities.title: Compare mode: percent of WHICH base?
feedback: If the pupil picks the 30% deal with no calculation, ask 'percent of WHAT?' and have them compute both actual savings on the two labelled bars.
If they compute one base and assume it applies to both, draw attention to the different bar totals and have them compute the second separately.
Two bars of different totals shown side by side, with each discount slice drawn to scale, can let the pupil SEE the 25%-of-£80 slice (£20) come out taller than the 30%-of-£60 slice (£18).
activities.rationale: The comparison is deliberately rigged so the smaller percentage gives the larger saving, which directly addresses the base-ignoring misconception; the underlying principle is that a percentage is a proportion of its own base. Drawing both slices to scale on different-height bars is a proposed way to make the relationship visible; its comparative efficacy over other formats is not established.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils solve problems involving the calculation of percentages (e.g. of measures, such as 15% of 360) and the use of percentages for comparison.

Documented common student errors include converting a percent to a decimal incorrectly (e.g. treating 6% as 0.6) and using inefficient benchmark-then-combine methods; the underlying idea is percentage as a proportion, and translating fluently between percents, decimals and fractions is a key difficulty.
learnerActions: Look at two bars of different totals side by side, e.g. an £80 coat at 25% off and a £60 jacket at 30% off.
First predict which deal saves more, then compute both actual savings: 25% of £80 = £20 and 30% of £60 = £18.
State the result: the COAT saves more (£20 > £18) even though its percentage is smaller, because the two percentages are taken of different prices.
Test the base explicitly: if the jacket had cost £100 instead of £60, recompute — 30% of £100 = £30 would now win — to show that the base matters.
Finish by writing a one-sentence explanation of why a smaller percentage can give a larger amount.
activities.intendedInsight: A percentage is relative to its own base; to compare two percentages of different amounts you must compute the actual amounts, not compare the percentages.

activities.title: Scored practice set with a base-ignoring distractor
feedback: Mark the 'bigger-percentage-wins' choice as a base error and prompt recomputation of both actual amounts.
If an answer is out by a factor of ten (e.g. 15% of 360 given as 5.4 or 540), flag the decimal/place-value slip and rebuild 15% = 0.15.
If the build-up blanks are inconsistent (10% right but 15% wrong), show 15% = 10% + 5%.
activities.rationale: A scored set can check percentage-of-amount and comparison cleanly, and a base-ignoring option is diagnostic; it consolidates and diagnoses rather than being the main place the comparison concept is constructed. Recognition-style items can check whether an answer is correctly classified but do not by themselves elicit the independent build-and-combine construction.
sourceClaims: Documented common student errors include converting a percent to a decimal incorrectly (e.g. treating 6% as 0.6) and using inefficient benchmark-then-combine methods; the underlying idea is percentage as a proportion, and translating fluently between percents, decimals and fractions is a key difficulty.
learnerActions: Complete fill-in build-ups: 10% of 360 = ☐, 5% of 360 = ☐, so 15% of 360 = ☐.
Answer a multiple-choice comparison of two discounts on differently-priced items, where one option is the 'bigger percentage must win' answer.
Use a slider to estimate a percentage on a 0-to-amount scale as a proportional sanity check before computing exactly.
Convert between forms in short items: write 15% as a fraction and a decimal and check decimal placement.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency with benchmark build-up and correct decimal conversion, plus recognising when a percentage-only comparison is wrong.

activities.title: 100-grid reference and shop-context discussion
feedback: If the pupil answers the shopkeeper by percentage alone, challenge with the rigged case where the smaller percentage wins and ask them to compute both actual amounts.

For '15% is 54 — roughly what fraction of 360 is that, and does that seem about right?', prompt a proportional check: 54 lies between a tenth of 360 (36) and a fifth (72), not 540 or 5.4. It is one and a half times 36 because 15% is one and a half times 10%.
activities.rationale: A static grid can anchor one worked percentage as a reference, and a conversational shop context can surface the base question and check reasoning; a conversation of this kind may prompt justification but does not itself drill computation, so repeated practice across cases is still needed for fluency.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils solve problems involving the calculation of percentages (e.g. of measures, such as 15% of 360) and the use of percentages for comparison.
learnerActions: On a 100-square where the whole grid is 360 and each cell = 1% (worth 3.6), reveal 10 cells (10% = 36), then a further 5 cells (5% = 18), then read 15 cells (15% = 54), as a benchmark reference.
Discuss a shopkeeper's competing deals on differently-priced items: 'which saves more?', and justify by computing actual amounts rather than comparing percentages.
Answer probing questions: 'How did you get 10% of 360 — and how do you know it isn't 3.6?'; 'Give me a quick way to find 5%, and 1%, of any amount.'
activities.intendedInsight: The 100-grid keeps 'parts per hundred' concrete, and talking through a real comparison forces 'percent of what?' into the reasoning.

constraints: 5% is HALF of 10% (÷2). It is not the amount ÷ 5, which gives 20%, and it is not 10% ÷ 5, which gives 2%. These are common slips to pre-empt.
Always make 'percent of what?' explicit in comparison problems — a bigger percentage of a smaller amount can be less than a smaller percentage of a bigger amount, so compute the actual amounts.
Check decimal placement: 15% = 0.15, not 1.5; misplacement gives tenfold errors.
The static 100-grid is a benchmark reference, not the main practice: fluency and comparison require the pupil to compute across multiple cases, not just view one worked example.

The scored set consolidates and diagnoses; recognition-style items can check whether an answer is right but do not by themselves elicit the independent build-and-combine construction, so they supplement rather than replace the bar work.

Bar/grid models are representations of proportion; keep the numeric meaning (parts per hundred) explicit so pupils do not treat the picture as the whole method. Percentages and fractions are comparable as numbers (e.g. 0.15 < 0.30) irrespective of any base; it is the actual amounts they produce that depend on the base, so when comparing represented portions use a common whole.

All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and the interactive mechanisms are optional illustrations of the learning mechanism, not mandatory tools or product features.

Self-audit of the worked numbers: 10% of 360 = 36, 5% = 18, 15% = 54 (correct). 25% of £80 = £20; 30% of £60 = £18, so the coat saves more (£20 > £18) — the comparison is correctly rigged. 30% of £100 = £30 (correct for the counterexample). No arithmetic errors found.

Tension in source claim 2: it describes 'benchmark-then-combine' as an inefficient method and a documented difficulty, whereas the pedagogy recommends it as the reliable Year 6 method. The claim is retained because it also supports percentage-as-proportion and decimal-conversion errors; it is NOT treated as evidence that benchmark-then-combine is efficient or best. Progression to a single multiplier (×0.15) once benchmarks are secure is kept to acknowledge the efficiency point.

Comparative efficacy of the interactive bar over static grid or quiz formats is not asserted; sources establish the curriculum objective and document misconceptions but do not establish necessity or superiority of any medium.

probeDeeper: 'How did you get 10% of 360 — and how do you know it isn't 3.6?' — checks the place-value meaning of 10%.
'You said 15% is 54 — roughly what fraction of 360 is that, and does that seem about right?' — checks a proportional sanity check (15% ≈ a bit more than a tenth).

Counterexample: 'If the jacket had been £100 instead of £60, would your answer change?' — a child who understands base recomputes (30% of £100 = £30 now wins); a percentage-only reasoner does not see why it would matter.
'Give me a quick way to find 5%, and 1%, of any amount' — surfaces whether the benchmark toolkit is fluent.
assess.correctAnswer: 15% of 360 = 54 (10% is 36, 5% is 18, total 54). Coat saving = 25% of £80 = £20; jacket saving = 30% of £60 = £18; so the COAT saves more (£20 > £18) even though its percentage is smaller, because the amounts are percentages of different prices.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares the percentages and ignores the different bases: 'the jacket, because 30% is more than 25%' — without working out the actual savings
errorPatterns.nextMove: Force 'percent of WHAT?' — compute both actual amounts on two labelled bars of different heights; show the smaller percentage taking the bigger slice. Reinforce percentage as relative to its own base.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child picks the bigger percentage as the bigger saving with no calculation, or calculates one base and assumes it applies to both

errorPatterns.pattern: Misplaces the decimal / mis-converts the percentage: takes 10% of 360 as 3.6 or 360, or treats 15% as 1.5, giving a tenfold error
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the 100-grid / 'parts per hundred': 10% means ÷10 (one whole chunk of the ten), 1% means ÷100; check 15% = 0.15 not 1.5. Rebuild the equivalence triple.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The percentage-of-amount answer is out by a factor of ten (e.g. 15% of 360 given as 5.4 or 540)

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot assemble the percentage from benchmarks, or takes 5% as 10% ÷ 5 instead of half of 10%
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach percentages — scaffold the benchmark relationships: 5% is HALF of 10%; 15% = 10% + 5%. A lapse in assembling, not a conceptual gap.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child finds 10% correctly but computes 5% as 360÷5 = 72, or cannot combine 10% and 5% into 15%

responseLevels.gap: Cannot find a percentage of an amount reliably (tenfold errors, faulty benchmarks) and compares discounts by percentage alone, ignoring the base.
responseLevels.full: Fluently builds any percentage of an amount from benchmarks (or a single multiplier), places decimals correctly, and when comparing always computes the actual amounts relative to each base, explaining why a smaller percentage can give a larger amount.
responseLevels.partial: Finds friendly percentages of an amount via 10%/5% build-up for the practised case, but the method is fragile (place-value slips, awkward percentages) or still compares percentages without consistently computing both bases when they differ.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two things, do them however you like and I'll watch. First, find 15% of 360. Second, two shops: a coat that normally costs £80 has 25% off, and a jacket that normally costs £60 has 30% off — work out which sale saves you more money.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The comparison is rigged so the SMALLER percentage (25%) gives the LARGER saving (£20 vs £18): a child who understands that a percentage is relative to its base computes both actual amounts and picks the coat; a child who treats the percentage as the whole story picks the jacket (30% > 25%) without computing. And 15% of 360 exposes the build-up method and the decimal placement — whether 10% is read as 36 (correct) or 3.6/360 (place-value slip). Watching, not asking, surfaces both.
