pedagogy.summary: This is the conceptual definition that underpins all percentage work: a percentage is a number of parts PER HUNDRED — a standardised proportion — which is why it can be written equivalently as a fraction (out of 100) and a decimal (45% = 45/100 = 0.45), why the same percentage of different wholes gives different amounts (it is relative to its base, not an absolute quantity), and why percentages can exceed 100% (150% = one and a half times the whole). Standardising 'out of 100' is precisely what makes percentages useful for COMPARING proportions with different totals. Teaching should ground the definition in the 100-grid, hammer the three-way fraction–decimal–percentage equivalence, and repeatedly confront the intuition that a percentage names a fixed amount rather than a proportion of a whole.
bestPractices: Define percentage on a 100-grid: shade 45 of 100 cells — 45% = 45/100 = 0.45 = the shaded proportion; the grid makes 'per hundred' literal.
Stress that a percentage is RELATIVE to its whole: 50% of a small quantity and 50% of a large quantity are different amounts — percentage is a proportion, not a fixed number.
Drill the three-way conversion (fraction ↔ decimal ↔ percentage) in both directions, watching decimal placement (7% = 0.07, not 0.7).
Introduce percentages over 100% deliberately (a 100-grid plus part of a second grid; 150% = 1.5 = one and a half wholes) so 100% is understood as 'the whole', not a ceiling.
Teach 'express A as a percentage of B' as A/B × 100, tying it back to proportion (A out of B, restated out of 100).
Use side-by-side comparison tasks (which class did better: 18/25 or 70/100?) so standardising to 'per hundred' is seen to be the point of percentages.
keyRepresentations: 100-grid (each cell = 1%), shaded to show a percentage as a proportion
Fraction–decimal–percentage equivalence triple (45% = 45/100 = 0.45)
Two differently-sized bars/quantities with the same percentage shaded (relative-to-whole)
A 100-grid plus a partial second grid to show >100% (150% = 1.5 wholes)
'A out of B, restated out of 100' bridge for expressing one quantity as a percentage of another
commonMisconceptions: Treats a percentage as a fixed absolute amount (50% is 'the same amount' regardless of the whole), not as a proportion of its base
Believes percentages cannot exceed 100% (100% is seen as a maximum rather than 'one whole')
Mis-converts between forms: 7% → 0.7 (decimal misplacement), or 0.45 → 4.5%
Confuses 'A as a percentage of B' with 'B as a percentage of A', or which quantity is the whole (the base)

learn.summary: A percentage is a number of parts per hundred — a standardised proportion — so it can be written equivalently as a fraction (out of 100) and as a decimal (45% = 45/100 = 0.45). Because a percentage is relative to its whole (base), the same percentage of different wholes gives different amounts, and percentages can exceed 100% (150% = one and a half wholes). Standardising 'out of 100' is what makes percentages useful for comparing proportions with different totals. Teaching grounds the definition in a 100-grid, drills the three-way fraction–decimal–percentage equivalence, and repeatedly confronts the intuition that a percentage names a fixed amount rather than a proportion of a whole.

activities.title: Shade a 100-grid to define 'per hundred'
feedback: If a learner writes 7% = 0.7, point back to the grid: 7 cells out of 100 is 7 hundredths = 0.07; 0.7 would be 70 out of 100 cells.
If a learner thinks the grid cannot be exceeded, give a second grid and ask them to shade 150 cells in total across the two, naming it as one and a half wholes.
Confirm when all three forms (45%, 45/100, 0.45) are matched to the same shaded region.
activities.rationale: Grounding the definition on a 100-grid makes 'per hundred' literal and ties the fraction and decimal forms to a single visible proportion; a second partial grid shows >100% concretely. Curriculum framing treats fractions, decimals and percentages as different ways of expressing proportions.
sourceClaims: Percentage is 'number of parts per hundred'; pupils interpret percentages as a fraction or decimal, express one quantity as a percentage of another, compare quantities using percentages, and work with percentages greater than 100% (Y5 non-statutory: FDP are 'different ways of expressing proportions').

Translating fluently between percents, decimals and fractions is a key difficulty; a documented error is converting a percent to a decimal incorrectly (treating a small percent as a large decimal, e.g. 7% → 0.7).
learnerActions: On a 10×10 grid (100 cells, each cell = 1%), shade 45 cells and write the result three ways: 45% = 45/100 = 0.45.
State in your own words what '45 out of 100' means by pointing at the shaded and unshaded parts of the grid.
Shade a second grid partly to show more than one whole: fill one full grid and 50 cells of a second, and write 150% = 1.5 = one and a half wholes.
Convert a small percentage carefully: shade 7 cells and record 7% = 7/100 = 0.07 (watch that it is 0.07, not 0.7).
activities.intendedInsight: A percentage literally means parts per hundred, so it is the same quantity expressed as a fraction (out of 100) and as a decimal; 100% is 'one whole', not a ceiling, and percentages can go beyond it.

activities.title: Same percentage, different wholes — 50% of two bags
feedback: If a learner predicts 'the same, because it's 50% of each', have them compute 50% of each whole (10 vs 20) and shade half of each: half of a larger whole is more.

If a learner says 'Bag B gives 20 more, because it has 20 more sweets', compute both halves — the gap is 10, not 20. The halves differ by 50% of the difference in the wholes; reason from 'half of each', not the raw total gap.
If a learner insists 100% must always beat 50%, return to the trap comparison: 100% of 10 = 10 is fewer than 50% of 40 = 20, because the percentages sit on different wholes.
Confirm when the learner both gets 'different amounts' AND justifies it by 'half of each whole, and the wholes differ'.
activities.rationale: The percentage-as-absolute misconception is the central error for this topic; predicting then computing and shading the same percentage on two different wholes directly confronts it, and the trap comparison blocks the shortcut '100% always beats 50%' by showing 50% of a larger whole exceeding 100% of a smaller one. A separate check distinguishes a correct 'no' reasoned proportionally from a 'no' reasoned from the raw total gap.
sourceClaims: Bassan Cincinatus & Sheffet (2016), a peer-reviewed study, documents the percentage-as-absolute misconception: learners treat a percentage as a fixed number added/subtracted regardless of its base — assuming '32% bigger' implies '32% smaller' the other way, and that 32% of one amount equals 32% of a different amount. It states 'a 32% value of one initial amount is not equal to a 32% value of another initial amount — it is important to find out from which whole the percentage is calculated', and that a price +20% then −20% does NOT return to the original.

Per the article abstract (personally fetched), percent is a 'privileged proportion' whose 'extremely concise language has lost its explicit referents, has misleading additive terminology for multiplicative meanings, and has multiple uses for the preposition of', and it 'forms a bridge between real-world situations and mathematical concepts of multiplicative structures' — explaining why learners default to additive schemas. (Abstract verified; full text paywalled.)
learnerActions: Predict first: Bag A has 20 sweets and Bag B has 40 sweets. If you take 50% of each, will you get the same amount from both, or more from one — and why? Write your reason before checking.
Compute 50% of each: 50% of 20 = 10, 50% of 40 = 20.
Shade half of two bars (or grids) sized to represent 20 and 40, and compare the shaded amounts.
Explain in one sentence why the same percentage gave different amounts.

Check a trap comparison: is 100% of a small 10-sweet bag more or fewer sweets than 50% of Bag B (40 sweets)? Compute both (10 and 20): 50% of the larger bag gives MORE than 100% of the smaller bag — so '100% always beats 50%' is false, because each percentage acts on its own whole.
activities.intendedInsight: A percentage is a proportion of its own whole (50% = half of whatever the whole is). Because the wholes differ, equal percentages give different amounts, so a percentage is not a fixed absolute quantity; a larger whole's 50% can even exceed a smaller whole's 100%.

activities.title: Convert fluently between fraction, decimal and percentage
feedback: If 0.45 is written as 4.5%, re-anchor: 0.45 = 45/100 = 45%; 4.5% would be 0.045.
If 7% is converted to 0.7, re-anchor to 7/100 = 0.07.
Confirm when conversions are correct in both directions, including a value over 100%.
activities.rationale: Fluent two-directional conversion, with attention to decimal placement, is a documented difficulty and a stated curriculum requirement. Recognition/matching is a useful check of whether a learner can identify equivalent forms, but it does not by itself show they can produce a conversion; so matching is paired with learner-produced conversions.
sourceClaims: Translating fluently between percents, decimals and fractions is a key difficulty; a documented error is converting a percent to a decimal incorrectly (treating a small percent as a large decimal, e.g. 7% → 0.7).

Percentage is 'number of parts per hundred'; pupils interpret percentages as a fraction or decimal, express one quantity as a percentage of another, compare quantities using percentages, and work with percentages greater than 100% (Y5 non-statutory: FDP are 'different ways of expressing proportions').
learnerActions: Match each percentage to its decimal and its fraction-out-of-100 (e.g. 45% ↔ 0.45 ↔ 45/100; 7% ↔ 0.07 ↔ 7/100; 150% ↔ 1.5 ↔ 150/100).
Go in both directions: given 0.08, write the percentage (8%); given 3/100, write the percentage (3%) and decimal (0.03).
Place a given value on a number line that passes 100%, locating 150% at one and a half wholes.
Explain the decimal-placement rule: converting a percent to a decimal divides by 100, moving two places, so a small percent becomes a small decimal (7% → 0.07).
activities.intendedInsight: The three forms are interchangeable notations for the same proportion; converting reliably in both directions depends on tracking the 'out of 100' divisor and decimal place.

activities.title: Express one quantity as a percentage of another, and compare
feedback: If a learner reports 18/25 as the loser without converting, have them compute 18/25 = 72/100 = 72%, which beats 70%.
If a learner confuses 'A as a % of B' with 'B as a % of A', mark which quantity is the whole in each phrasing and recompute both.
Confirm when the learner identifies the base correctly and uses A/B × 100.
activities.rationale: Expressing one quantity as a percentage of another and comparing via a common 'out of 100' base are explicit curriculum goals; confusing which quantity is the base is a listed misconception, so direction is checked deliberately.
sourceClaims: Percentage is 'number of parts per hundred'; pupils interpret percentages as a fraction or decimal, express one quantity as a percentage of another, compare quantities using percentages, and work with percentages greater than 100% (Y5 non-statutory: FDP are 'different ways of expressing proportions').
learnerActions: Write 'A as a percentage of B' as A/B × 100, and say aloud 'A out of B, restated out of 100'.
Compare two results: one class had 18 out of 25 pass, another 70 out of 100. Convert 18/25 to a percentage (72%) and decide which class did better.
Explain why percentages make this comparison easy: both are restated out of the same total, 100.
Check direction: is 'A as a percentage of B' the same as 'B as a percentage of A'? Try A=10, B=40 (10/40×100 = 25% vs 40/10×100 = 400%) and state which quantity is the whole each time.
activities.intendedInsight: Standardising to 'per hundred' lets you compare proportions with different totals; the base (the 'of B' quantity) is the whole, and swapping A and B changes the question and the answer.

constraints: Keep the base explicit at all times: every percentage is 'of' some whole; when amounts are involved, state the whole before computing.

Matching and multiple-choice checks confirm recognition of equivalent forms but do not, on their own, show the learner can produce conversions or justify the proportional reasoning; pair them with learner-constructed answers and spoken/written explanations.

A static shaded 100-grid is a strong, honest picture of the 'per hundred' definition and the equivalence triple; to let a learner test that the SAME percentage yields different amounts on different wholes, they need to act on at least two different wholes themselves (compute, shade, or physically share), whether with paper grids/bars or an interactive model.

Optional interactive supports — a grid whose fraction and decimal update as cells are shaded, a side-by-side panel shading the same percentage on two differently-sized bars, a drag-past-100% mode onto a second grid, and an 'A as % of B' tool that restates A/B out of 100 — make the mechanism concrete but are not required; the same learning can be reached with paper grids, drawn bars, or shared counters.
Distinguish the diagnostic prediction step from the explanation: the reason given BEFORE observing is what reveals the absolute-vs-proportion view.
Do not teach '100% always beats 50%': supply a counterexample, e.g. 100% of a 10-sweet bag (10) is fewer than 50% of a 40-sweet bag (20), so 50% of a larger whole can exceed 100% of a smaller one.
Percentages compare proportions directly because each one is restated out of a common whole of 100. Comparing the actual amounts still needs each whole: 50% of 40 (20) is more than 100% of 10 (10).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support the underlying teaching principle rather than proving any specific activity was tested.

Scope gap: the objective/evidence includes 'calculate percentage increases and decreases', but no activity builds this (only percentages >100% are represented). The original learn field likewise did not build it, so the rewrite is faithful, but this target is NOT covered and should not be read as taught. The Bassan '+20% then −20%' content is cited for the percentage-as-absolute principle in Activity 2, not for a change-calculation task.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 50% of 20 = 10 and 50% of 40 = 20 (difference 10, not 20); the trap comparison 100% of 10 = 10 is fewer than 50% of 40 = 20; 18/25 = 72% > 70%; 10/40 = 25% and 40/10 = 400%; 7% = 0.07, 45% = 0.45, 0.45 = 45% (not 4.5%), 150% = 1.5, 0.08 = 8%, 3/100 = 0.03 = 3% — all verified consistent.

Trap-comparison restored to the source form: '100% of a 10-sweet bag (10) vs 50% of Bag B (40) = 10 vs 20', which vividly shows 50% of a larger whole exceeding 100% of a smaller one. An equal-case variant reusing only Bags A and B (100% of 20 vs 50% of 40 = 20 vs 20) is also mathematically valid and refutes '100% always beats 50%'; reviewers may prefer it for setup economy.

The second misconception ('reaches no by raw total difference') is subtle: the halves differ by 10, which is 50% of the 20-sweet difference in the wholes — preserved in Activity 2 feedback as stated in the source.

The 'conversation/tutor' alternative and the 'per-hundred static grid' explainer from the source are preserved as approaches within activities and constraints rather than as separate ranked artefacts; comparative-efficacy phrasing was softened because the cited sources do not establish one medium as superior.
Source claims are marked 'verified' in the legacy row, but no re-verification occurred here; evidence strength should not be read as freshly confirmed.

assess.poeTask: Show the child two chocolate bars of clearly different sizes — a small one and a large one. Say you will give them 50% of each. PREDICT before breaking anything: will they get the same amount of chocolate from both, or more from one — and WHY? (A child answering 'the same, because it's 50% of each' is treating the percentage as absolute; the reason given before observing is the diagnostic part.) OBSERVE: break each bar in half — the large bar's half is visibly much more chocolate. EXPLAIN: 50% means half of EACH bar's own whole; because the wholes differ, the halves differ — a percentage is a proportion of its base, not a fixed amount.
probeDeeper: 'Write 50% as a fraction and as a decimal' — checks the parts-per-hundred equivalence (1/2, 0.5), and watch for decimal slips.
'Can you ever have more than 100% of something? Give me an example' — surfaces whether 100% is understood as 'the whole' rather than a ceiling.

Counterexample: 'Bag C has 10 sweets — is 100% of bag C more or fewer sweets than 50% of bag B?' — 100% of 10 (=10) equals 50% of 40 (=20)? No: 10 vs 20 — a child who reasons proportionally computes both; an absolute-view child assumes 100% always beats 50%.
'In one class 18 out of 25 passed; in another 70 out of 100 passed — which did better, and why are percentages useful here?' — tests standardising to 'per hundred' for comparison.
assess.correctAnswer: No. 50% of bag A is 10 sweets and 50% of bag B is 20 sweets. A percentage is a proportion of its OWN whole (50% means half of whatever the whole is), so because the bags have different totals, the same percentage gives different amounts.

errorPatterns.pattern: Percentage-as-absolute: 'Yes, 50% is 50%, so you get the same number of sweets from each bag' — treats the percentage as a fixed amount, not a proportion of the whole
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront with the two bags: compute 50% of each (10 and 20) and shade half of each on a grid; a percentage is half of ITS whole, and the wholes differ. Rebuild percentage as a proportion of the base.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — 50% is 50%, so you get the same number of sweets from each bag
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child answers 'yes, the same', or computes only one bag and assumes it holds for both; the percentage is treated as an absolute quantity

errorPatterns.pattern: Reaches 'no' by the raw difference in totals rather than by proportion: 'bag B gives 20 more, because it has 20 more sweets'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compute both halves (10 and 20, a gap of 10, not 20): the percentage acts on each whole, so the difference in the results is 50% of the difference in the wholes. Anchor to 'half of each'.
errorPatterns.distractor: No — bag B gives 20 more sweets, because it has 20 more sweets than bag A
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says the halves differ by 20 (the difference in the bags) instead of 10; reasons from the absolute gap, not 50% of each whole

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes percentages cannot exceed 100% (100% is a maximum, so 150% is impossible or meaningless)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show 100% = one whole (the full grid); 150% = one and a half wholes on a grid-plus-half-grid. Percentages describe proportions that can exceed the whole (e.g. prices rising to 150% of the original).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked (probe) about 150%, child says 'you can't have more than 100%' or caps it at 100

responseLevels.gap: Treats a percentage as a fixed amount ('50% is the same in both'), or insists percentages cannot exceed 100%; cannot connect percentage to a fraction/decimal of the whole.
responseLevels.full: Defines percentage as parts per hundred / a proportion of its whole, so equal percentages of different wholes give different amounts; converts fluently among fraction, decimal and percentage; interprets and uses percentages greater than 100%; and standardises 'out of 100' to compare proportions with different totals.
responseLevels.partial: Recognises the amounts differ and can compute 50% of each for the practised case, but explains it by the raw difference in totals rather than 'a proportion of each whole', or is shaky on ↔fraction/decimal conversion or on percentages over 100%.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Bag A has 20 sweets and bag B has 40 sweets. Is 50% of bag A the same amount of sweets as 50% of bag B? And — this is the important part — how do you know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The prompt forces the relative-vs-absolute distinction and, via the second tier, the REASON. A child who understands percentage as a proportion of the whole says 'no' and explains it by the different wholes; a child holding the absolute view says 'yes, 50% is 50%'. Crucially the tier-two reason also separates a child who reaches 'no' for the RIGHT reason (proportion of each whole) from one who reaches 'no' for a wrong reason (e.g. 'B has 20 more sweets so its half is 20 more') — hard to answer correctly without the proportional idea.

sources.claim: Percentage is 'number of parts per hundred'; pupils interpret percentages as a fraction or decimal, express one quantity as a percentage of another, compare quantities using percentages, and work with percentages greater than 100% (Y5 non-statutory: FDP are 'different ways of expressing proportions').
sources.source: DfE, National curriculum in England: mathematics programmes of study (KS3 ratio/proportion; Y5 FDP) (Crown copyright)

sources.claim: Bassan Cincinatus & Sheffet (2016), a peer-reviewed study, documents the percentage-as-absolute misconception: learners treat a percentage as a fixed number added/subtracted regardless of its base — assuming '32% bigger' implies '32% smaller' the other way, and that 32% of one amount equals 32% of a different amount. It states 'a 32% value of one initial amount is not equal to a 32% value of another initial amount — it is important to find out from which whole the percentage is calculated', and that a price +20% then −20% does NOT return to the original.
sources.source: Bassan Cincinatus, R. & Sheffet, M. (2016), 'With Percentages the 100 is Always in the Denominator', Int. Journal of Research in Education and Science 2(2) (ERIC EJ1105176)

(Abstract verified; full text paywalled.)

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Percentages (age 12+)
topic.description: Solve problems involving percentage increase, percentage decrease, finding the original value after a percentage change, and calculating simple interest
evidence: Calculate a 15% increase on £240 using a decimal multiplier (× 1.15)
Find the original price before a 20% discount resulted in a sale price of £64
Calculate simple interest on £500 at 3% per annum for 4 years
topic.assessmentPrompt: If a bike originally costs £250 and its price goes up by 8%, can {{name}} work out the new price — and if a savings account earns 3% simple interest per year, how much interest would £500 earn in 4 years?

pedagogy.summary: This topic extends percentages to CHANGE: increasing and decreasing by a percentage, finding the original value after a change (reverse percentages), and simple interest. The single most powerful idea — emphasised by the research — is that every percentage change is a MULTIPLICATION by a scale factor: a 15% increase is ×1.15, a 20% decrease is ×0.8. This reframing replaces error-prone add-on/subtract-off methods and makes reverse problems tractable (divide by the multiplier) and reveals why an increase then a decrease by the same percentage does NOT return to the start (the multipliers are not reciprocals: 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96). Teaching should build the decimal multiplier explicitly, show increases and decreases as ×(1 ± r), teach reverse percentages as dividing by the multiplier, and confront the 'it cancels out' intuition head-on. Simple interest is then repeated addition of a fixed percentage of the ORIGINAL each period (contrast with compound).
bestPractices: Teach every percentage change as a single multiplier: increase by r% is ×(1 + r/100), decrease by r% is ×(1 − r/100) — e.g. +15% is ×1.15, −20% is ×0.8.
Explicitly correct the multiplier: a 5% increase is ×1.05, NOT ×1.5; a 6% amount is ×0.06, not ×0.6 — decimal placement is the classic slip.
Teach reverse percentages as the inverse operation: if the new value is the original ×0.8, then original = new ÷ 0.8 — never 'add the percentage back onto the new value'.

Confront 'increase then decrease by the same % returns to the start' directly: show 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, and the classic case that a price up 50% must then fall by 33⅓% (not 50%) to return — because the base has changed.
Distinguish simple interest (a fixed percentage of the ORIGINAL principal each period, so total = P × r × t) from compound (interest on a growing balance); keep the base fixed for simple interest.
Use a bar/100-grid and pair decimal multipliers with their reverse (×1.25 pairs with ×0.8) so the reciprocal relationship of reverse percentages is visible.
keyRepresentations: Decimal-multiplier form of change: ×(1 + r/100) and ×(1 − r/100)
Paired multiplier cards showing reverse = reciprocal (×1.25 ↔ ×0.8, product 1)
Bar model where the original is 100% and the change adds/removes a shaded strip
Reverse-percentage arrow: original →(×0.8)→ new, so new →(÷0.8)→ original
Simple-interest table: same interest (r% of P) added each year for t years
commonMisconceptions: Treats a percentage change as addition/subtraction rather than a single multiplication (e.g. 240 + 0.15 or 240 + 1.15 rather than ×1.15)
Reverse-percentage error: to find the original before a 20% discount, adds 20% of the SALE price back on (64 + 20% of 64) instead of dividing by 0.8
Assumes an increase then a decrease by the same percentage returns to the original (subtracts percents: 20% up then 20% down = no change), not seeing the base has changed
Builds the wrong multiplier: 5% increase as ×1.5, or 6% as ×0.6 (decimal misplacement)
Computes simple interest on a growing balance (compound) or forgets to multiply by the number of years

learn.summary: Percentage change taught as a single multiplication by a scale factor: increase by r% is ×(1 + r/100), decrease by r% is ×(1 − r/100). This reframing makes reverse percentages tractable (divide by the multiplier), exposes why an increase then an equal-percentage decrease does not return to the start (1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, because the second change acts on a changed base), and distinguishes simple interest (a fixed percentage of the original principal each period) from compound. Learners build the decimal multiplier explicitly, solve forward and reverse problems, confront the 'it cancels out' intuition with computation, and compute simple interest on a fixed base.

activities.title: The price-changer: every change is a multiplier
feedback: If a learner writes £240 + 15 = £255, or ×1.5 (£360), or ×0.15 (£36): rebuild the multiplier — +15% means 100% + 15% = 115% = ×1.15; check the decimal, 15% = 0.15 so the multiplier is 1 + 0.15 = 1.15.
If a learner confuses ×1.15 with ×1.5: point out ×1.5 is a 50% increase; put ×1.15 and ×1.5 side by side on the same value to show the gap.
Confirm a correct multiplier by reading the bar: ×1.15 on £240 is £276, which is 15% more than £240.
activities.rationale: Treating every percentage change as a single multiplier by (1 ± r/100) replaces error-prone add-on/subtract-off methods; the classic slip is decimal misplacement, which explicit contrast of ×1.05 vs ×1.5 targets. A live bar/multiplier display may make the scale factor and resulting value visible together, but the multiplier can equally be built on paper; the display is one optional medium, not a requirement.
sourceClaims: All percentage changes are multiplications by a scale factor; documented student errors include treating percent change as addition/subtraction, mis-converting the multiplier, dividing by the wrong base, and assuming an increase then decrease by the same percent cancels out (0.8 × 1.25 = 1; the inverse of a percent increase is not a decrease by the same percent) — e.g. a price up 50% must fall 33⅓% to return.
KS3 pupils solve problems involving percentage change (increase, decrease and original-value problems) and simple interest in financial mathematics, and interpret percentages as operators.
learnerActions: Start with a value shown as a bar (drawn on paper or on screen), e.g. £240, apply a 15% increase, write the change as a single multiplication ×1.15, and read off the new value (£276).
Apply a 20% decrease to a value and write it as ×0.8; write a 6% decrease as ×0.94 (100% − 6% = 94%).
Deliberately contrast ×1.15 with ×1.5 and ×0.15 for a 15% increase, stating which is correct and why (100% + 15% = 115% = 1.15).
Match pairs of multiplier cards and check which pairs multiply to 1 (e.g. ×1.25 ↔ ×0.8), noticing the multiplier that UNDOES a change is its reciprocal.
OPTIONAL interaction if a live tool is available: drag or set the percentage and watch the bar grow/shrink while the displayed multiplier and new value update together.
activities.intendedInsight: A percentage increase or decrease is one multiplication by (1 ± r/100), not an add-on or subtract-off, and the decimal multiplier must be built carefully: a 5% increase is ×1.05, not ×1.5; and finding 6% OF a value is ×0.06, not ×0.6 (distinct from a 6% decrease, which is ×0.94).

activities.title: Reverse percentages: undo by dividing
feedback: If a learner computes 20% of £64 and adds it (£76.80), or otherwise treats £64 as the base: reframe as a multiplier — sale price = original ×0.8, so original = £64 ÷ 0.8. Show that 20% of the true original £80 is £16, confirming £80 → £64; the percentage is of the ORIGINAL.
Reinforce the self-check: a correct original survives 'reduce by 20%' and lands back on £64; the add-back answer (£76.80) does not, falling to £61.44.
activities.rationale: The reverse problem is the key discriminator between an additive model and a multiplicative model of percentage change; teaching it as the inverse operation (divide by the multiplier) and requiring a reversal check directly confronts the documented add-back error.
sourceClaims: All percentage changes are multiplications by a scale factor; documented student errors include treating percent change as addition/subtraction, mis-converting the multiplier, dividing by the wrong base, and assuming an increase then decrease by the same percent cancels out (0.8 × 1.25 = 1; the inverse of a percent increase is not a decrease by the same percent) — e.g. a price up 50% must fall 33⅓% to return.
KS3 pupils solve problems involving percentage change (increase, decrease and original-value problems) and simple interest in financial mathematics, and interpret percentages as operators.
learnerActions: Given a sale price of £64 that is already 20% off, find the original price by recognising sale = original ×0.8, so original = £64 ÷ 0.8 = £80.
Check the answer: reduce the found original by 20% and confirm it returns to the sale price (20% of £80 is £16, so £80 → £64).
Explicitly compare the correct method (÷0.8) with the common wrong method (£64 + 20% of £64 = £76.80) and check which one survives the reversal test (£76.80 reduced by 20% gives £61.44, not £64).
Draw a reverse arrow: original →(×0.8)→ new, so new →(÷0.8)→ original.
activities.intendedInsight: To find an original value before a percentage change, divide by the multiplier that produced the change; the percentage is taken of the original, not of the new/sale value, so adding the percentage back onto the new value is wrong.

activities.title: Does it cancel out? Chaining changes on a changing base
feedback: If a learner says the price returns to the start: compute ×1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96 and track £100 → £120 → £96; point out the 20% decrease is taken from the larger £120 base.
If a learner assumes the restoring fall equals the rise: show the £20 → £30 case needs a 33⅓% fall, because 33⅓% is taken of £30, not £20.
activities.rationale: The 'it cancels out' belief is a documented, seductive misconception; confronting it with direct computation and a visibly changed base, rather than assertion, lets learners see the multiplicative structure. Prediction-before-computation surfaces the belief so it can be challenged.
sourceClaims: All percentage changes are multiplications by a scale factor; documented student errors include treating percent change as addition/subtraction, mis-converting the multiplier, dividing by the wrong base, and assuming an increase then decrease by the same percent cancels out (0.8 × 1.25 = 1; the inverse of a percent increase is not a decrease by the same percent) — e.g. a price up 50% must fall 33⅓% to return.
learnerActions: Predict first: if a price goes up 20% and then down 20%, is it back where it started?
Compute the chain as multipliers: ×1.2 then ×0.8 = ×0.96, a 4% net fall; test on a concrete value, e.g. £100 → £120 → £96.
Identify why: after the increase the base is larger (£120), so the 20% decrease removes more (£24) than the 20% increase added (£20).
Explore the classic case: a £20 item up 50% becomes £30; find what percentage fall returns it to £20 (£10 off £30 is 33⅓%, not 50%).
OPTIONAL interaction if a chain tool is available: apply +20% then −20% and watch the bar land short of the start, with the post-increase base highlighted.
activities.intendedInsight: Equal up-then-down percentages do not cancel, because each percentage acts on whatever base is current; the two multipliers are not reciprocals (1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, not 1), so the net result is a fall. (Note this differs from the reciprocal pair that UNDOES a single change, e.g. ×1.25 then ×0.8 = 1.)

activities.title: Simple interest on a fixed base
feedback: If a learner gives one year's interest (£15) only: remind them to multiply by the number of years, £15 × 4 = £60.
If a learner grows the balance each year (compounds): clarify that simple interest keeps the base at the ORIGINAL £500 every year; interest = £500 × 0.03 × 4 = £60.
activities.rationale: A frequent error is computing interest on a growing balance (compound) or omitting the time factor; keeping the base fixed and tabulating equal yearly additions makes the structure of simple interest explicit and separates it from compound. The cited curriculum source establishes simple interest as a KS3 objective; the specific error pattern is drawn from the inherited misconception analysis and was not re-verified here.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils solve problems involving percentage change (increase, decrease and original-value problems) and simple interest in financial mathematics, and interpret percentages as operators.
learnerActions: Compute simple interest on £500 at 3% per annum for 4 years: find one year's interest (£500 × 0.03 = £15), then multiply by the number of years (£15 × 4 = £60).
Build a year-by-year table showing the same £15 added each year because it is always 3% of the original £500.
Contrast briefly with compound: ask whether year 2's interest would still be £15 if interest were added to the balance each year (under compound it would not, because the base grows).
activities.intendedInsight: Simple interest is a fixed percentage of the ORIGINAL principal each period, so total interest = P × r × t; it must be multiplied by the number of periods, and the base stays fixed (unlike compound interest, which grows the base).

constraints: A scored set of items (fill-in-the-multiplier, a reverse-percentage selection item with the '£64 + 20%' add-back as a distractor, a true/false on 'up 20% then down 20% returns to start' where the misconception is the incorrect option, and a simple-interest item with a compound distractor) can diagnose which model a learner holds, but selecting among options does not by itself elicit the independent construction of a multiplier or a dividing-by-the-multiplier method; include tasks where the learner writes or builds the method.

A static worked example or tap-to-reveal diagram (e.g. tap +15% to reveal ×1.15, tap a reverse problem to reveal ÷0.8) can present the method as a reference, but it is fixed and cannot be re-based by the learner, so the 'base changes under you' insight is better met by actually applying a sequence of changes and tracking the new base.

A shop/bank persona dialogue can pose sale and interest problems and raise the 'does it cancel' challenge, but learners still need to carry out the multiplier computation themselves rather than only hear it explained.
Keep the base fixed for simple interest; do not let it drift into compound unless deliberately contrasting.

When checking reverse-percentage answers, require a reversal test (apply the original percentage change to the found original, e.g. reduce it for a sale or increase it for a price rise, and confirm it returns to the given value) rather than accepting the numeric answer alone.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit (arithmetic, confirmed correct): £240 × 1.15 = £276; £64 ÷ 0.8 = £80, and 20% of £80 = £16 so £80 − £16 = £64; add-back error £64 + 20%×£64 = £76.80, and £76.80 × 0.8 = £61.44; chain ×1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96 so £100 → £120 → £96 (4% net fall); £20 × 1.5 = £30, and to return to £20 the fall is £10/£30 = 33⅓%; simple interest £500 × 0.03 × 4 = £60 with £15 per year; 6% decrease = ×0.94. All internally consistent.

Subtle distinction preserved from the source: ×1.25 and ×0.8 ARE reciprocals (product 1), so a ×0.8 undoes a ×1.25 (a 20% decrease undoes a 25% increase); but applying the SAME percentage up then down is NOT reciprocal (1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96; 1.25 × 0.75 = 0.9375). The card-matching concerns undoing the same change, whereas the 'cancels out' misconception concerns the same percentage in opposite directions — these are different comparisons and must not be conflated.

The source states the inverse of a percentage increase is not a decrease by the same percent; this is a mathematical fact (demonstrated by computation) and is retained as such, not as an untested effectiveness claim.

The simple-interest misconceptions (compounding the balance, omitting the time factor) come from the legacy row's misconception list; neither cited source claim documents them, so activity 4 cites only the curriculum-objective claim.

Efficacy of the optional live tool, quiz set, tap-to-reveal diagram and persona dialogue is not established; they are proposed scaffolds with scoped affordances and limits, not evidenced as superior to one another.

probeDeeper: 'You got £80 — check it: what is £80 reduced by 20%?' — a correct method survives the check (→£64); the add-back error does not (£76.80 reduced by 20% is £61.44).
'A price goes up 20% and then down 20% — is it back to what it was? Why?' — directly surfaces the cancels-out misconception and the changing base.
'Write the 15% increase as a single multiplication' — checks the ×1.15 scale-factor idea rather than an add-on method.
Counterexample for interest: 'What if it were compound interest instead — would year 2's interest still be £15?' — tests whether the fixed-base of SIMPLE interest is understood.
assess.correctAnswer: Original jacket price = £64 ÷ 0.8 = £80 (since sale price = original ×0.8). Increase: £240 × 1.15 = £276.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverse-percentage error: to undo a 20% discount, adds 20% of the SALE price back (64 + 20% of 64 = £76.80), treating the new value as the base
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe as a multiplier: sale price = original ×0.8, so original = £64 ÷0.8. Show 20% of £80 (the true original) is £16, confirming £80 → £64; the percentage is of the ORIGINAL, not the sale price.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child computes 20% of £64 and adds it, or otherwise works from £64 as the original; answer £76.80 rather than £80

errorPatterns.pattern: Add/subtract instead of multiply, or wrong multiplier: does 240 + 15, or ×1.5, or ×0.15, instead of ×1.15
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build the multiplier explicitly: +15% means 100% + 15% = 115% = ×1.15; contrast ×1.15 with ×1.5. Check the decimal (15% = 0.15).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The increase answer is £255 (+15 flat), £360 (×1.5), or £36 (×0.15) rather than £276

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes an increase then a decrease by the same percentage returns to the original (subtracts percents / 'it cancels out')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compute it: ×1.2 then ×0.8 = ×0.96, a 4% net fall; show the second percentage acts on the larger base. Use the £20 blouse (+50% then must fall 33⅓% to return).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked (probe), child says a price up 20% then down 20% is back to the start; does not see the base changed

errorPatterns.pattern: Simple interest computed on a growing balance (compound) or without multiplying by the number of years
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach percentages — clarify simple interest is r% of the ORIGINAL each year, kept constant: interest = £500 × 0.03 × 4. Contrast briefly with compound.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For £500 at 3% for 4 years, child gives one year's interest (£15), or compounds the balance, instead of £15 × 4 = £60

responseLevels.gap: Uses add/subtract for changes and the add-back method for reverse problems; believes same-percentage up-then-down cancels; cannot form the multiplier.
responseLevels.full: Treats every percentage change as ×(1±r), solves reverse problems by dividing by the multiplier and checks the result, explains why equal up/down percentages don't cancel (changed base), and computes simple interest as a fixed percentage of the original per period.
responseLevels.partial: Handles a straightforward increase/decrease with a multiplier for practised numbers, but reverts to add-back on reverse problems, mis-forms awkward multipliers, or is unsure whether up-then-down cancels; simple interest sometimes compounded or missing the time factor.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A jacket was reduced by 20% in a sale and now costs £64. Find its original price before the sale. Then, separately, increase £240 by 15%. Do both however you like — I'll watch.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The reverse problem is the discriminator: a child who understands percentage change as a multiplier sees £64 = original ×0.8 and divides (£80); a child using add/subtract intuition adds 20% of £64 back (£64 + £12.80 = £76.80) — the documented reverse-percentage error — giving a wrong answer that is itself diagnostic. The increase task reveals the multiplier: ×1.15 (correct) versus +15 flat, ×1.5, or ×0.15. Watching the method shows which model of percentage change the child holds.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Ratio Problems
topic.description: Solve problems involving the relative sizes of two quantities where missing values can be found by using integer multiplication and division facts
evidence: If the ratio of red to blue beads is 3:5 and there are 15 blue beads, find the number of red beads
Use multiplication facts to find the missing value: 'For every 2 apples there are 5 oranges; if there are 20 oranges, how many apples?'
Explain the multiplicative relationship between two quantities in a ratio context
topic.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe uses 3 eggs for every 200g of flour, can {{name}} work out how many eggs would be needed for 600g of flour?

pedagogy.summary: This is the first sustained problem-solving procedure of the strand: given a ratio and one known quantity, find the missing one using multiplication and division ('red:blue is 3:5, there are 15 blue — find red'). The reliable method is to find the multiplier that maps the known ratio-part to the actual amount (15 ÷ 5 = 3, so ×3), then apply it to the other part (3 × 3 = 9), or equivalently to find the value of one 'share' via a bar model. The central teaching battle is against ADDITIVE reasoning — children who reason 'blue went up by 10, so red goes up by 10' (a constant difference) instead of scaling by a constant multiplier. Teaching must make the multiplicative relationship explicit and visible, using bar models, ratio tables and 'for every' language so that scaling, not adding, becomes the natural move.
bestPractices: Draw a bar model first: equal blocks for each part make 'find one block' (the multiplier/share value) the obvious pivot, and expose the structure before any arithmetic.
Name the multiplier explicitly: 'what do we multiply the ratio by to get the real amounts?' (15 = 5 × 3, so ×3 everywhere) — this directly counters additive thinking.
Use a ratio table so equivalent ratios (3:5, 6:10, 9:15) are seen as scalings of the same relationship, and the constant multiplier is visible down the columns.

Confront the additive error head-on with a comparison task: show that 'add 10 to both' changes the relationship (3:5 vs 13:15 are different mixtures) whereas multiplying keeps it — ideally with a concrete mixing/colour context where the change is perceptible.
Keep 'for every' language central ('for every 3 red there are 5 blue') so scaling up in whole groups feels natural before formal multiplier work.
Vary which quantity is known and use non-unit and non-integer multipliers so children cannot rely on simple build-up alone.
keyRepresentations: Bar model with equal blocks per part (find one block = the share/multiplier)
Ratio table showing the constant multiplier down the columns (3:5, ×3 → 9:15)
Double number line aligning the two quantities at 0
'For every a there are b' grouping with counters/cubes
Arrow diagram showing '×3' mapping ratio to real amounts
commonMisconceptions: Additive/constant-difference reasoning: 'blue rose by 10, so red rises by 10' (or 'the difference is 2, keep it') instead of scaling by a constant multiplier
Applies the multiplier to only one quantity, or adds the multiplier instead of multiplying
Uses the wrong direction (multiplies when should divide to find the multiplier, or vice versa)
Build-up strategy that works for whole-number cases but collapses when the multiplier is non-integer

learn.summary: Learners solve missing-value ratio problems (given a ratio and one known quantity, find the other) by finding and applying a constant multiplier, e.g. 'red:blue is 3:5, there are 15 blue — find red' (15÷5=3, so ×3, red = 3×3 = 9). The central challenge is overcoming ADDITIVE reasoning — 'blue rose by 10, so red rises by 10' or 'keep the same difference' — by making the multiplicative relationship visible through bar models, ratio tables and 'for every' language, and by letting learners see that adding the same amount to both unequal parts changes the relationship while multiplying both parts by the same factor preserves it.

activities.title: Scale a mixture and compare adding versus multiplying
feedback: If the learner adds the difference (e.g. 15−5=10, then red = 3+10 = 13): show that 13:15 produces a different mixture/shade from 3:5, then ask 'what do we multiply 5 by to get 15?' and apply that same factor to red.
If the learner finds ×3 but applies it to only one part: highlight that both bar/table columns move together, so the same multiplier acts on red and blue.
If the learner multiplies when they should divide (or the reverse): ask 'is 15 bigger or smaller than 5? so are we scaling up or down?' before choosing the operation.
When correct: name the multiplier explicitly ('5 became 15, that is ×3, so red 3 becomes 9') and connect it to one 'share' on the bar model.
activities.rationale: A live outcome that visibly changes under adding but stays the same under multiplying can make the multiplicative structure perceptible, which may help with additive-strategy interference. Ratio tables and bar/double-number-line models that move both parts together are commonly recommended supports for this error.
sourceClaims: NCETM documents that in scaling/missing-value problems 'students often assume that relationships are additive... in situations where the actual relationship is multiplicative' — e.g. for '5 miles = 8 km, how many km is 7 miles?' students say 'two more miles means two more km', and for a ratio 2:5 assume a constant £3 difference rather than scaling. The remedy is to find the constant multiplier (functional/scalar) using ratio tables and bar/double-number-line models that move both parts together.

Year 6 pupils 'solve problems involving the relative sizes of two quantities where missing values can be found by using integer multiplication and division facts', and recognise proportion when quantities are in the same ratio (recipes, similar shapes).
learnerActions: Meet the problem 'red:blue is 3:5 and there are 15 blue — how many red?' alongside a visible outcome such as rows of beads or a paint shade produced by the ratio.
Scale the ratio up a ratio table (3:5, 6:10, 9:15) and watch two bars (one per part) grow together, stating the multiplier that turns 5 into 15 (×3) and applying the same ×3 to red to get 9.

Try two contrasting moves on the mixture: 'add 10 to each part' (giving 13:15) and 'multiply each part by 3' (giving 9:15), and observe which move keeps the mixture/shade the same and which changes it.
Say in words why multiplying by 3 keeps the same relationship but adding 10 to both does not.

As an optional extension beyond the integer-fact objective, keep red:blue 3:5 but switch to a measurable paint mixture: with 12 ml blue the multiplier is 12÷5 = 2.4, so red = 3×2.4 = 7.2 ml. This shows that building up in whole groups of 3:5 cannot reach the answer. (A bead count could not be 7.2, so use continuous amounts here.)
activities.intendedInsight: The two quantities in a ratio are linked by a constant multiplier, not a constant difference: scaling both parts by the same factor preserves the relationship, while adding the same amount to both breaks it whenever the two parts are unequal.

activities.title: Build a bar model to find one share
feedback: If the learner cannot start: cover the arithmetic and ask 'if these 5 equal blocks hold 15 altogether, how much is in one block?'
If a learner gives one block the whole known total: remind them the known amount is shared equally across its blocks, not placed in one.
When correct: link the 'per block' value to the multiplier so the two methods are seen as the same idea.
activities.rationale: Drawing equal blocks first exposes the structure and makes 'find one block' the obvious pivot, giving a route to the answer via equal shares that supports multiplicative reasoning.
sourceClaims: NCETM documents that in scaling/missing-value problems 'students often assume that relationships are additive... in situations where the actual relationship is multiplicative' — e.g. for '5 miles = 8 km, how many km is 7 miles?' students say 'two more miles means two more km', and for a ratio 2:5 assume a constant £3 difference rather than scaling. The remedy is to find the constant multiplier (functional/scalar) using ratio tables and bar/double-number-line models that move both parts together.
learnerActions: Draw a bar model with equal blocks for each part of the ratio (3 blocks red, 5 blocks blue).
Match the known quantity to its blocks and work out the value of one block (15 blue ÷ 5 blocks = 3 per block).
Multiply the value of one block by the number of blocks in the unknown part (3 × 3 = 9 red).
Explain, pointing at the model, why the red count is that number because every block holds the same amount.
activities.intendedInsight: Finding the value of a single equal 'share' or block reveals the constant multiplier and makes the equal-grouping structure of a ratio explicit before any symbolic arithmetic.

activities.title: Solve varied missing-value problems and catch the additive trap
feedback: If the learner answers 17 for the apples: that is 2 + (20−5), adding the difference; show that 5 scaled to 20 is ×4, so apples go 2 × 4 = 8.

If the learner stalls on the non-integer case: extend build-up by asking 'how many groups of 5 is 20?' to turn counting-in-groups into ×4. Then note that 12 is 2 groups of 5 and 2 more, i.e. 2 and 2/5 = 2.4 groups, and apply ×2.4.
If the learner inverts the direction: compare the sizes of the two known amounts to decide scale up or down before computing.
When correct across varied cases: confirm the multiplier is found by division of matching parts and applied by multiplication to the other part.
activities.rationale: Varying which quantity is known and including non-integer multipliers prevents reliance on simple build-up and makes the constant-multiplier method the robust strategy; additive distractors are diagnostic of the core misconception.
sourceClaims: Year 6 pupils 'solve problems involving the relative sizes of two quantities where missing values can be found by using integer multiplication and division facts', and recognise proportion when quantities are in the same ratio (recipes, similar shapes).

NCETM documents that in scaling/missing-value problems 'students often assume that relationships are additive... in situations where the actual relationship is multiplicative' — e.g. for '5 miles = 8 km, how many km is 7 miles?' students say 'two more miles means two more km', and for a ratio 2:5 assume a constant £3 difference rather than scaling. The remedy is to find the constant multiplier (functional/scalar) using ratio tables and bar/double-number-line models that move both parts together.
learnerActions: Solve a set of missing-value problems where the known quantity varies between the two parts and multipliers are sometimes non-integer, e.g. 'for every 2 apples there are 5 oranges; with 20 oranges, how many apples?' (×4 → 8 apples).
For each, state the multiplier and show it applied to both parts.

Compare a tempting additive answer with the correct scaled answer and explain which relationship each uses, e.g. for 2 apples : 5 oranges with 20 oranges, the additive move gives 2+15 = 17 while the correct scaled answer is 2×4 = 8.

As an optional extension, tackle one non-integer case using measurable quantities (e.g. 2 cups juice : 5 cups water with 12 cups water → ×2.4 → 4.8 cups juice) to test that the method still works when whole-group build-up cannot reach the number.
activities.intendedInsight: The same constant multiplier applies to both parts regardless of which quantity is known, and multiplicative reasoning works even when the multiplier is not a whole number — unlike repeated adding.

activities.title: Talk it through: is it still the same drink?
feedback: If the learner accepts 'add 10 to each': ask them to compare the mixture before and after and notice that, because the two parts are unequal, the taste/shade would change (e.g. 3:5 becomes 13:15).
If the learner scales correctly: prompt them to state the multiplier explicitly and connect 'for every' groups to multiplication.
activities.rationale: Posing 'for every' problems and probing additive suggestions keeps scaling language central; discussion can surface a learner's reasoning, though the preserving-versus-breaking contrast is often clearer when the outcome can be seen as well as discussed.
sourceClaims: NCETM documents that in scaling/missing-value problems 'students often assume that relationships are additive... in situations where the actual relationship is multiplicative' — e.g. for '5 miles = 8 km, how many km is 7 miles?' students say 'two more miles means two more km', and for a ratio 2:5 assume a constant £3 difference rather than scaling. The remedy is to find the constant multiplier (functional/scalar) using ratio tables and bar/double-number-line models that move both parts together.
learnerActions: Take on a recipe or juice-bar scenario where orders must be scaled up while keeping the same taste/mixture.
When a character suggests 'just add 10 more of each', decide and explain whether the drink stays the same, then propose the correct scaling.
Use 'for every' language ('for every 3 red there are 5 blue') to justify scaling up in whole groups before naming the formal multiplier.
activities.intendedInsight: Keeping a ratio the same means scaling both parts by the same factor; 'for every' grouping language supports this before formal multiplier notation.

constraints: This is procedural problem-solving: learners should construct and solve problems and state the multiplier, not merely recognise a correct answer from options.

Build-up (repeatedly adding the ratio unit) is a valid stepping stone and should be extended toward the multiplier ('how many groups of 5 is 20?'), not discouraged. Non-integer multipliers, where whole-group build-up fails, are an optional extension beyond the integer-fact objective and should use measurable (continuous) quantities.

A worked example that only reveals one scaling (e.g. tap to show ×3) is a reference scaffold; it does not by itself give practice solving varied problems or confronting the additive alternative, so pair it with learner-constructed solutions.

Scored item sets with additive distractors (e.g. 17 for 2:5 with 20 known) can check and diagnose the additive misconception, but selecting a correct option does not by itself require the learner to produce the method or justify why the multiplier applies to both parts, so pair them with learner-constructed, explained solutions.

Vary which quantity is known, include non-unit multipliers and scaling down, and offer non-integer multipliers only as an optional extension with measurable quantities (or ratios not in simplest form that give whole answers, e.g. 4:6 with 15 → ×2.5 → 10), so correctness does not depend on whole-number build-up alone.
Keep each activity's ratio consistent within its own worked examples (e.g. activity 1 stays 3:5), so learners are not silently switched between different ratios mid-task.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 15÷5=3 and 3×3=9 (red beads) correct; for 2 apples:5 oranges with 20 oranges, 20÷5=4 and 2×4=8 (correct), additive error 2+(20−5)=17 (correctly labelled as the misconception, not a valid answer); non-integer case in activity 1 keeps 3:5 so 12÷5=2.4 and 3×2.4=7.2, and in activity 3 uses 2:5 so 12÷5=2.4 and 2×2.4=4.8 (both correct). These values are presented as intended.

The non-integer answers 7.2 (beads, activity 1) and 4.8 (apples, activity 3) are mathematically correct from their stated setups but are not whole-object counts; treat them as numerical scaling exercises, or choose a context where fractional values make sense.

The claim that a visible interactive contrast 'directly defeats' the misconception is a design rationale only; the cited sources establish the misconception and recommend ratio-table/bar/number-line remedies but do not establish comparative efficacy of a particular interactive outcome. Stated here as a proposal with its affordance, not as proven superiority.

probeDeeper: 'How did you decide to multiply by 4?' — checks the multiplier comes from 20÷5, not a guess.
'Does adding the same number to both parts keep the same relationship? Why or why not?' — directly surfaces additive vs multiplicative thinking.

Counterexample: 'What if there were 12 oranges instead of 20 — how many apples?' (multiplier ×2.4) — a child with true multiplicative reasoning scales to 4.8; a build-up-only or additive child stalls or mis-adds.
'Show me on a bar model why the apples are 8' — forces the equal-share structure to justify the answer.
assess.correctAnswer: 8 apples. The oranges scaled from 5 to 20, which is ×4, so the apples scale the same way: 2 × 4 = 8. (Equivalently, one 'share' logic via a bar model gives 8.)

errorPatterns.pattern: Additive / constant-difference reasoning: 'oranges went up by 15, so apples go up by 15' (→ 17), or 'the difference stays 3' — uses a constant difference instead of a constant multiplier
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront additively vs multiplicatively on a perceptible mixture: show 'add the difference' makes a different mixture, while scaling keeps it. Rebuild via 'what do we multiply 5 by to get 20?' and a bar model. This is documented additive-strategy interference, not carelessness.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child computes 20−5 = 15 (or the 3 gap) and adds it to the apples rather than finding ×4; answer 17 (or a gap-preserving value)

errorPatterns.pattern: Scales only one quantity, or adds the multiplier instead of multiplying: finds ×4 for oranges but leaves apples at 2, or does 2+4
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reinforce that the SAME multiplier acts on both parts (the ratio table columns move together); use the bar model where every block scales identically.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child finds the multiplier but applies it to one part only, or treats ×4 as +4 (giving 6)

errorPatterns.pattern: Wrong direction of scaling: divides when should multiply (or vice versa), e.g. treats 20 as the small amount
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach ratio — scaffold 'which is bigger, 5 or 20? so are we scaling up or down?' before choosing the operation. A set-up lapse.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child sets up 5 ÷ 20 or scales apples down; the multiplier is inverted

errorPatterns.pattern: Build-up that only works for whole-number multipliers: repeatedly adds the ratio unit (2,5 → 4,10 → ...) but cannot cope when the multiplier is non-integer
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT discourage build-up — it is a sound stepping stone; extend it toward the multiplier by asking 'how many groups of 5 is 20?' so counting-in-groups becomes ×4. It matures into multiplicative reasoning.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child successfully counts up in 2s-and-5s to reach 20 oranges but is stuck if asked about, say, 12 oranges

responseLevels.gap: Uses additive reasoning (adds the difference) or cannot set up the problem; gets 17 and defends it, or scales the wrong quantity/direction with no self-correction.
responseLevels.full: Finds the constant multiplier and applies it to both parts (or reasons via equal shares/bar model), explains why adding a constant would break the relationship, and transfers reliably to non-integer multipliers and either-quantity-known problems.
responseLevels.partial: Solves whole-number cases by build-up or by finding the multiplier for the practised numbers, but the reasoning is fragile — reverts to additive or stalls when the multiplier is non-integer or the known quantity changes; can find a multiplier but not always justify why it applies to both parts.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: For every 2 apples in a fruit bowl there are 5 oranges. A bigger bowl keeps the same relationship and has 20 oranges. Work out how many apples are in the bigger bowl — however you like, I'll watch.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The numbers are chosen so the additive and multiplicative strategies give clearly different answers: a child scaling multiplicatively finds ×4 and gets 8; a child reasoning additively sees oranges rose by 15 (from 5 to 20) and adds 15 to the apples, giving 17 — or keeps the difference of 3 and gives 17. Watching the method (do they seek a multiplier/scale the bars, or do they add the difference?) reveals which relationship the child is using, which is the entire conceptual hinge of ratio.
