topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Understanding fractions
topic.description: Solve problems involving unequal sharing and grouping using knowledge of fractions and multiples
evidence: Share 40 sweets between two children in the ratio 3:5
Solve: 'Tom gets twice as many as Sam and Sam gets three times as many as Jo. If there are 30 altogether, how many does each get?'
Use fraction knowledge to explain why sharing in ratio 2:3 means one person gets 2/5 of the total
topic.assessmentPrompt: If three friends share a bag of 24 sweets so that one person gets twice as many as each of the others, can {{name}} work out how many each person receives?

pedagogy.summary: Unequal sharing means splitting a quantity so the parts follow a given ratio rather than being equal. The reliable method is the 'find one part' routine: add the ratio numbers to get the TOTAL number of equal parts, divide the quantity by that total to find the value of ONE part, then multiply each share by its number of parts. The conceptual anchor — and the thing children most often get wrong — is that sharing in the ratio 2:3 gives fractions of the WHOLE of 2/5 and 3/5 (denominator = a+b), NOT 2/3. Chained comparisons ('Tom gets twice as many as Sam') must first be turned into a single ratio before sharing. Bar models make the equal-parts structure visible and are the canonical representation.
bestPractices: Teach the explicit routine: total parts = sum of the ratio numbers → one part = quantity ÷ total parts → each share = its parts × one part.
Draw the bar model FIRST (a strip cut into a+b equal segments), label the whole, find one segment, then read off each share — diagram before arithmetic.
Make the part-to-whole fractions explicit: in 2:3, one child gets 2/5 and the other 3/5; contrast sharply with the wrong 2/3 to fence the misconception.
Convert chained/multiplicative language ('twice as many', 'three times as many') into a single ratio before sharing (Jo:Sam:Tom = 1:3:6), using the smallest quantity as one part.
Check by adding the shares back to the original total — a fast self-verification pupils can run every time.
keyRepresentations: Bar model / tape diagram cut into a+b equal segments
The 'one part' unit (quantity ÷ total parts) as the building block
Part-to-whole fraction strip (2/5 and 3/5 of the whole for 2:3)
Ratio table linking parts to values
commonMisconceptions: Reading the ratio 2:3 as fractions 2/3 and 3/3 (or 2/3 of the total) instead of 2/5 and 3/5 — using one part as the denominator rather than the sum of parts.
Sharing equally, ignoring the ratio (40 ÷ 2 = 20 each).
Finding the value of one part but forgetting to multiply each share back (reporting the number of parts, or one-part, as the answer).
Unable to combine chained comparisons into a single ratio, so treating 'twice as many' and 'three times as many' as unrelated.

learn.summary: Unequal sharing splits a quantity so the parts follow a given ratio rather than being equal. The reliable routine: add the ratio numbers to find the TOTAL number of equal parts, divide the quantity by that total to find the value of ONE part, then multiply the value of one part by each person's number of parts to get their share. The core idea children most often get wrong is that sharing in the ratio 2:3 gives fractions of the WHOLE of 2/5 and 3/5 (denominator = sum of parts), NOT 2/3. Chained comparisons ('Tom gets twice as many as Sam') must first be turned into a single ratio before sharing. A bar/tape diagram cut into (a+b) equal segments makes the equal-parts structure visible and is the canonical representation.

activities.title: Cut the sharing bar into the right number of parts
feedback: If a learner tries to cut 3:5 into 3 or 5 segments, point out the two children's parts together must fill the whole strip: 3 + 5 = 8 segments, so neither 3 nor 5 can be the total.
If they answer '5 and 5' after 40 ÷ 8 = 5, respond: 'That is the value of ONE part — how many parts does each child have?' and prompt the final multiply, then the add-back check 15 + 25 = 40.

If they say the 3-part child gets 3/5 of the sweets, have them count the segments on the bar: the denominator is the TOTAL number of parts, so it is 3/8. Contrast 3/8 with 3/5 explicitly, then test the wrong rule on its own terms — if the 3-child got 3/5, by that same rule the 5-child would get 5/5 (all of them), so the two shares would be 3/5 + 5/5 = 8/5 of the sweets, more than the whole, which is impossible. That is why the denominator must be the total, 8.
If they share equally (40 ÷ 2 = 20 each), return to the bar: 3:5 means one child's part is bigger, so the numbers of segments are not equal.
If they treat 'twice' and 'three times' as unrelated, make Jo one part, so Sam is 3 parts and Tom is 6; the total is 10 parts and one part = 3 (for a 30 total). Build the 1:3:6 bar before sharing.
activities.rationale: The routine is procedural and benefits from a visible equal-parts structure: a bar the learner cuts and fills gives immediate feedback when the segment count or the total is wrong, and forcing the choice of 8 (not 3 or 5) segments brings the a/(a+b) idea into the open, which is where the common 'fraction of the total is a/b' error arises.
sourceClaims: In a part-to-part ratio a:b, one part is a/(a+b) of the whole — ratio compares part to part, proportion compares a part to the whole; the classic error is reading a:b as the fraction a/b of the whole.
Pupils should solve problems involving unequal sharing and grouping using knowledge of fractions and multiples (Year 6 ratio and proportion).
learnerActions: Take a ratio such as 3:5 and draw an empty strip (a tape/bar diagram) to represent the whole quantity.

Decide how many EQUAL segments to cut the strip into so that both children's parts together fill it exactly (try 3, 5 or another number and check), then explain in your own words why the sum 3 + 5 = 8 is the simplest count that works.
Place the total quantity (40) across the strip and work out the value of one segment: 40 ÷ 8 = 5.
Colour 3 segments for the first child and 5 for the second, then read off 3 × 5 = 15 and 5 × 5 = 25.
State what fraction of the WHOLE each child gets: 3/8 and 5/8, and check these sum to 1 (and that 15 + 25 = 40).

In a second round, turn chained language ('Tom gets twice as many as Sam, Sam three times as many as Jo') into one ratio Jo:Sam:Tom = 1:3:6 by making the smallest quantity one part, then build that 10-part bar before sharing.
activities.intendedInsight: The ratio a:b needs (a+b) equal parts, so each share is a/(a+b) and b/(a+b) of the whole — not a/b. One part is the building block; chained comparisons must become a single ratio before sharing.

activities.title: Explain and check the shares
feedback: Correct full response: 3 + 5 = 8 equal parts, one part = 40 ÷ 8 = 5, shares are 15 and 25 (which sum to 40), and the 3-part child gets 3/8 of all the sweets.
If the add-back does not reach 40, a part value or a multiply was wrong — recount segments and recompute one part.

On the 3/8-vs-5 test: 2/5 is the CORRECT complement of 3/5 (3/5 + 2/5 = 1), so 'they fit the whole' does NOT excuse the 3/5 error. Apply the misconception's own rule instead — it treats the 5-child's number of parts (5) as if it were the total, giving the 5-child 5/5, so 3/5 + 5/5 = 8/5 exceeds the whole. That contradiction shows the denominator must be the total number of parts, 8, giving 3/8 and 5/8.
For the chained problem with 30: one part = 30 ÷ 10 = 3, so Jo = 3, Sam = 9, Tom = 18 (which sum to 30).
activities.rationale: Short reasoning prompts and an add-back check let the learner verify their own work and expose whether they counted (a+b) parts or mistakenly used a or b as the total; the fraction question forces the a/(a+b) idea into the open, where 3/8 versus 3/5 is a clean diagnostic split.
sourceClaims: In a part-to-part ratio a:b, one part is a/(a+b) of the whole — ratio compares part to part, proportion compares a part to the whole; the classic error is reading a:b as the fraction a/b of the whole.
learnerActions: Answer: how many EQUAL parts are there altogether in 3:5, and where does that number come from?
Add your two shares back together — do they make 40? Say what it would tell you if they did not.

You said the fraction is 3/8 — why is 8 on the bottom and not 5? Test the wrong rule on its own terms: if the 3-part child got 3/5, then by that same rule the 5-part child would get 5/5 (all of them) — do 3/5 and 5/5 fit inside one whole?
Given 'Tom gets twice as many as Sam and Sam three times as many as Jo, 30 altogether', turn it into one ratio (Jo:Sam:Tom = 1:3:6) before sharing, and find each share.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding the shares back to the original total is a fast self-check, and articulating why the denominator is the sum of parts secures the part-to-whole fraction and the handling of chained comparisons.

activities.title: Short questions to consolidate the routine
feedback: For 'share 40 in 3:5', the shares are 15 and 25; an answer of 20 and 20 is equal sharing that ignores the ratio.

For the fraction, 3/8 is correct; 3/5 wrongly uses the other child's number of parts (5) as the denominator instead of the sum of parts. By that wrong rule the 5-child would get 5/5 (all of them), so the two 'shares' (3/5 and 5/5) would exceed the whole — a quick sign the denominator must be the sum of parts, 8, not 5.
For a chained problem, first state the single ratio (e.g. 1:3:6) — the multipliers are related, not separate.
activities.rationale: Targeted recall questions with distractors built from the known errors (equal sharing, a/b as the whole-fraction) help check whether the routine and the part-to-whole idea are secure. Recognition-style questions assess and reinforce but do not by themselves require the learner to construct and cut the bar, so pair them with the bar-building task.
sourceClaims: In a part-to-part ratio a:b, one part is a/(a+b) of the whole — ratio compares part to part, proportion compares a part to the whole; the classic error is reading a:b as the fraction a/b of the whole.
learnerActions: Share 40 in the ratio 3:5 and write the two shares.
Choose what fraction of the whole the '3' child gets.
Read a chained-comparison problem and state the combined single ratio before working out the shares.
activities.intendedInsight: Separating the share values from the part-to-whole fraction lets the learner spot and discard the 'equal share' and 'a/b of the total' errors.

constraints: A static labelled bar model (cut into a+b parts, with tap-to-reveal values and part-to-whole fractions) is a useful reference/scaffold, but it does not let the learner cut and check their own segmentation — the choice of how many segments is where the key misconception surfaces, so include an activity where the learner decides the segment count themselves.
Recognition/short-answer questions assess and reinforce the routine but do not elicit independent construction of the bar or the shares; use them alongside, not instead of, the building task.
Always convert chained/multiplicative language into a single ratio (using the smallest quantity as one part, and scaling up if needed so all parts are whole numbers) before sharing.

Keep the part-to-whole fraction explicit (3/8 and 5/8 for 3:5) and contrast it directly with the wrong 3/5 to fence the misconception — and when demonstrating why 3/5 is wrong, in EVERY learner prompt and feedback item apply the misconception's own rule (3/5 and 5/5) so the contradiction (exceeding the whole) is visible, rather than its correct complement (3/5 and 2/5), which wrongly looks consistent.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy entry asserted that an interactive manipulable bar 'defeats' the misconception and that a dialogue or 3D representation 'adds nothing'; these are catalog-style comparative claims not established by the cited sources, so they have been softened to a narrowly scoped affordance (visible equal-parts structure and immediate feedback on segment count). A fixed/static bar can still teach the routine.

Arithmetic was independently checked: 3+5=8; 40÷8=5; 3×5=15; 5×5=25; 15+25=40; fractions 3/8 and 5/8 sum to 1. Chained example with 30 total: 1+3+6=10 parts, 30÷10=3, giving Jo 3, Sam 9, Tom 18 (sum 30) — all consistent.

Independent-review correction: the flawed 3/5 counterexample survived not only in feedback but in a LEARNER PROMPT in the explain-and-check activity ('where would the matching second share come from, and could the two still fit inside the whole?'), which invites the correct 2/5 complement and can reinforce the error. Because 3/5 + 2/5 = 1 fits the whole, that framing wrongly validates the misconception. Every learner-facing occurrence now applies the misconception's own rule (the 5-child gets 5/5, so 3/5 + 5/5 = 8/5 exceeds the whole), matching the original row's description of the error (reading 2:3 as 2/3 and 3/3).
The illustration that 3/5 of 40 = 24 can still be used to show the wrong path in feedback, but it is never presented as a valid share.

probeDeeper: How many EQUAL parts are there altogether in 3:5? Where does that number come from?
Add your two shares back together — do they make 40? What would it tell you if they didn't?
You said the fraction is 3/8 — why 8 on the bottom and not 5? (counterexample: if it were 3/5, what would the two shares add up to?)
If instead Tom gets twice as many as Sam and Sam three times as many as Jo with 30 in total, how would you turn that into one ratio before sharing?
assess.correctAnswer: 15 and 25. There are 3 + 5 = 8 equal parts, so one part = 40 ÷ 8 = 5; the 3-part child gets 3 × 5 = 15 and the 5-part child gets 5 × 5 = 25. The 3-part child gets 3/8 of all the sweets.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads 3:5 as the fraction 3/5 of the whole — uses one part as the denominator instead of the sum of parts
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the bar cut into 3+5 = 8 equal segments; count them. The denominator is the TOTAL parts, so it's 3/8. Contrast 3/8 with 3/5 explicitly. Reteach part-to-part vs part-to-whole vocabulary.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the 3-part child gets 3/5 of the sweets (or works 3/5 of 40 = 24), never forming the total of 8 parts

errorPatterns.pattern: Shares equally, ignoring the ratio
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the bar: 3:5 means the second child's part is bigger — the segments are not equal in NUMBER between children. Reteach relative-size ratio reasoning.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 40 ÷ 2 = 20 each, disregarding that 3:5 means unequal shares

errorPatterns.pattern: Finds one part but forgets to multiply each share back (reports the parts count or the one-part value as the answer)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold: 'that's the value of ONE part — how many parts does each child have?' Prompt the final multiply and the add-back check (15 + 25 = 40).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computes 40 ÷ 8 = 5 and answers '5 and 5', or gives '3 and 5' as the numbers of sweets

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot combine chained comparisons into a single ratio
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make Jo one part; Sam is 3 parts, Tom is 6; total 10 parts, one part = 3. Build the 1:3:6 bar before sharing. Reteach missing-value ratio reasoning.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On 'Tom twice Sam, Sam three times Jo, 30 altogether', treats the multipliers separately and cannot state Jo:Sam:Tom = 1:3:6

responseLevels.gap: Shares equally, or uses 3/5 as the fraction and shares wrongly; does not form the total of 8 parts.
responseLevels.full: Sums to 8 parts, finds one part = 5, gives 15 and 25, states the fraction of the whole as 3/8, checks by adding back to 40, and transfers the method to a chained three-way comparison (1:3:6).
responseLevels.partial: Finds one part and the correct shares (15, 25) via 8 parts, but gives the whole-fraction as 3/5, or cannot combine chained 'twice/three times' language into a single ratio — the part-whole idea or transfer is not yet secure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Share 40 sweets between two children in the ratio 3:5. Work out how many each child gets. Then tell me: what fraction of ALL the sweets does the child with 3 parts get? Show your working.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands adds the parts to get 8, so their shares total 40 and the fraction is 3/8. A child treating the ratio as a part-whole fraction says 3/5 (and often shares wrongly). Watching the working shows whether they counted 8 parts or used 3 or 5 as the total — and the fraction question forces the a/(a+b) idea into the open; 3/8 versus 3/5 is a clean split.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Dividing Quantities by Ratio
topic.description: Divide a given quantity into two parts in a given part:part or part:whole ratio, and express the division as a fraction of the whole
evidence: Share £60 between two people in the ratio 2:3 by finding the value of one part
Express the result of sharing 24 sweets as 10 and 14 in ratio form as 5:7
Solve problems involving three-part ratios (e.g. divide 180 in the ratio 1:2:3)
topic.assessmentPrompt: If £60 is shared between two people in the ratio 2:3, can {{name}} work out how much each person gets?

pedagogy.summary: Dividing a quantity in a given ratio is the formal KS3 procedure: for a ratio a:b (or a:b:c), the TOTAL number of parts is a+b(+c); one part = quantity ÷ total parts; each share = its parts × one part. Two things distinguish this from earlier unequal-sharing work: it extends cleanly to THREE-part ratios (divide 180 in 1:2:3), and it goes both ways — pupils must also express a completed division back AS a ratio in simplest form (10 and 14 becomes 5:7), and read off a part as a fraction of the whole. The persistent hazard is using a part rather than the SUM of parts as the denominator; the fix is the same find-one-part routine, kept visible on a bar model.
bestPractices: Standardise the routine explicitly: total parts = sum of all ratio numbers → one part = quantity ÷ total → multiply each ratio number by one part.
Extend to three-part ratios immediately (1:2:3 → 6 parts) so the 'sum ALL the parts' step is generalised, not tied to two shares.
Practise the reverse direction: given the actual shares, write them as a ratio and simplify (10:14 → 5:7), and state a share as a fraction of the whole.
Keep the bar model as the check: the number of equal segments equals the sum of the ratio numbers; adding the shares must return the original quantity.
Distinguish part-to-part (a:b) from part-to-whole (a out of a+b) in the notation, since the same numbers appear in both.
keyRepresentations: Bar model / tape diagram with a+b(+c) equal segments
The 'one part' unit (quantity ÷ total parts)
Ratio table (parts | value) extended to three columns for three-part ratios
Simplest-form ratio from actual shares (divide by the HCF)
commonMisconceptions: Dividing by a single part rather than the sum of parts (÷3 or ÷5 instead of ÷8), or in a 3-part ratio forgetting to include every part in the total.
Sharing the quantity equally among the number of terms (180 into three equal 60s for 1:2:3).
When reversing, writing the shares as a ratio without simplifying (10:14 left un-reduced), or reversing the order.
Confusing part-to-part with part-to-whole — stating a share as a/b of the whole rather than a/(a+b).

learn.summary: Divide a quantity in a given ratio using the find-one-part routine: total parts = sum of ALL ratio numbers; one part = quantity ÷ total parts; each share = its ratio number × one part. The guidance generalises this to three-part ratios (divide 180 in 1:2:3 = 6 parts, not 3) and works both directions: express a completed division back as a simplest-form ratio (10 and 14 → 5:7) and state a share as a fraction of the whole. The persistent hazard is using one part, rather than the sum of parts, as the denominator; a bar/tape model with the correct number of equal segments keeps the correct total visible as a check.

activities.title: Ratio-divider on a tape diagram (forward direction)
feedback: If the strip is cut into three segments for 1:2:3, flag it: count that 1+2+3 = 6 segments are needed before the fill unlocks.

If the learner divides by the number of ratio terms or by a single term instead of the sum of parts (e.g. 180 ÷ 3 = 60) or shares equally (60, 60, 60), show the six-segment bar and recompute one part = 180 ÷ 6 = 30.
If the learner finds one part but stops (answers '30', or '1, 2, 3'), prompt that 30 is only ONE part: ask how many parts each share has, then multiply (1×30, 2×30, 3×30 → 30, 60, 90).
If the shares don't sum to the original quantity, prompt a recount of segments — the total must return 180.
activities.rationale: An optional interactive tape diagram that refuses an incorrect number of segments can make the '÷ total parts' step explicit and give immediate feedback; because the learner segments and fills the bar, the task lets them produce the working rather than only recognise a finished answer. The refusal mechanism is one illustrative design, proposed rather than required or uniquely effective, and its efficacy is not source-verified; it teaches the National Curriculum objective of dividing a quantity in a given ratio.
sourceClaims: Pupils should divide a given quantity into two (or more) parts in a given part:part or part:whole ratio, and express a division as a fraction of the whole (KS3 ratio, proportion and rates of change).
learnerActions: Enter a ratio such as 1:2:3 and cut the strip into the SUM of the parts — six equal segments for 1:2:3, not three.
Let the quantity (e.g. 180) distribute across the equal segments and read off one part = 180 ÷ 6 = 30.
Colour 1, 2 and 3 adjacent segments to read the shares 30, 60 and 90, then add them to check they return 180.
Repeat with a two-part ratio (e.g. share £60 in 2:3: 5 parts, one part = 12, shares 24 and 36, summing to 60).
activities.intendedInsight: A three-part ratio 1:2:3 needs six equal parts, not three; dividing once by the total number of parts and then scaling each term is the whole routine, and the shares must add back to the original quantity.

activities.title: Reverse station: write shares as a simplest-form ratio
feedback: If the learner leaves 10:14 un-simplified, prompt: what common factor divides both? Divide by 2 to get 5:7.
If the order is reversed to 14:10, point back to which share came first (10) and restore the matching order.
activities.rationale: The forward division task does not test simplification, so a separate reverse task is needed to secure it. Casting simplification as dividing both terms by the HCF connects to prior fraction work.
sourceClaims: In a part-to-part ratio a:b(:c), a part is a/(a+b(+c)) of the whole; ratio compares part to part and must be reduced to simplest form — the classic error is reading a:b as a/b of the whole.
learnerActions: Take two actual shares (e.g. 24 sweets shared as 10 and 14) and write them as a ratio 10:14.
Simplify by dividing both terms by their highest common factor (÷2) to reach 5:7, keeping the order matching the shares as stated.
Explain how this is like simplifying a fraction, and check you have not reversed the order (14:10 is wrong for 10 then 14).
activities.intendedInsight: A completed division can be expressed back as a ratio, and a ratio must be reduced to simplest form by dividing by the common factor — directly analogous to simplifying a fraction.

activities.title: Part of the whole as a fraction
feedback: If a learner writes the middle share of 1:2:3 as 2/3, point to the six segments: the denominator is the total parts, so it is 2/6 = 1/3.
Compare 2/6 and 2/3 side by side so the distinction between part-to-part and part-to-whole is visible.
activities.rationale: Confusing a:b with a/b of the whole is a documented classic error; anchoring the denominator to the counted total parts on the bar addresses it directly.
sourceClaims: In a part-to-part ratio a:b(:c), a part is a/(a+b(+c)) of the whole; ratio compares part to part and must be reduced to simplest form — the classic error is reading a:b as a/b of the whole.
Pupils should divide a given quantity into two (or more) parts in a given part:part or part:whole ratio, and express a division as a fraction of the whole (KS3 ratio, proportion and rates of change).
learnerActions: For 1:2:3, state what fraction of the whole each share is: 1/6, 2/6 (=1/3) and 3/6 (=1/2), using the TOTAL of 6 parts as the denominator.
Contrast part-to-part with part-to-whole explicitly: the middle share is 2 parts out of 6 total, so 2/6, NOT 2/3.
Optionally toggle a colour band to light each part and reveal its fraction of the whole.
activities.intendedInsight: When stating a share as a fraction of the whole, the denominator is the SUM of all parts (a+b+c), not another single term; part-to-part and part-to-whole use the same numbers differently.

activities.title: Checks for understanding (written/selected response)
feedback: For 60, 60, 60: that divides equally rather than in 1:2:3 — re-form the total of 6 parts and scale each term.
For 10:14 chosen as final: it is not yet simplified — divide both terms by 2 to reach 5:7.
For 2/3: the denominator should be the total of 6 parts, giving 2/6 = 1/3.
activities.rationale: Selected/short responses efficiently reveal the equal-share and un-simplified-ratio errors, but they confirm recognition and recall rather than requiring the learner to build the segmented bar and produce the working; use alongside the construction tasks.
learnerActions: Fill in: divide 180 in 1:2:3 → __, __, __ (answer 30, 60, 90; the equal-share response 60, 60, 60 is a common error).
Choose the simplest-form ratio for shares of 10 and 14 (answer 5:7; the un-simplified 10:14 is a distractor).
State what fraction of the whole the middle share of 1:2:3 is (answer 2/6 = 1/3).
activities.intendedInsight: Three-part division, reverse-to-ratio, and part-of-whole can each be checked, with 'shared equally' and 'un-simplified ratio' as the diagnostic error responses; add a two-part item (e.g. £60 in 2:3) if two-part division is also to be checked.

constraints: Treat the forward division and the reverse (shares → simplest-form ratio) as distinct objectives: the forward task does not exercise simplification, so include a separate reverse task.

A static segmented reference bar (e.g. six equal segments for 1:2:3) with tap-to-reveal 'one part = total ÷ sum of parts' can consolidate the routine but does not let the learner segment, fill, or reverse a division themselves — it is a reference card, not a substitute for construction.
Selected-response checks confirm recognition/recall; they do not require the learner to build the bar or produce the working, so pair them with construction tasks for full evidence.
Always re-include every term in the total: a three-part ratio must sum all parts (1+2+3 = 6), and the shares must add back to the original quantity as a check.
Keep part-to-part (a:b) and part-to-whole (a out of a+b+c) distinct in notation, since the same numbers appear in both.
After finding one part, scale each term (×1, ×2, ×3) — reporting one part alone, or '1, 2, 3', is incomplete.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit (arithmetic/logic checked): 180 ÷ 6 = 30; shares 30+60+90 = 180 ✓. £60 in 2:3 → 5 parts, 60 ÷ 5 = 12, shares 24 and 36, sum 60 ✓. 10:14 ÷2 = 5:7 ✓. Middle share of 1:2:3 = 2/6 = 1/3 ✓; largest share 3/6 = 1/2 ✓.

The legacy entry asserted a dividing procedure 'gains nothing' from dialogue and that 3D 'adds nothing' because partitioning is one-dimensional. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been dropped rather than propagated as universal laws; the tape/bar model is retained as a well-fitted representation without claiming other media cannot teach this.
The 'refusal to cut into three segments' is preserved as one optional, illustrative feedback mechanism, not a mandatory or uniquely effective design; its efficacy is untested.

Restored the original assessment's 'performance' error pattern (finds one part but forgets to multiply each term back) as explicit feedback in the forward-division activity, as it was missing from the source candidate.

The original probeDeeper listed '3/3, 3/6, or 3/1' as candidate answers for the largest share; only the correct 3/6 = 1/2 is used, and the erroneous options were not migrated as learner-facing choices.

probeDeeper: How many equal parts are there altogether in 1:2:3? Why 6 and not 3?
Add your three amounts together — do they make 180? What would it mean if they didn't?
What fraction of the whole 180 is the largest share? (counterexample: is it 3/3, 3/6, or 3/1 — and why?)
For 10:14, how did you get 5:7 — what did you divide by, and how is that like simplifying a fraction?
assess.correctAnswer: For 180 in 1:2:3: total parts = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, so one part = 180 ÷ 6 = 30; the shares are 30, 60 and 90 (which add to 180). For the reverse: 10:14 simplifies (÷2) to 5:7.

errorPatterns.pattern: Divides by a single part or by the number of terms rather than the SUM of all parts
errorPatterns.nextMove: Draw the bar cut into 1+2+3 = 6 equal segments and count them; one part = 180 ÷ 6. Check the shares add back to 180. Reteach ratio notation and the total-parts idea.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 180 ÷ 3 = 60 and gives 60, 60, 60 (equal), or 180 ÷ 1 / ÷2 / ÷3 separately; total parts of 6 never formed

errorPatterns.pattern: When reversing, writes the shares as a ratio without simplifying (or reverses the order)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Treat it like simplifying a fraction: divide both by the common factor (2). Keep the order matching the shares as stated. Reteach ratio simplification.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 10:14 as the final answer, or writes 14:10, not dividing by the HCF to 5:7

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses part-to-part with part-to-whole — states a share as a/b of the whole rather than a/(a+b+c)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to the six segments: the denominator is the TOTAL parts. Contrast 2/6 with 2/3 explicitly. Reteach the vocabulary of part-to-part vs part-to-whole.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a follow-up, says the middle share of 1:2:3 is 2/3 of the whole rather than 2/6 = 1/3

errorPatterns.pattern: Finds one part correctly but forgets to multiply each term back
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold: 'that's ONE part — how many parts does each share have?' Prompt the multiply and the add-back check.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computes 180 ÷ 6 = 30 and answers '30' or '1, 2, 3' rather than 30, 60, 90

responseLevels.gap: Shares equally (60,60,60) or divides by one part; cannot form the total of 6 parts, and leaves a reversed ratio un-simplified.
responseLevels.full: Sums all parts to 6, finds one part = 30, gives 30/60/90 checked to 180, simplifies 10:14 to 5:7, and correctly states a share as its fraction of the whole (e.g. 2/6 = 1/3) — handling both directions and three-part ratios.
responseLevels.partial: Divides 180 correctly via 6 parts to 30/60/90, but leaves 10:14 un-simplified, or states a share as part-of-part not part-of-whole — the reverse direction or the fraction interpretation is not yet secure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Divide 180 in the ratio 1:2:3. Work out the three amounts, and show your working. Then, separately: 24 sweets were shared as 10 and 14 — write that sharing as a ratio in its simplest form.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A pupil who has the routine sums all three parts to 6, divides once, and scales — shares total 180. A pupil dividing by the number of terms shares equally (60, 60, 60) or divides by one part; a pupil who cannot reverse leaves 10:14 un-simplified. Watching the working shows exactly which step fails, and the reverse task separately tests simplification, which the forward task does not.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: One Quantity as a Fraction
topic.description: Express one quantity as a fraction of another where the result may be less than 1 or greater than 1, and interpret the meaning in context
evidence: Express 45 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours (= 3/8)
Express a larger quantity as a fraction of a smaller one and explain why the result exceeds 1
Simplify the resulting fraction and interpret its meaning in the original context
topic.assessmentPrompt: If there are 15 boys and 20 girls in a class, can {{name}} express the number of boys as a fraction of the whole class and say whether that fraction is less than or greater than a half?

pedagogy.summary: Expressing one quantity as a fraction of another means writing 'a as a fraction of b' = a/b, where the quantity AFTER 'of' is the denominator (the whole) and the other is the numerator (the part). Two ideas make it conceptual rather than mechanical: (1) both quantities must be in the SAME UNIT before you form the fraction (45 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours is 45/120 = 3/8, not 45/2), and (2) the result can be MORE THAN ONE when the first quantity is bigger than the second (3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours = 3/2), which contradicts the young child's belief that a fraction is always less than a whole. Mastery is forming, simplifying, and INTERPRETING such a fraction in context.
bestPractices: Foreground the phrase structure: 'a as a fraction of b' → the thing after 'of' is the denominator. Rehearse identifying which quantity is the whole before writing anything.
Always convert to a common unit first; make 'same units?' a required checkpoint (45 min and 2 h → 45 min and 120 min).
Deliberately include cases where the answer exceeds 1 (e.g. 150 cm as a fraction of 1 m) so pupils accept improper-fraction results and interpret them as 'more than the whole'.
Simplify and then interpret in words — '3/8 of the two hours' — so the fraction is tied back to the situation, not left as a bare number.
Connect to ratio and percentage: a/b is the same comparison expressed as a fraction, and ×100 gives the percentage — building the ratio–fraction–percentage web.
keyRepresentations: Bar / double number line with both quantities in a common unit (45 out of 120 minutes shaded)
The sentence frame 'a as a fraction of b = a/b' with 'of' → denominator
Fraction-of-a-quantity strip that can exceed one whole (improper result)
Equivalent-fraction simplification chain (45/120 → 3/8)
commonMisconceptions: Writing the raw numbers without converting to a common unit (45/2 for 45 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours).
Putting the quantities the wrong way round — ignoring that the quantity after 'of' is the denominator.
Believing a fraction must be less than 1, so being unable to accept or interpret a result greater than 1 (3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours = 3/2).
Forgetting to simplify, or simplifying incorrectly, leaving the comparison obscured.

learn.summary: Learners express one quantity as a fraction of another: 'a as a fraction of b' = a/b, where the quantity after 'of' is the denominator (the whole). Mastery requires (1) converting both quantities to the SAME unit before forming the fraction (45 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours is 45/120 = 3/8, not 45/2), (2) accepting results greater than one whole when the first quantity is bigger (3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours = 3/2), and (3) simplifying and interpreting the fraction back in context.

activities.title: The fraction-of bench: convert units, then form the fraction
feedback: If a learner writes 45/2, ask: 'Are minutes and hours the same unit?' Convert 2 hours to 120 minutes on the bar, then re-form 45/120 = 3/8.

If a learner writes 120/45 or 8/3, rehearse the sentence frame: 'a as a fraction of b' means b (after 'of') is the whole/denominator; test it on 1 hour as a fraction of 2 hours, which must be 1/2, not 2.

If a learner refuses 3/2, flips it to 2/3, or says 'that can't be a fraction', return to the overflowing bar: 3 hours shaded past the 2-hour whole is 3/2 = 1½ wholes — an improper fraction meaning more than the whole amount.
If a learner stops at 45/120, prompt them to simplify and then say the answer in context ('3/8 of the two hours').
activities.rationale: Seeing both quantities on a common-unit bar grounds the part–whole comparison; a strip that overflows one whole makes an improper result visible rather than abstract, which targets the belief that a fraction must be less than 1. An optional unit toggle that withholds the fraction until units match makes the 'convert first' step explicit at the moment the error would occur. Laying both quantities on a shared scale is a concrete way to reason multiplicatively about part relative to whole.
sourceClaims: KS2/KS3 pupils should express one quantity as a fraction of another and solve problems involving relative sizes of two quantities, including where units must be made common and results simplified.
Comparing two quantities as a fraction is part of the ratio–fraction–proportion web; reasoning multiplicatively about part relative to whole underpins it.
learnerActions: Start with two quantities in different units, e.g. 45 minutes and 2 hours, and say in words which quantity is the whole (the one after 'of' — here 2 hours).
Before writing any fraction, convert both to a common unit: split the 2-hour bar into 120 minute-segments and highlight the 45.
Form the fraction from the shaded bar: 45 out of 120, then simplify the equivalent-fraction chain 45/120 → 9/24 → 3/8.

In a second round, take 3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours: shade 3 hours against a 2-hour whole bar so the shading runs past the end of one whole and spills into a second bar; read the fraction as 3/2.
State what 3/2 means here in words: '3 hours is one and a half times the two hours' / 'more than the whole'.
Check yourself with an obvious case: 1 hour as a fraction of 2 hours should be 1/2 — confirm your method gives it.
activities.intendedInsight: Both quantities must be in the same unit before forming a fraction, the quantity after 'of' is the denominator, and the comparison fraction can exceed one whole when the first quantity is larger.

activities.title: Form, simplify and interpret — including improper results
feedback: For 45/2: this did not convert hours to minutes; 2 h = 120 min, so the fraction is 45/120 = 3/8.
For 150/1: 1 m = 100 cm, so 150 cm as a fraction of 1 m is 150/100 = 3/2, not 150/1.
For 2/3 on the 150 cm item: the quantity after 'of' (1 m = 100 cm) is the whole/denominator, so 150 goes on top — the answer 3/2 is greater than 1.
Connect a/b to percentage: ×100 turns 3/8 into 37.5% and 3/2 into 150%, linking the fraction, ratio and percentage.
activities.rationale: Short constructed and selection items let learners rehearse forming, simplifying and interpreting the fraction and confront targeted distractors (no conversion, wrong way round, improper result). Recognition/selection confirms the rule but does not by itself require the learner to build the common-unit bar, so it complements rather than replaces the hands-on forming activity.
sourceClaims: KS2/KS3 pupils should express one quantity as a fraction of another and solve problems involving relative sizes of two quantities, including where units must be made common and results simplified.
learnerActions: Fill in the blank: '45 min as a fraction of 2 h = ___', giving the simplified fraction (3/8) and rejecting the un-converted 45/2.
Identify which quantity is the denominator in a given 'a as a fraction of b' statement and justify why.
Tackle an item whose answer exceeds 1: write 150 cm as a fraction of 1 m in simplest form (= 3/2), avoiding 2/3 (wrong way round) and 150/1 (no conversion).
After each answer, write one sentence interpreting the fraction in the original context.
activities.intendedInsight: Forming, simplifying and interpreting the fraction — including when it is greater than 1 — is a single connected skill, with the not-converting and wrong-way-round errors as the key pitfalls.

activities.title: Annotated reference bar: 'of → denominator' and 'convert units first'
feedback: If a learner still mixes up the order, point back to the tapped 'of → denominator' annotation and re-test on 1 hour as a fraction of 2 hours = 1/2.
If a learner forgets conversion, re-reveal the 2 h = 120 min step on the bar.
activities.rationale: A fixed annotated bar consolidates the rule and serves as a reference card. As a static scaffold it cannot make the learner perform the conversion or watch a fraction overflow one whole, so it supports but does not substitute for the interactive forming activity.
learnerActions: Study a bar showing 45 of 120 minutes shaded; tap the word 'of' to reveal that it marks the whole/denominator.
Tap the bar to reveal the common-unit conversion (2 h = 120 min) that had to happen first.
Use this card as a quick check before forming any 'fraction-of' answer.
activities.intendedInsight: The phrase 'a as a fraction of b' always puts the quantity after 'of' as the denominator, and units must be made common before the fraction is formed.

constraints: Always require a 'same units?' checkpoint before any fraction is written; converting to a common unit must precede forming the fraction.
Deliberately include cases where the answer exceeds 1 (e.g. 3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours = 3/2, 150 cm as a fraction of 1 m = 3/2) so learners accept and interpret improper results.
Simplify and then interpret the fraction in words tied to the situation ('3/8 of the two hours'); do not leave it as a bare number.
Selection/recognition items confirm the rule and surface distractors but do not elicit independent construction of the common-unit comparison; pair them with hands-on forming.
The static annotated bar is a reference scaffold: it cannot make the learner perform the conversion or dynamically witness a fraction exceeding one whole.
Connect to ratio and percentage (a/b as the same comparison; ×100 for percentage) to build the ratio–fraction–percentage web.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original 'persona dialogue' and '3D' entries were rated poor-fit; those were catalog-fit judgements for this one-dimensional comparison, not established pedagogical laws, so they are omitted rather than asserted as universal claims about the media.

The claim that only the overflowing-bar visual can dismantle the 'fractions are always <1' misconception is a catalog preference; it is presented here as a well-motivated proposal, not proven necessity.

Independent editor arithmetic/coherence check: 45/120 = 9/24 = 3/8; 150/100 = 3/2; 1 h/2 h = 1/2; 120/45 = 8/3; 3/8 = 37.5% and 3/2 = 150% all verify. 45/2 and 120/45 (=8/3) are framed only as errors, never as valid answers, and no denominator-'flip' claim is made (the unit-fraction comparison here fixes the numerator and varies the whole, so no 'flipping rule' is implied).

probeDeeper: Are 45 and 2 measured in the same unit? What do you have to do before you can compare them?
Which is the WHOLE here — the 45 minutes or the 2 hours? How does the wording tell you which goes on the bottom?
Now write 3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours. Can the answer be bigger than 1? What does 3/2 mean here? (counterexample forcing an improper result.)
Check yourself: 1 hour as a fraction of 2 hours — what should that be? Does your method give that?
assess.correctAnswer: 3/8. Because 2 hours = 120 minutes, 45 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours is 45/120, which simplifies to 3/8. (Both quantities must be in the same unit — minutes — before forming the fraction.)

errorPatterns.pattern: Does not convert to a common unit — writes 45/2 straight from the numbers as they appear
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'are minutes and hours the same unit?' Convert 2 hours to 120 minutes on a bar, then re-form 45/120. Make 'same units first' a fixed checkpoint.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer is 45/2 or 22.5, and the explanation is 'the 45 goes over the 2' with no mention of minutes vs hours

errorPatterns.pattern: Puts the quantities the wrong way round — ignores that the amount after 'of' is the denominator
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rehearse the sentence frame: 'a as a fraction of b' → b (after 'of') is the whole/denominator. Check with an obvious case: 1 hour as a fraction of 2 hours must be 1/2, not 2.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 120/45 (or 8/3), treating the first-mentioned or larger quantity as the whole

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes a fraction must be less than 1, so cannot accept or interpret a result greater than one whole
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the overflowing bar: 3 hours shaded past the 2-hour whole gives 3/2 = 1½ wholes. Name it an improper fraction and interpret it as 'more than the whole amount'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a case like 3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours, refuses 3/2, flips it to 2/3, or says 'that can't be a fraction'

responseLevels.gap: Writes 45/2 (or flips to 120/45) without converting units or identifying the whole; treats it as a bare number-placing exercise.
responseLevels.full: Converts 2 h to 120 min, forms 45/120 with the correct quantity as denominator, simplifies to 3/8, interprets it in context, AND accepts and interprets an improper result such as 3/2 for 3 hours as a fraction of 2 hours.
responseLevels.partial: Converts to a common unit and forms 45/120 but stops without simplifying, or simplifies yet cannot handle a result greater than 1, or cannot say which quantity is the whole and why.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Write 45 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours, as simply as you can. Then explain how you got it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands must first notice the units differ and convert 2 hours to 120 minutes; the answer 3/8 can ONLY be reached that way. A child who just writes the numbers gives 45/2 (or 22.5) and their reason reveals they never converted. The reason-tier separates 'I made the units the same first' from 'I put 45 over 2', so the two children give different answers and different explanations.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Proportional Reasoning Vocabulary
topic.description: Know and use advanced vocabulary of multiplicative reasoning — direct proportion, inverse proportion, ratio, rate, unit rate, compound unit, scale factor — accurately in problem-solving contexts
evidence: Distinguish between 'direct proportion' and 'inverse proportion' with real-world examples
Use 'rate', 'speed', and 'density' correctly and explain what units they are measured in

topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is solving a problem about speed or density, can they explain what 'compound unit' means and tell the difference between direct proportion (more of one means more of the other) and inverse proportion (more of one means less of the other)?

pedagogy.summary: This is the precise VOCABULARY of multiplicative reasoning — direct proportion, inverse proportion, ratio, rate, unit rate, compound unit, scale factor — used accurately in context. The teaching goal is not reciting definitions but USING each term correctly to describe real situations and knowing what units a rate/compound measure carries. The two words that cause most trouble are 'proportion' (whose everyday sense, 'a large proportion', drifts from the mathematical one) and the direct/inverse pair (pupils label anything with 'more' as 'direct'). Vocabulary is best taught with examples AND non-examples, tied to situations, and rehearsed in speaking and writing rather than as a glossary.
bestPractices: Teach each term through examples and NON-examples that fence its boundary (a directly proportional situation vs an inverse one vs a non-proportional one), following explicit-vocabulary practice (e.g. Frayer-style).
Always attach units when using rate/speed/density (mph, m/s, kg/m³) — a rate without units is incomplete.
Contrast the everyday and mathematical senses of 'proportion' directly, so the technical meaning (a multiplicative part-to-whole relationship) is distinguished from loose usage.
Rehearse the direct/inverse distinction in full sentences ('as one increases the other DEcreases, so it is inverse'), not as a label to guess.
Give pupils the terms to USE in describing and solving problems (calculate the speed of a car doing 120 miles in 2 hours and NAME it a rate), not to define in isolation.
keyRepresentations: Frayer-style word map (definition, characteristics, examples, non-examples) for each term
Paired example/non-example situation cards (direct | inverse | neither)
Unit tags for each compound measure (speed = mph or m/s; density = kg/m³)
Sentence frames ('as … increases, … so this is … proportion')
commonMisconceptions: Using 'proportion' in its loose everyday sense ('a large proportion') rather than the mathematical multiplicative meaning.
Labelling any 'more → more' situation 'direct proportion' and failing to identify inverse proportion (more workers → less time).
Using 'rate', 'speed' or 'density' without units, or treating 'ratio' and 'rate' as interchangeable.
Confusing 'scale factor' with an additive change rather than a multiplier.

learn.summary: Learners (ages 11–14) build precise command of multiplicative-reasoning vocabulary — direct proportion, inverse proportion, ratio, rate, unit rate, compound unit, scale factor — by USING each term accurately to describe real situations and stating the units a rate/compound measure carries. The goal is correct use in context, not reciting glossary definitions. The two persistent trouble spots are 'proportion' (whose everyday sense 'a large proportion' drifts from the mathematical multiplicative meaning) and the direct/inverse pair (learners label anything with 'more' as 'direct'). Vocabulary is taught with examples AND non-examples tied to situations, and rehearsed in speaking and writing.

activities.title: Talk it through with a market-stall trader (or science reporter)
feedback: When the learner calls 'more workers → less time' direct, don't supply the label — ask which way EACH quantity moves, then ask what happens to the time if the workers double (assuming each works at the same rate); let them hear themselves say 'opposite, and doubling halves it, so inverse.'
If 'proportion' is used loosely ('a large proportion'), ask: do you mean the everyday amount or the maths relationship where two quantities change in a constant ratio?
If a rate is named without units, ask for the units and why 'per' matters (miles PER hour compares distance to time).

Name the tell back to them: 'both increase together in a constant ratio → direct; one up while the other goes down with a constant product (double one, halve the other) → inverse' — and note that both increasing without a constant ratio, or one decreasing without a constant product, is neither.
activities.rationale: A LANGUAGE objective — using terms accurately in context — is well served by open dialogue where a character can probe loose usage in real time and push the learner toward precise use and units. The unscripted push, not a fixed script, drives self-correction. This is a research-informed proposal, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: The word 'proportion' has an everyday sense that drifts from its mathematical meaning; a directly proportional relationship is a constant multiplicative relationship between two quantities, distinct from ratio (part-to-part).

Students over-apply 'direct proportion' and fail to recognise inverse proportion (e.g. driving twice as fast halves the time); the properties of direct proportion must be named and contrasted with inverse and non-proportional situations.
learnerActions: Respond in-role to a character who throws real situations at you and listens for the right word: '3 apples for £1 — what do we call this, and what are its units?' (target: it is a rate; its unit rate is 'pounds per apple', found by sharing £1 across 3 apples ≈ £0.33 per apple — or equivalently 3 apples per pound).

When you label 'more workers, fewer hours' as direct, answer the follow-up: 'I add two workers and the time drops — are those two quantities moving the SAME way or opposite?' and revise to 'opposite — and if every worker works at the same rate, doubling the workers halves the time (workers × hours stays constant), so it is INVERSE proportion.'
Describe at least one directly proportional situation, one inverse, and name a rate aloud WITH its units (e.g. '120 miles in 2 hours is 60 miles per hour — a rate/speed, miles per hour').
Say a full sentence that explains WHY, e.g. 'as the petrol increases, the cost increases with it in a constant ratio, so it is direct proportion.'
activities.intendedInsight: A term is pinned to the behaviour it names — you decide 'direct' vs 'inverse' by checking whether the quantities move together in a constant ratio (direct) or oppositely with a constant product, so doubling one halves the other (inverse), not by spotting the word 'more'. If neither holds, the relationship is not proportional. A rate is incomplete without its units.

activities.title: Sort-and-tag: direct / inverse / neither, with unit tags
feedback: When a card is binned, state the reason: 'both quantities increase together in a constant ratio → direct' or 'one increases while the other decreases with a constant product (doubling one halves the other) → inverse.'
If a rate is tagged without units or with wrong units, prompt the X-per-Y form (miles per hour, kg per cubic metre).

Reinforce that 'neither' is a real category — not every 'more → more' situation is direct and not every 'more → less' situation is inverse; two quantities can both rise without a constant ratio, or one can fall as the other rises without a constant product.
activities.rationale: Sorting situations by the right term and tagging rates with units gives immediate feedback and builds the direct/inverse/neither boundary through examples and non-examples (Frayer-style fencing). A strong companion to the dialogue for boundary practice. Research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Explicit vocabulary instruction uses definitions with examples AND non-examples to fence a term's boundary, with active use rather than rote definition (Frayer model).

Students over-apply 'direct proportion' and fail to recognise inverse proportion (e.g. driving twice as fast halves the time); the properties of direct proportion must be named and contrasted with inverse and non-proportional situations.
learnerActions: Sort situation cards into three bins: direct proportion, inverse proportion, and neither (non-proportional).
Attach the correct unit tag to each rate card (speed = mph or m/s; density = kg/m³).
Complete sentence frames using the vocabulary, e.g. 'as … increases, … so this is … proportion.'
Read the feedback that names the tell ('both increase together in a constant ratio → direct') and re-sort any you placed wrongly.
activities.intendedInsight: The boundary between direct, inverse, and non-proportional situations becomes visible through contrasting examples and non-examples; every rate carries units.

activities.title: Frayer-style term map (reference and consolidation)
feedback: Check that each map includes a genuine non-example, not just an example reworded.
If 'scale factor' is described as 'add 3', correct it to a multiplier ('×3').

Tie the mathematical meaning of 'direct proportion' to 'as one changes, the other changes in a constant ratio', and of 'inverse proportion' to 'as one changes, the other changes so that their product stays constant.'
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal or written term map consolidates meanings and supports explicit-vocabulary practice. It is a reference/consolidation scaffold: it does not by itself require the learner to PRODUCE a term in a novel context, which the assessment targets — so it should accompany, not replace, the productive tasks. Research-informed proposal, not a tested intervention.
sourceClaims: Explicit vocabulary instruction uses definitions with examples AND non-examples to fence a term's boundary, with active use rather than rote definition (Frayer model).
learnerActions: For each term (direct proportion, inverse proportion, ratio, rate, unit rate, compound unit, scale factor), fill a four-box map: definition, characteristics, an example, and a non-example.
Add the units for each rate/compound measure (speed: mph or m/s; density: kg/m³).
Explicitly contrast the everyday sense of 'proportion' (an amount) with the mathematical sense (a multiplicative part-to-whole relationship / constant ratio).
Note that 'scale factor' is a MULTIPLIER, not an additive change.
activities.intendedInsight: Each term has a fenced meaning with clear examples, non-examples, and (for rates) units; 'proportion' and 'scale factor' have specific mathematical senses distinct from loose everyday use.

activities.title: Check and probe: use the words, generate your own examples
feedback: If both situations are called 'direct', have the learner say which way EACH quantity moves and whether doubling one halves the other; opposite movement with a constant product → inverse. Re-sort more example/non-example pairs rehearsing 'as … doubles, … halves, so inverse', including opposite-moving non-examples that are neither.
If 60 mph is called 'a ratio' or a 'rate' without units, insist on the X-per-Y units and explain a rate is a ratio of two different quantities with units.
If the learner can label but not generate a fresh inverse example, their use is recognitional, not yet productive — prompt for a new everyday situation.
activities.rationale: Correct-use judgements are assessable via categorisation and explanation, with loose-'proportion' and direct-for-inverse as sharp error patterns. Requiring self-generated examples distinguishes productive command from recognition. A selection/categorisation check verifies correct choice but does not on its own elicit the independent spoken/written use that is the objective, so it is paired with explain-and-generate tasks. Research-informed proposal, not a validated intervention.

The word 'proportion' has an everyday sense that drifts from its mathematical meaning; a directly proportional relationship is a constant multiplicative relationship between two quantities, distinct from ratio (part-to-part).
learnerActions: Given two situations — (1) the more workers dig the trench, the less time it takes (assume every worker digs at the same rate); (2) the more petrol you buy, the more it costs (at a fixed price per litre) — state for EACH whether the quantities are in direct or inverse proportion and say a sentence explaining why.
For a car travelling 120 miles in 2 hours, state what '60 miles per hour' is called and what makes it that (a rate/speed, a compound unit comparing distance to time, miles PER hour).
Generate your OWN fresh example of an inverse proportion and your own example of a direct proportion.
Distinguish 'rate' from 'ratio': a rate is a ratio of two DIFFERENT quantities carrying units (X per Y).
activities.intendedInsight: Real command shows in how you USE the words in an explaining sentence and in whether you can PRODUCE a correct fresh example — not in label-matching.

constraints: Always attach units when using rate/speed/density (mph, m/s, kg/m³); a rate stated without units is incomplete.
Teach each term through examples AND non-examples that fence its boundary (direct vs inverse vs non-proportional), with active use rather than rote definition.
Contrast the everyday and mathematical senses of 'proportion' directly so the technical multiplicative meaning is distinguished from loose usage.

Rehearse the direct/inverse distinction in full sentences ('as one increases the other decreases so that their product stays constant — doubling one halves the other — so it is inverse'), not as a label guessed from 'more'. One quantity going down as the other goes up is not enough on its own to make it inverse.
Direct proportion requires quantities that increase together IN A CONSTANT RATIO; 'both increase' alone is not sufficient and may be non-proportional, so keep 'neither' a live category.
Give learners the terms to USE in describing and solving problems, not to define in isolation (e.g. compute the speed of a car doing 120 miles in 2 hours and NAME it a rate).

The term map is a consolidation/reference scaffold: it supports recognition but does not require independent production of the term in a novel context, which the productive tasks and assessment target.

A multiple-choice or categorisation check verifies correct selection; it does not on its own elicit the independent spoken/written USE of a term that is the main objective — pair recognition items with explain-and-generate tasks.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source assessment's worked rate 120 miles ÷ 2 hours = 60 miles per hour is arithmetically correct and retained.

One source claim (IRIS Center / Frayer model) is flagged verified:false in the row; the examples/non-examples principle is widely used but its citation here is unverified — treat as supporting a teaching principle, not as evidence the proposed activities were tested.

The curriculum 'use and understand the vocabulary' claim is a general objective/necessity assertion. It states the overall objective but does not support any individual activity's teaching METHOD, so it has been removed from all activity sourceClaims (including the dialogue, where the prior draft had retained it inconsistently).

The inherited feedback tell 'both increase together → direct' was corrected to 'both increase together IN A CONSTANT RATIO → direct' at every occurrence, because unqualified it reinforces the targeted over-application misconception and contradicts the 'neither/non-proportional' category present in the same activity.

Inherited phrasing names '3 apples for £1' a 'unit rate, in pounds per apple'; strictly '3 apples for £1' is a rate, and its unit rate is £1 ÷ 3 ≈ £0.33 per apple (equivalently 3 apples per pound). The learner action now makes the normalisation to one unit explicit.

probeDeeper: In situation (1), which way does the TIME move as workers increase? So are the quantities moving the same way or opposite — and which word is that?
You used the word 'proportion' — do you mean it the everyday way (an amount) or the maths way (two quantities changing together in a constant ratio)?
What are the UNITS of the car's speed, and why does 'per' matter?
Give me your OWN example of an inverse proportion, and one of a direct proportion. (counterexample-generation: can they produce, not just label?)
assess.correctAnswer: (1) Inverse proportion — as the number of workers increases, the time DEcreases (one goes up as the other goes down). (2) Direct proportion — as the petrol increases, the cost increases with it (both go up together, in a constant ratio). '60 miles per hour' is a RATE (a compound unit/speed), because it compares distance to time — miles PER hour.

errorPatterns.pattern: Labels any 'more → more/less' situation 'direct proportion', missing inverse
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have them say which way EACH quantity moves; if they move oppositely it is inverse. Give more example/non-example pairs to sort, rehearsing the sentence 'as … up, … down, so inverse'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the workers-and-time situation 'direct' because there are 'more workers', without noticing the time goes DOWN

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses 'proportion' in its everyday sense rather than the mathematical multiplicative meaning
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the two senses explicitly; keep the mathematical meaning tied to 'as one changes, the other changes in a constant ratio'. Rehearse in full sentences about specific situations.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says things like 'a large proportion of workers' or uses 'proportion' to mean 'amount', not a relationship between two quantities

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses 'rate', 'speed' or 'density' without units, or treats 'ratio' and 'rate' as the same word
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist a rate carries its units (X PER Y); a rate is a ratio of two DIFFERENT quantities with units, distinct from a plain ratio. Tag several rates with their units.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names 60 mph 'a ratio', or calls it a rate but cannot say the units are miles per hour

responseLevels.gap: Calls both situations 'direct', or uses 'proportion'/'rate' loosely and without units; cannot tie a term to the behaviour it names.
responseLevels.full: Correctly identifies inverse (workers/time) and direct (petrol/cost) BY describing the opposite/together movement, names 60 mph a rate/speed with units (miles per hour), distinguishes rate from ratio, and generates own correct examples of each term.
responseLevels.partial: Uses direct/inverse correctly for the given cases and names 60 mph a rate, but omits units, or cannot generate a fresh example of inverse proportion — use is recognitional, not yet productive.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are two situations. (1) The more workers dig the trench, the less time it takes. (2) The more petrol you buy, the more it costs. For EACH one, tell me whether the two quantities are in direct proportion or inverse proportion, and say a sentence explaining why. Then: a car travels 120 miles in 2 hours — what do we call the '60 miles per hour', and what makes it that?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who owns the vocabulary attaches 'inverse' to the workers case BY describing the opposite movement, and 'direct' to petrol by the together-movement, and names 60 mph a rate with its units. A child guessing from 'more' calls both 'direct'. Listening for how they USE the words in the explaining sentence — not whether they can define them — is what separates real command from label-matching.
