topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Understanding fractions
topic.description: Solve problems involving scaling by simple fractions and problems involving simple rates
evidence: A recipe for 4 people needs 200 g of flour — how much for 6 people?
If 3 kg costs £12, how much does 5 kg cost?
Scale a shape by a factor of 1/2 and find the new dimensions
topic.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe serves 4 and {{name}} wants to make it for 6, can they scale up each ingredient — for example, changing '2 cups of flour' to '3 cups'?

pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; solve problems involving scaling by simple fractions and simple rates (recipe for 4→6 people; 3 kg costs £12 → 5 kg; scale a shape by 1/2).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5–Y6 'solve problems involving … scaling by simple fractions and problems involving simple rates'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): connects to 4.OA.2 (multiplicative comparison) and 6.RP.1–3 (ratios and unit rates) — this topic is the bridge from whole-number scaling to proportional reasoning.
• Operational details — two related structures: SCALING by a fraction (multiply a quantity by a fraction >1 or <1: enlarge/reduce; e.g. ×6/4 for the recipe, ×1/2 for the shape) and RATES (a per-unit relationship: £12 per 3 kg → £4 per kg → ×5). The powerful general strategy is the UNITARY METHOD — find the value of one unit, then scale — supported by the double number line and ratio table. Children must see scaling as multiplicative (a fraction/rate multiplier), not additive. This is the conceptual launchpad for ratio and proportion (a separate domain) and must stay grounded in known multiplicative-comparison ideas.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): scale a quantity by a simple whole factor and by 1/2 with a double number line. Tier B (age 9–10): solve a rate problem via the unitary method (3 kg=£12 → 1 kg=£4 → 5 kg=£20) and a fraction-scaling recipe problem. Tier C (age 10): choose unitary vs scale-factor efficiently and justify with a ratio table / double number line.
bestPractices: Teach the unitary method — find one unit then scale — as the reliable general strategy, supported by a double number line and ratio table.
Represent rates on a double number line (kg vs £) so the proportional (multiplicative) relationship is visible and both quantities scale together.
Treat scaling as multiplicative (× a fraction/rate), explicitly contrasting with additive change, to prevent the classic 'add the difference' error.
Use both directions — scale up and scale down (×1/2) — and connect fraction-of-quantity skills to scaling.
Ground problems in authentic contexts (recipes, prices, maps/shapes) and check reasonableness.
keyRepresentations: Double number line (two quantities scaling together) — core rate/scaling tool
Ratio table — unit value and scaled values
Bar model — fraction scaling of a quantity
Scale-factor arrow (×6/4, ×1/2) linking original to scaled
commonMisconceptions: Scaling additively — adding the difference in people/kg instead of multiplying by the ratio (recipe for 6 = recipe for 4 + 2 portions of everything, done wrongly).
Not finding the unit value, so unable to scale to a new amount.
Inverting the rate (£12 per 3 kg treated as £3 per kg).
Confusing scaling up with down, or mis-applying ×1/2.
Treating rate problems as unrelated to multiplicative comparison / fractions.

learn.summary: For 9–10 year olds: solve problems involving scaling by simple fractions and simple rates (e.g. a recipe for 4→6 people; 3 kg costs £12 → cost of 5 kg; scale a shape by 1/2). The through-line is the UNITARY METHOD — find the value of one unit, then scale — supported by a double number line, ratio table and bar model. Learners should experience scaling as multiplicative (× a fraction or rate), explicitly contrasted with the common additive 'add the difference' error, across authentic contexts (recipes, prices, maps/shapes). Activities range from a manipulable double-number-line scaler that builds the proportional feel, through a Socratic unit-rate dialogue, a worked annotated exemplar, to checkable practice with targeted distractors.

activities.title: Double-number-line scaler: find one unit, then scale
feedback: When the child finds 1 kg = £4 and reaches £20 for 5 kg, affirm the unitary route: 'you found the cost of one, then multiplied by five'.

If the additive-trap attempt is tried, point out that adding the same number to both quantities (£12 + 2 = £14 for 5 kg) knocks the two lines out of alignment and gives a wrong amount. The rate holds only when each quantity changes by matching amounts (2 kg with £8), which is the same as scaling by the unit rate.
In recipe mode, if a learner adds 200 g for the '2 extra people', show that per-person is 50 g, so 6 people need 300 g, not 400 g.
activities.rationale: Direct manipulation of two locked quantities makes the multiplicative nature of scaling tangible and exposes the unitary method; sliding one quantity and watching the other move proportionally helps learners feel why adding the same amount to both quantities breaks the relationship. The additive-trap comparison is one optional device for making the contrast visible, not a claim that only manipulation can teach this.
sourceClaims: The unitary method, double number line and ratio table support scaling/rate problems; scaling must be treated as multiplicative, not additive.
learnerActions: On two parallel lines locked by a rate (e.g. kilograms against cost in pounds, £), slide to mark 3 kg opposite £12.
Use a 'find 1 unit' action to collapse the lines to 1 kg = £4, then slide on to 5 kg and read off £20.
Switch to a recipe mode: scale ingredients by ×6/4 (e.g. 200 g flour for 4 people → how much for 6?) shown on a bar model.
Switch to a shape mode: halve every dimension (×1/2) and read the new measurements.

Try the 'additive trap' toggle: add the same number to both lines (3 kg + 2 = 5 kg, so £12 + 2 = £14), then compare with the locked-rate result of £20. Notice that adding matching amounts instead (2 kg and its value, £8) keeps the lines aligned and gives £20.
activities.intendedInsight: Scaling and rates are proportional, multiplicative relationships: finding the value of one unit unlocks any target amount, and adding the same difference to both quantities does not preserve the relationship.

activities.title: Unit-rate dialogue: 'what does one cost?'
feedback: If the learner gives the unit value and scales correctly, name the strategy: 'you used the unitary method'.
If the learner answers the additive-objection probe by defending adding 200 g, redirect to per-person value (50 g) and ask them to total for 6.
For the 4→10 stretch, confirm that per-person value scales to any target, unlike hunting for a whole-number factor.
activities.rationale: A Socratic dialogue builds the unitary habit and can pose rich, varied contexts and challenge the additive misconception verbally. It cannot render a manipulable double number line, so it complements rather than replaces the interactive scaler.
sourceClaims: The unitary method, double number line and ratio table support scaling/rate problems; scaling must be treated as multiplicative, not additive.
learnerActions: Respond to a market-trader or chef character posing rate and recipe problems: 'If 3 kg costs £12, what does ONE kilogram cost? So what about five?'
State the unit value aloud or in writing, then state how you scale it to the target amount.
Answer the probe 'Someone said 6 people is 2 more than 4, so add 200 g more — what's wrong with that?' and explain the flaw.
Tackle a stretch case ('a recipe for 4, but you need it for 10') and say whether the unit-value method still works.
activities.intendedInsight: Routing every proportional problem through 'the value of one, then times the target' is a reliable general habit that works even when the scale factor is not a whole number.

activities.title: Worked exemplar: annotated double number line and ratio table
feedback: After revealing each step, restate the move: 'divide by 3 to get one, then multiply by 5'.
Prompt the learner to apply the same two-step reveal to their own new problem rather than only reading the exemplar.
activities.rationale: A worked, tap-to-reveal exemplar is a useful reference for the structure of the method, but a fixed image cannot provide new problems to solve, so it should be paired with independent problem-solving.
sourceClaims: The unitary method, double number line and ratio table support scaling/rate problems; scaling must be treated as multiplicative, not additive.
learnerActions: Study an annotated double number line (kg vs £) and a ratio table with a unit-value column.
Reveal the unitary steps one at a time: 3 kg = £12 → 1 kg = £4 → 5 kg = £20.
Read the ratio table to see the unit column (1 person = 50 g) and how scaled values follow from it.
Use the exemplar as a reference, then solve a new, different rate/scaling problem yourself.
activities.intendedInsight: The unit value is the key column of a ratio table / anchor point of a double number line; scaled values are multiples of it.

activities.title: Checkable practice with additive-error distractors
feedback: For a chosen additive distractor, explain that it adds an amount that does not match the change (e.g. adding 200 g, the amount for 4 people, for only 2 extra people, or adding 2 to the quantity) rather than scaling; show the per-unit route: 50 g per person, so 2 more people need 100 g, giving 300 g.

If division is inverted (e.g. 4 ÷ 200 or 3 kg treated as £3 per kg), prompt labelling units (g per person, £ per kg) to orient the division and check the unit value is reasonable (50 g per person, not 0.02).
activities.rationale: Rate and scaling answers are checkable, so targeted distractors can verify the method and surface the additive and inversion misconceptions. This format is better suited to checking and diagnosing than to first building the proportional feel, so it works best after the interactive and dialogue activities.
learnerActions: Fill in the unitary steps: 3 kg = £12 → 1 kg = □ → 5 kg = □.
Choose the correct recipe-for-6 amount from options that include an additive distractor (e.g. 400 g from 'add 200 g for 2 more people' vs the correct 300 g).
Select the correct multiplier for a scaling problem (e.g. ×6/4 = ×1.5, ×1/2).
Use a slider to set the scaled quantity and check it against the unit value.
activities.intendedInsight: Correct proportional answers come from multiplying the unit value or applying the right fractional multiplier; additive answers are identifiable errors.

constraints: Scaling must be taught as multiplicative (× a fraction or rate), explicitly contrasted with additive 'add the difference' change.
Use both directions — scale up and scale down (×1/2) — and connect fraction-of-quantity skills to scaling.
Include at least one non-integer scale factor (e.g. 4→6, factor 6/4) so learners cannot rely on whole-number multiples; the unit-value route always works.
Ground problems in authentic contexts (recipes, prices, maps/shapes) and check reasonableness of the unit value (e.g. 50 g per person, not 0.02).
This topic is the launchpad for formal ratio and proportion (a separate domain); keep it grounded in known multiplicative-comparison and fraction ideas rather than introducing formal ratio notation.

The worked exemplar and quiz are scaffolds/checks: a fixed image and recognition items cannot by themselves elicit independent solving of new problems, so pair them with activities where the learner constructs the solution.

The 'additive trap' toggle and live sliders are optional devices for making the mechanism concrete; they are illustrative, not mandatory, and manipulation is not asserted to be the only way to learn this.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Self-audit of arithmetic: 200÷4 = 50 g per person, ×6 = 300 g (scale factor 6/4 = 1.5, 200×1.5 = 300) — correct; £12÷3 = £4 per kg, ×5 = £20 — correct. These match the source's correctAnswer.

The source lists an error pattern '200÷4 = 40' as an example of a performance slip; the correct value is 50. It is presented in the source as a learner error, not as a taught fact, so it is not reproduced as correct in any activity.

Two of three cited sources are marked verified:false in the row (CCSS bridge claim and NCETM guidance); the DfE claim is verified:true. No new verification is asserted here. The CCSS bridging claim was not used as a sourceClaim since no activity's rationale depends on it directly.

The DfE curriculum claim is a topic-level claim and was not attached to activities whose rationales turn on the multiplicative/unitary principle (activity 1) or answer-checkability (activity 4); the NCETM claim, which states the teaching principle, is used instead.
The source's artefact-fit note that '3D adds no proportional insight' is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law, and has been omitted rather than asserted as universal.

Activity 4's rationale was softened from a categorical 'verifies rather than builds' to a relative affordance (better suited to checking than to first building the feel) to avoid an unsupported 'quiz only assesses' claim.

probeDeeper: How much flour would ONE person need? How did that help you get to 6?
Someone said '6 people is 2 more than 4, so add 200 g more'. What's wrong with that?
If 3 kg costs £12, what does 1 kg cost — and how do you know?
What if the recipe were for 4 people and you needed it for 10 — would your method still work?
assess.correctAnswer: Flour: 300 g (200 ÷ 4 = 50 g per person, × 6 = 300; or scale factor 6/4 = 1.5, 200 × 1.5). Cost: £20 (£12 ÷ 3 = £4 per kg, × 5 = £20). The teacher watches for a multiplicative route — unit rate or scale factor — not additive 'add 2 more people so add 200 g'.

errorPatterns.pattern: uses additive reasoning instead of multiplicative — '6 is 2 more than 4, so add 200 g' giving 400 g, or 'add £12 again'
errorPatterns.nextMove: set up a ratio table (people | flour) and fill the unit column (1 person = 50 g) so scaling becomes 'per one, then times'; contrast with the wrong additive jump side by side.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child changes the quantity by the DIFFERENCE between the two situations rather than by a ratio

errorPatterns.pattern: finds the unit rate but then multiplies by the wrong quantity, or inverts the division (4 ÷ 200)
errorPatterns.nextMove: label units on every number (g per person) so the division is oriented correctly; check the unit rate is 'reasonable' (50 g per person, not 0.02).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child divides the wrong way (people by grams) or scales by the original count not the target

errorPatterns.pattern: can only scale by whole-number factors — stalls when 6/4 is not a whole multiple of 4
errorPatterns.nextMove: route through the unit value (per one person) which always works, rather than hunting for a whole-number scale factor.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child solves 3→6 (×2) confidently but freezes on 4→6

errorPatterns.pattern: sets up the proportion correctly but slips in the arithmetic (200÷4 = 40)
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach proportion; have the child check the unit rate against the original (50 × 4 = 200?).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: correct method, wrong division/multiplication result

responseLevels.gap: scales additively (adds the difference) or inverts the rate; answer bears no multiplicative relationship to the given values.
responseLevels.full: routes reliably through unit rate or scale factor for both integer and non-integer cases, orients the division by units, and rejects additive scaling with a reason.
responseLevels.partial: solves whole-number-multiple cases (3→6) by scaling but stalls on non-integer factors (4→6), or finds a unit rate inconsistently.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child rate/scaling problems to solve, watching their method: 'A recipe for 4 people needs 200 g of flour — how much for 6 people?' and 'If 3 kg costs £12, how much does 5 kg cost?' Watch whether they find a unit value or a scale factor, or whether they just add on a difference.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The signature error in proportional reasoning is additive: '4→6 people is +2, so +2 of something'. Watching the method (unit rate vs adding a constant) reveals whether the child reasons multiplicatively. The non-integer scale factor (6/4) also catches children who can only scale by whole numbers.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Scale and similar shapes
topic.description: Solve problems involving similar shapes where the scale factor is known or can be found
evidence: Find the missing side of a similar rectangle given a scale factor of 3
Determine the scale factor between two similar triangles from given side lengths
Use a scale factor to enlarge or reduce a shape and verify that all sides are in the same ratio
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has a scale drawing where 1 cm represents 5 m, and a room measures 3.5 cm on the plan, can they work out the real length of the room?

pedagogy.summary: Two shapes are SIMILAR when one is a scaled copy of the other: corresponding angles are equal and every pair of corresponding sides is in the SAME ratio (the scale factor). Solving similar-shape problems means (1) finding the scale factor from a known pair of corresponding sides, then (2) multiplying (to enlarge) or dividing (to reduce) the other sides by it. The pedagogical crux is that enlargement is MULTIPLICATIVE, not additive: every side is multiplied by the SAME factor, so the shape keeps its proportions. Children must resist adding a constant to each side (which distorts the shape) and, when area comes in, must learn that a length scale factor k multiplies AREA by k².
bestPractices: Establish 'same shape, sides in the same ratio, equal angles' as the definition of similar before any calculation; contrast a genuine enlargement with a stretched (distorted) copy.
Find the scale factor first from a matched pair of corresponding sides (new ÷ old), then apply it to every other side — make 'multiply by the SAME number' explicit.

Confront the additive error directly: show that adding the same amount to each side changes the shape (a 2×5 rectangle + 4 to each side is 6×9, no longer similar), whereas multiplying keeps it similar.
When perimeter/area appear, build the k² result from a diagram: doubling the sides of a rectangle makes FOUR copies fit inside, so area ×4 not ×2 (MAP Enlargements).
Use a ratio table / double number line pairing corresponding sides so the constant multiplier is visible across all pairs.
keyRepresentations: Ratio table pairing corresponding sides (old side | new side), scale factor as the column multiplier
Overlaid/nested shapes on a grid showing the enlargement from a centre
Area grid showing k² tiling (double sides → four sub-rectangles)
The scale-factor arrow (×k) applied to every corresponding side
commonMisconceptions: Additive enlargement — adding the same amount to each side instead of multiplying by the scale factor (distorts the shape; the classic Hart/CSMS rectangle error).
Treating 'similar' as 'roughly the same shape' or as 'congruent/identical', not checking that all sides share one ratio.
Believing that doubling the lengths doubles the area (area actually scales by k²; MAP Enlargements documents this as a persistent error).
Applying the scale factor to only one side, or using new÷old for one pair and old÷new for another (inconsistent direction).

learn.summary: Similar shapes are scaled copies: corresponding angles are equal and every pair of corresponding sides shares one ratio (the scale factor). Learners find the scale factor from a known matched pair (new ÷ old), then multiply the other sides by that same factor (a factor greater than 1 enlarges; a factor less than 1, such as 1/3, reduces — equivalently, when reducing you can divide by the enlargement factor). The pedagogical crux is that enlargement is MULTIPLICATIVE, not additive — adding a constant to each side generally distorts the shape (e.g. any non-square rectangle; a square or equilateral triangle is an exception) — and that a length scale factor k scales area by k² (and volume by k³ for solids).

activities.title: Enlargement studio: grab, scale, and compare with additive mode
feedback: If you scaled only one side: ask whether the new shape is still the same shape — overlay it and check that EVERY corresponding side grew by the same multiplier.

If additive mode looked 'about right', overlay it on the original's diagonal: a true enlargement stays on the diagonal; the additive copy of a non-square rectangle slides off it, showing distorted proportions.
When you predicted area, compare your guess with the tiled count: doubling sides gives four tiles (×4), tripling gives nine (×9) — area follows k².
activities.rationale: Live manipulation with a locked aspect ratio plus a contrasting additive mode may make the multiplicative nature of enlargement observable, so the documented additive error becomes visible rather than merely asserted. The tiling overlay builds the k² area result from a concrete diagram. The additive mode, ratio table, diagonal check and tiling overlay are optional illustrative mechanisms, not the only way to teach this.
sourceClaims: Students apply inappropriate ADDITIVE strategies to multiplicative scaling situations (adding a constant rather than multiplying by a scale factor) — a documented error in proportional-reasoning classroom trials.

Doubling the length and width of a rectangle multiplies its area by 4, not 2; for similar shapes the area scale factor is the square of the scale factor (k²) and the volume scale factor is k³ — documented as a persistent student misconception (treating price/area as scaling linearly).
learnerActions: Work on a grid with a non-square rectangle or triangle whose aspect ratio is locked. Drag a corner to enlarge it and watch a live scale-factor readout while every side multiplies by the same factor and the angles stay unchanged; for a rectangle enlarged from a fixed corner, notice the dragged opposite corner moves along the original's diagonal, showing it is the same shape.
Fill a ratio table alongside (old side | new side for each pair) and check that the same column multiplier appears for every pair of corresponding sides.

Flip to an 'additive mode' that instead ADDS your chosen number to each side of the non-square rectangle; observe it stretch lopsided and fall off the original's diagonal — it is no longer similar. Compare directly with the multiplicative result.
Turn on a grid-tiling overlay: with a scale factor of 2, see FOUR copies of the original tile the new shape; with a factor of 3, nine copies fit — connect this to area × k².
If a scaling touches only one side, use the flag that highlights the unchanged side and correct it so every corresponding side is scaled.
activities.intendedInsight: Enlargement multiplies every corresponding side by the SAME factor, preserving shape and angles; adding the same amount to each side of a non-square rectangle distorts it. Because the shape grows in two dimensions, area scales by k², not by k.

activities.title: Confront the additive error on paper
feedback: Compare the two ratios as numbers: 6/9 (= 2/3) does not equal 2/5, so the additive version is not a true enlargement.
If unsure, draw both shapes to scale and overlay a corner — the similar one nests exactly along the diagonal.
activities.rationale: Explicitly performing and comparing the additive versus multiplicative transformation targets the classic Hart/CSMS rectangle error. Worked on paper this needs no device and makes the ratio check the decider.
sourceClaims: Students apply inappropriate ADDITIVE strategies to multiplicative scaling situations (adding a constant rather than multiplying by a scale factor) — a documented error in proportional-reasoning classroom trials.
learnerActions: Take a 2×5 rectangle. Add 4 to each side to get a 6×9 rectangle, and draw both. Check whether the side ratios match: 2:5 versus 6:9 — they do not, so the shapes are not similar.
Now enlarge the same 2×5 rectangle by a scale factor, multiplying each side by 3 to get 6×15, and confirm 2:5 and 6:15 are the same ratio.
State in your own words why 'add the same to each side' changes the shape while 'multiply each side by the same number' keeps it.
activities.intendedInsight: Adding a constant to every side changed the proportions of the 2×5 rectangle (as it does for any non-square rectangle); multiplying every side by a common factor always keeps corresponding sides in a single ratio and preserves the shape.

activities.title: Solve and judge similar-shape problems
feedback: If you wrote 21, you added the 12 difference; instead find the factor (×3) and apply it — the correct missing side is 27 cm.
If you said the area is 3× bigger, tile it: a factor of 3 fits nine copies, so area is ×9 (54 → 486 cm²).

On a reduction, sense-check direction: the answer should be SMALLER than the side you began with, so divide by the enlargement factor (e.g. ÷3) or, equivalently, multiply by the new ÷ old factor (e.g. ×1/3).
Keep new ÷ old consistent — do not use new ÷ old for one pair and old ÷ new for another.
activities.rationale: These items make the scale factor, the additive distractor, the direction-of-application slip and the area-scaling error separately assessable. Watching the working (e.g. 27 via ×3 versus 21 via +12) reveals which strategy a learner used; recognition items alone would not elicit this production. Pair it with the manipulation activities so the rule is understood, not just recognised.
sourceClaims: Pupils should solve problems involving similar shapes where the scale factor is known or can be found (Year 6 ratio and proportion).

Doubling the length and width of a rectangle multiplies its area by 4, not 2; for similar shapes the area scale factor is the square of the scale factor (k²) and the volume scale factor is k³ — documented as a persistent student misconception (treating price/area as scaling linearly).
learnerActions: Given a rectangle 6×9 enlarged so 6→18, find the scale factor (18 ÷ 6 = 3) and the missing side (9 × 3 = 27 cm). Beware of adding the difference 12 to get 21 — that is the additive error, not a valid answer.
Find the scale factor between two similar triangles from a matched pair of side lengths, keeping new ÷ old consistent for the comparison.

Judge whether two given shapes are similar by testing EVERY pair of corresponding sides for the same ratio, not by appearance, and by checking that corresponding angles are equal (for triangles, matching side ratios are enough; for other polygons they are not, e.g. a square and a non-square rhombus). One mismatched ratio means not similar.

For a REDUCTION (e.g. 18 back to 6), decide first whether the answer should be bigger or smaller than the side you start from; then divide by the enlargement factor (÷3), which is the same as multiplying by the new ÷ old factor (6 ÷ 18 = 1/3).
On an area follow-up for the 6×9→18×27 rectangle, reason that area scales by k² = 3² = 9 (54 cm² → 486 cm²), not by 3.
activities.intendedInsight: Problem solving means finding the scale factor from a known pair, applying it in the correct direction to every side, checking similarity by shared ratio, and using k² for area.

activities.title: Optional extension: scaling a solid to feel k² and k³
feedback: If you expected volume to double when edges double, count the unit cubes: eight small cubes fit, so volume is ×8 (2³).
Keep the core objective in view — this 3D view is an extension beyond the 2D similar-shapes task.
activities.rationale: A solid-scaling sandbox may give a concrete feel for how area and volume grow with dimension, complementing the 2D work. This is explicitly optional and exceeds the stated 2D objective; it should not replace the primary 2D activities.
sourceClaims: Doubling the length and width of a rectangle multiplies its area by 4, not 2; for similar shapes the area scale factor is the square of the scale factor (k²) and the volume scale factor is k³ — documented as a persistent student misconception (treating price/area as scaling linearly).
learnerActions: Enlarge a cube or cuboid with a slider and watch surface area grow by k² and volume by k³.
Fill the enlarged solid with unit cubes to count that doubling every edge of a cube gives 2³ = 8 times the volume, and relate the growing faces to k² area.
Return to a flat similar-shapes problem and restate: length ×k, area ×k², and for solids volume ×k³.
activities.intendedInsight: Scaling length by k scales area by k² and, for solids, volume by k³ — the same multiplicative idea extended by dimension.

constraints: Establish the definition — same shape, equal angles, ALL corresponding sides in one ratio — and contrast a true enlargement with a stretched copy BEFORE any calculation.
Find the scale factor first from a matched pair (new ÷ old), then apply the SAME factor to every other side; make 'multiply by the same number' explicit.

A static nested-shapes diagram with tap-to-reveal '×k per side' and 'area ×k²' can consolidate the rule as a reference card, but does not let the learner manipulate and watch the additive distortion occur; use it after, not instead of, hands-on work.

Multiple-choice/recognition items (e.g. choosing which pair is similar) assess discrimination but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction of finding and applying a scale factor; include fill-in and show-your-working tasks for production.
Keep the direction of division consistent (new ÷ old) within a comparison, and sense-check whether the answer should be larger or smaller before computing.
The 3D solid-scaling activity is an optional extension that goes beyond the 2D similar-shapes objective and must not be the main teaching artefact.

Illustrative interface features (locked aspect ratio, live scale-factor readout, additive-mode toggle, diagonal check, tiling overlay, ratio table, single-side flag) are examples of the learning mechanism, not mandatory requirements.

The additive-mode distortion demonstration should use a non-square rectangle, since a square keeps its shape under equal additions; present the additive result (e.g. 21) only as a flagged error, never as a valid answer option.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support the underlying principle, not the specific activity designs.

Self-audit (arithmetic/logic): 18 ÷ 6 = 3 and 9 × 3 = 27 are correct; the additive distractor 21 comes from 9 + 12 where 12 = 18 − 6. For a scale factor of 3, nine copies tile the area (3² = 9) and area 6×9 = 54 cm² becomes 486 cm² (18×27=486=54×9). Volume for a doubled edge is 2³ = 8, correct. In Activity 2, 2+4=6 and 5+4=9 (additive, not similar: 2/5≠2/3); 2×3=6 and 5×3=15 (multiplicative, similar: 2/5=6/15).

The original design used a scale-factor-2 tiling example showing FOUR copies (2²=4), while the worked problem uses factor 3 giving nine copies (3²=9); both are internally consistent and kept distinct to avoid conflating the example with the problem.

Activity 1 keeps the enlargement studio's aspect ratio locked; otherwise a free corner-drag would change width and height independently and distort the shape, contradicting the same-factor/angle-preserving behaviour.

The additive-mode 'falls off the diagonal' behaviour holds for non-square rectangles; a square would remain similar under equal additions, so the demonstration is scoped to non-square cases and treated as an illustrative affordance, not an invariant law.

The original artefact framing asserted a conversation 'cannot exercise' the skill and that 3D 'overshoots'; these are softened to scoped limits (in-role dialogue is a poor fit for this spatial-procedural practice; 3D is an optional extension) rather than universal pedagogical laws.

The double-number-line representation from the original was folded into the ratio-table scaffold rather than dropped; centre-of-enlargement detail was not emphasised as it exceeds the stated scale-factor objective.

probeDeeper: Is your enlarged rectangle the SAME shape as the original — how could you check that all the sides grew in the same way?
What is the scale factor here, and what does it mean to say the sides are 'in the same ratio'?
Now think about AREA: the original is 6×9 = 54 cm². What is the area of the enlarged one — is it 3 times bigger? (counterexample forcing the k² idea: it is 9 times bigger.)
If instead I SHRANK the rectangle so the 18 went back to 6, what would you do to the other side — multiply or divide, and by what?
assess.correctAnswer: 27 cm. The scale factor is 18 ÷ 6 = 3, so every side is multiplied by 3: the 9 cm side becomes 9 × 3 = 27 cm.

errorPatterns.pattern: Additive enlargement — adds the constant difference (here +12) to each side instead of multiplying by the scale factor
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'is the new rectangle the SAME shape as the old one?' Draw both and overlay — the additive version is distorted. Rebuild on a ratio table: every side ×3. Reteach multiplicative missing-value ratio.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 9 + 12 = 21, having taken the 18−6 = 12 increase from the known side and added it to the other; no scale factor computed

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats 'similar' as 'roughly the same shape' or 'congruent', not checking that all sides share one ratio
errorPatterns.nextMove: Restate the definition: same shape, equal angles, ALL sides in the same ratio. Test each side pair — one mismatched ratio means not similar. Reteach the vocabulary of ratio/proportion/scale.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When judging whether two given shapes are similar, decides on appearance ('they both look like rectangles') without comparing side ratios, or assumes similar means identical

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes doubling the lengths doubles the area (ignores that area scales by the square of the scale factor)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Tile the enlarged rectangle with copies of the original on a grid — a scale factor of 3 fits 9 copies. Establish length ×k → area ×k². Reteach area of rectangles.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On an area follow-up, says the enlarged rectangle's area is 3× (or 2×) the original instead of 3² = 9×; treats area like a length

errorPatterns.pattern: Finds the scale factor correctly but applies it in the wrong direction (multiplies when reducing, or divides when enlarging)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: ask 'is the answer meant to be bigger or smaller than the side you started from?' before computing, as a sense-check on the direction.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computes the factor as 3 but on a REDUCTION problem multiplies anyway, giving a bigger shape when it should be smaller

responseLevels.gap: Adds the constant difference to the other side (21), or judges similarity by appearance; does not find or apply a scale factor.
responseLevels.full: Finds the scale factor (×3), applies it to give 27, explains that all corresponding sides share that ratio so the shape is preserved, correctly reasons that area scales by k² (×9), and handles a reduction by dividing — transferring the method to an unfamiliar shape.
responseLevels.partial: Finds the scale factor and the missing side correctly for lengths, but slips on area (says ×3 not ×9) or cannot reliably judge whether two new shapes are similar — the multiplicative rule is not yet secure across cases.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a rectangle 6 cm by 9 cm. I enlarge it so the 6 cm side becomes 18 cm, and the new rectangle is similar to the old one. Work out the length of the other side. Show your working.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child reasoning multiplicatively finds the scale factor (×3) and applies it to the other side, giving 27 — a value only that method produces. A child using the additive strategy sees the 6→18 side grew by 12 and adds 12 to the other side, giving 21. The two children produce different numbers by different routes, and watching the working (not asking them to state a rule) shows immediately which they used.

topic.name: Scale drawings and maps
topic.description: Use a scale, given as a ratio (e.g. 1:50), as a statement such as '1 cm represents 2 m', or as a scale factor, to work out actual lengths from a scale drawing or map and drawing lengths from actual lengths; reproduce a scale drawing at a different scale by finding each new drawing length, either through the actual length or from the ratio of the two scales; and solve map, room-plan and design problems with consistent units, converting between mm, cm, m and km before or after scaling. evidence: On a 1:50 room plan, find that a 9 cm wall is 450 cm = 4.5 m long, and that a 1.2 m doorway should be drawn 2.4 cm wide

pedagogy.summary: A scale diagram or map represents real distances by a fixed multiplicative scale, written as a ratio like 1:25000 (1 unit on the map = 25000 of the same units in real life). Fluency means (1) reading the scale as a pure multiplier, (2) going the right way — MULTIPLY a map measurement to get the real distance, DIVIDE a real distance to get the map measurement — and (3) converting units so the answer is sensible (1:25000 gives cm → cm, then convert to m or km). The two recurring hazards are direction (multiplying vs dividing) and the unit conversion buried in the scale; both are procedural and best caught by a magnitude sense-check ('should the real distance be far bigger?').
bestPractices: Read the scale ratio aloud as 'one centimetre on the map is 25000 centimetres in real life' so the shared unit and the multiplier are explicit before any arithmetic.
Establish the direction rule with a sense-check: real life is bigger, so map→real MULTIPLY, real→map DIVIDE; estimate the size of the answer first.
Do the unit conversion as a deliberate final step (cm → m ÷100 → km ÷1000), tracking units, rather than leaving an answer in centimetres.
Have pupils both READ a map (find a real distance) and CREATE a scale diagram (draw a room to a chosen scale), so the divide-direction is practised, not just the multiply-direction.
Use a double number line pairing map-cm with real-distance to keep the proportional relationship visible.
keyRepresentations: Scale ratio 1:n read as 'one unit = n units'
Double number line / ratio table (map distance | real distance)
Scale bar on the map for direct measure-and-read
Unit-conversion chain cm → m → km as an explicit final step
commonMisconceptions: Forgetting the unit conversion — leaving the real distance in centimetres (200000 cm) instead of converting to metres/kilometres, or converting with the wrong factor.
Going the wrong direction — dividing a map measurement instead of multiplying (or vice versa), producing a real distance smaller than the map one.
Misreading the ratio — treating 1:25000 additively, or reading it as '1 cm = 25000 km' (unit slip).
Applying the scale to only part of the problem, or mixing map units and real units without a common basis.

learn.summary: Learners work with scale on maps and diagrams, reading a ratio such as 1:25000 as a same-unit multiplier (1 cm on the map = 25000 cm in real life). The two recurring hazards are direction (multiply map→real, divide real→map) and the unit conversion buried in the scale (cm → m → km). Both are best caught with a magnitude sense-check and are practised in BOTH directions — reading a real distance off a map AND creating a scale diagram of a room.

activities.title: Measure, scale and convert on a map
feedback: If the working stops at 200000 and cm: 'That's the real distance in centimetres — now convert. How many centimetres are in a metre? In a kilometre? Walk the cm → m → km chain.'
If the real distance comes out tiny (e.g. 0.00032): 'Which is bigger, the map or real life? If the map is smaller, map→real should MULTIPLY, not divide. Re-estimate the size first.'

If the ratio was read as '1 cm = 25000 km': 'The 25000 is in the same unit as the 1, so both are centimetres. Keep the units the same while you scale, then convert carefully, for example by multiplying first and then converting cm to m to km.'

If arithmetic slips (e.g. 20000 or 2000000, or ÷10 instead of ÷100): 'Your method is right — estimate the order of magnitude first (hundreds of thousands of cm, a couple of km) and check your answer against it.'
activities.rationale: Direction and unit conversion are procedural hazards; reading the ratio aloud, estimating magnitude, and tracking units through an explicit conversion chain target both directly. A double number line or ratio table pairing map-cm with real distance can keep the proportional relationship visible.
sourceClaims: Pupils should use scale factors, scale diagrams and maps (e.g. a scale such as 1:25000), interpreting and creating scale drawings and solving problems involving proportional reasoning and metric units.
Students apply inappropriate additive strategies to multiplicative scaling situations, so scaling must be taught as a consistent multiplier applied in the correct direction.
learnerActions: Read the scale ratio aloud before calculating, e.g. 'one centimetre on the map is 25000 centimetres in real life' — emphasise that both sides share the SAME unit.

Measure the map distance between two points (e.g. two villages 8 cm apart on a 1:25000 map). Optionally, drag a ruler on a map and use a live panel that unfolds measured map-cm, multiplication by25000, then the cm-to-m-to-km conversion, with the scale bar alongside for checking.
Before calculating, estimate: real life is bigger than the map, so map→real MUST multiply — predict roughly how big the real distance should be.
Do the unit conversion as a deliberate final step, tracking units: 200000 cm ÷ 100 = 2000 m, then ÷ 1000 = 2 km.
Apply the scale to the whole measurement, keeping both quantities in a common unit — do not scale only part of the problem.
Cross-check against the scale bar on the map and against your estimate: is 2 km between villages sensible?
activities.intendedInsight: Scale is a consistent multiplier: going from a map measurement to the real distance means multiplying by the scale denominator for this reduced map; the reverse means dividing. Track the units at each step and express the answer in the units requested, here kilometres.

activities.title: Draw a room to scale (the divide direction)
feedback: If the drawn room balloons far larger than the reference doorway: 'A scale drawing is smaller than reality — you multiplied where you should divide. Real→map means DIVIDE by the scale factor.'
If the learner forgets to convert m to cm before dividing: 'Get both lengths into the same unit first (4 m = 400 cm), then divide by 100.'
If correct: 'Your 4 cm line represents a 4 m wall — explain how you'd go the other way, from the drawing back to the real wall.'
activities.rationale: Practising the divide-direction, not just the multiply-direction, prevents a one-directional, insecure procedure. Laying out against a known reference provides an immediate, concrete magnitude check.
sourceClaims: Interpreting and using scale drawings is a proportional-reasoning task requiring metric-unit work; a formative lesson is built around planning a layout to scale.

Pupils should use scale factors, scale diagrams and maps (e.g. a scale such as 1:25000), interpreting and creating scale drawings and solving problems involving proportional reasoning and metric units.
learnerActions: Choose a scale (e.g. 1:100) for drawing your own bedroom.
For each real wall length, work out the line to draw: divide the real length by the scale factor (e.g. a 4 m wall at 1:100 → 4 m = 400 cm, 400 ÷ 100 = 4 cm on the diagram).
Draw the walls at the computed lengths and compare the result against a reference object of known size (e.g. a doorway) to sanity-check.
Say aloud why this is a divide: 'the diagram is smaller than real life, so real→map DIVIDES.'

Check: if the drawn room looks absurdly large, you probably multiplied instead of dividing, so revisit the direction rule. If it shrinks to a dot, check your units. For example, dividing 4 m by 100 without first converting to centimetres gives 0.04, which is far too small to draw.
activities.intendedInsight: Going from real distances to a scale drawing requires dividing by the scale factor; seeing the room come out the wrong SIZE against a familiar reference makes the direction error concrete.

activities.title: Direction and conversion practice with sharp distractors
feedback: If 200000 is chosen: 'That is the real distance in centimetres — the question asked for kilometres. Convert cm → m → km.'
If 0.00032 is chosen: 'You divided; real life is bigger than the map, so map→real multiplies.'
If the wrong direction is picked for drawing: 'A drawing is smaller than reality, so real→map divides.'
activities.rationale: Items with error-patterned options can surface whether learners spot direction and conversion mistakes; this is a check that reinforces the correct-direction multiplier. It does not by itself elicit the independent construction of a scale drawing, which requires learners to compute and draw the lines themselves in the tasks above.
sourceClaims: Students apply inappropriate additive strategies to multiplicative scaling situations, so scaling must be taught as a consistent multiplier applied in the correct direction.
learnerActions: Answer targeted items such as: '8 cm on a 1:25000 map → ___ km' (correct: 2 km).
Identify and reject the error value 200000 (the real distance left unconverted, in cm).
Identify and reject the error value ≈0.00032 (the result of dividing instead of multiplying).
Decide which operation (multiply or divide) applies when drawing a room to scale versus reading a real distance.
Choose a sensible scale for a given object and justify it.
activities.intendedInsight: The common errors — leaving the answer in cm, and dividing instead of multiplying — produce predictably wrong magnitudes that a sense-check would have caught.

activities.title: Annotated map reference card
feedback: Prompt the learner to restate: 'Does 1:25000 mean 1 cm = 25000 cm = 250 m? Why not 25000 km?'
activities.rationale: A static annotated map consolidates reading and the conversion chain, but it does not let the learner measure a distance of their own choosing or draw to scale — so it supports, rather than replaces, the measuring and drawing tasks.
learnerActions: Reveal the scale meaning on a worked map, e.g. 'one cm here = 250 m out there' (for a 1:25000 map, 25000 cm = 250 m).
Follow a worked real-distance calculation between two named towns, with each conversion step shown.
Use the scale bar directly to cross-check a distance.
activities.intendedInsight: The reading of a scale and its worked conversion can be consolidated as a reference, reinforcing the same-unit meaning of the ratio.

constraints: Practise BOTH directions: reading a real distance from a map (multiply) AND creating a scale diagram (divide). A procedure learned in only one direction is not yet secure.

For real-distance questions requesting kilometres, show the explicit conversion chain with units (cm to m: divide by100; m to km: divide by1000). Do not stop at an unconverted centimetre value for those questions. Scale-drawing lengths may appropriately be given in centimetres.
Read the ratio as a same-unit multiplier — both sides of 1:25000 are the same unit — to block additive readings and unit slips like '1 cm = 25000 km'.
Apply the scale consistently to the whole measurement, keeping map and real quantities on a common-unit basis; do not scale only part of a problem.

The annotated/reference map is a scaffold for reading and consolidation; it cannot provide practice in measuring a self-chosen distance or in drawing to scale, so it should not be the primary teaching activity.

Recognition/multiple-choice items check whether errors are spotted; they do not elicit the independent construction of a scale drawing, which requires the learner to compute and draw the lines themselves.

A live-computing map tool and interactive layout are optional means to make the measure-scale-convert and divide-direction feedback immediate; the same learning can be reached with a paper map, ruler, scale bar and squared paper.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic checked: 8 × 25000 = 200000 cm; ÷100 = 2000 m; ÷1000 = 2 km. The dividing value 8 ÷ 25000 ≈ 0.00032 and the unconverted 200000 cm are consistent with the stated error patterns. A 4 m wall at 1:100 → 400 cm ÷ 100 = 4 cm line, matching the probe counterexample. For 1:25000, 25000 cm = 250 m, so 'one cm here = 250 m out there' is correct.

The original misconception 'applying the scale to only part of the problem, or mixing map units and real units without a common basis' is represented via the same-unit reading plus a whole-measurement constraint and learner action, rather than a dedicated activity.

The recognition-item rationale's point that such items are a 'check, not a substitute' is an unvalidated design observation about the affordance of recognition items, not a source-backed finding; the attached source supports only the correct-direction multiplier principle the distractors probe.

The original marked 'conversation' and '3D' as poor fit with reasoning that they 'add nothing'; this is a catalog ranking, not an established pedagogical law, so it was not propagated as a universal claim. The planar nature of maps is retained only as a neutral observation about this specific task.

probeDeeper: Which is bigger — the distance on the map or the real distance? So should you multiply or divide? Does your answer fit that?
What does the '25000' in 1:25000 actually mean — 25000 of what?
Now go the other way: your bedroom wall is 4 m long and you want to draw it at 1:100 — how long is the line on your diagram? (counterexample forcing the divide-direction: 4 cm.)
Your answer is in centimetres — talk me through turning it into kilometres. How many centimetres are in a kilometre?
assess.correctAnswer: 2 km. Real distance = 8 × 25000 = 200000 cm; convert: 200000 ÷ 100 = 2000 m, then ÷ 1000 = 2 km.

errorPatterns.pattern: Forgets the unit conversion — leaves the answer as 200000 (cm) or fails to reach km, or converts with the wrong factor
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do the conversion as an explicit final step with units tracked: cm ÷100 → m ÷1000 → km. Sense-check: 2 km between villages is reasonable; 200000 km is not. Reteach unit conversion.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 8 × 25000 = 200000 and stops, or gives '200000 km' / '2000 km' having muddled the cm→m→km chain

errorPatterns.pattern: Goes the wrong direction — divides the map measurement by 25000 instead of multiplying (treats the map as bigger than reality)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor the sense-check first: real life is far bigger than the map, so map→real MUST multiply. Estimate the answer's size before calculating. Reteach the scale-factor direction from similar shapes.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 8 ÷ 25000 (≈ 0.00032) and reports a tiny real distance, or on a draw-to-scale task multiplies when they should divide

errorPatterns.pattern: Misreads the ratio 1:25000 — reads it additively, or as '1 cm = 25000 km', or ignores that both sides share a unit
errorPatterns.nextMove: Read the ratio aloud: '1 cm on the map = 25000 cm in real life' — SAME unit both sides. Only after multiplying do you convert. Reteach the precise meaning of scale factor / ratio notation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Adds 25000, or converts 8 cm to 200000 km directly, treating the 25000 as already in kilometres

errorPatterns.pattern: Correct method but a place-value / arithmetic slip in the ×25000 or the conversion
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: have them estimate the order of magnitude first (≈ hundreds of thousands of cm ≈ a couple of km) and check the answer against it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sets up 8 × 25000 correctly but writes 20000 or 2000000, or divides by 10 instead of 100 in the cm→m step

responseLevels.gap: Divides the wrong way, or leaves the answer in centimetres, or misreads the ratio; cannot produce a sensible real distance in km.
responseLevels.full: Multiplies 8 × 25000 and converts cleanly to 2 km, explains that real life is bigger so map→real multiplies (and real→map divides), reads the ratio as a same-unit multiplier, and transfers to drawing a scale diagram of a room.
responseLevels.partial: Multiplies correctly to 200000 cm but stumbles on the unit conversion (wrong factor or stops at cm), or can do map→real but not the reverse (real→map) — the procedure is one-directional and not yet secure on units.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: On a map with scale 1:25000, two villages are 8 cm apart. Work out the real distance between them, and give your answer in kilometres. Show your working.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A pupil who understands both the direction (map→real multiplies) and the unit conversion reaches 2 km — a value only that full chain produces. Watching the working exposes exactly where a pupil stops: at 200000 (no conversion), at a tiny number (divided the wrong way), or at a wrong magnitude (bad conversion factor). Because the answer is demanded in km, the unit step cannot be skipped unnoticed.

topic.name: Compound Units
topic.description: Use compound units such as speed (distance ÷ time), unit pricing (cost ÷ quantity), and density (mass ÷ volume); solve problems involving compound units
evidence: Calculate average speed given distance and time, converting between km/h and m/s if needed

topic.assessmentPrompt: If a car travels 150 miles in 2.5 hours, can {{name}} work out its average speed — and use the same idea to solve problems about price per kilogram or density of a material?

pedagogy.summary: Compound units measure one quantity PER another — speed (distance per time), density (mass per volume), unit price (cost per gram/item), flow rate. Fluency means (1) computing the rate by dividing the right way round, (2) using the rate to scale up or down and to compare (best-buy, faster-of-two), and (3) converting units correctly, including two-stage conversions like km/h ↔ m/s. The recurring procedural trap is average speed: it is TOTAL distance ÷ TOTAL time, NOT the mean of two speeds. Teaching should build the rate from a double number line or ratio table so 'per one' is visible, and treat the formula triangle with caution because it lets pupils get answers without proportional understanding.
bestPractices: Derive every compound measure as a UNIT RATE first ('how much for exactly one?') using a double number line or ratio table, before any formula.
For best-buy comparisons, insist on a common basis — cost per 100 g for both products — rather than comparing raw price to raw size.
Teach average speed as total distance ÷ total time by working a two-leg journey where the naive mean-of-the-two-speeds answer is demonstrably wrong.
Do km/h↔m/s as a deliberate two-step chain (×1000 m per km, ÷3600 s per hour) with units tracked through each step, not a memorised single factor.
Prefer double number lines / ratio tables over the formula 'magic triangle', which can block proportional reasoning by reducing it to symbol-shuffling (NCETM).
keyRepresentations: Double number line pairing the two quantities (e.g. km against hours, cost against grams)
Ratio table for scaling a rate up and down and for unit conversion
Unit-rate label ('£ per 100 g', 'm per s') as the object of comparison
Distance–time context for average speed (total over total)
commonMisconceptions: Averaging two speeds directly (60 and 40 → '50') instead of using total distance ÷ total time.
Dividing the wrong way round when forming a rate (time ÷ distance for speed, or cost basis inverted).
Comparing unit prices on different bases (price of the big pack vs unit price of the small) and concluding the cheaper total is the better value.
Botching km/h↔m/s by using a single wrong factor (e.g. ×60 or ÷60) instead of the ×1000÷3600 chain.
Treating the formula triangle as the concept — getting a number without knowing whether it should be bigger or smaller.

learn.summary: Compound units measure one quantity PER another: speed (distance per time), density (mass per volume), unit price (cost per gram/item), flow rate. Fluency means (1) computing the rate by dividing the right way round, (2) using the rate to scale up/down and to compare (best-buy, faster-of-two), and (3) converting units correctly, including two-stage chains like km/h↔m/s. The recurring trap is average speed: it is TOTAL distance ÷ TOTAL time, not the mean of two speeds. Build every rate as a visible 'per one' using a double number line or ratio table before any formula, and treat the formula triangle cautiously because it can reduce proportional reasoning to symbol-shuffling. The activities below span an interactive rate workshop, a paper performance task, a short check, and a consolidation reference card, each with a distinct purpose.

activities.title: Rate workshop: best-buy, two-leg journey, and km/h↔m/s converter
feedback: If the pupil writes (60+40)÷2 = 50, show the two leg times (1 h vs 1.5 h) and ask which speed the cyclist spent more time at; more time at 40 pulls the average below 50. Rebuild on a double number line, total over total.

If a division is done the wrong way round (e.g. 40÷60 instead of 60÷40 for the time of a 60 km leg at 40 km/h, or size÷price for a unit price), anchor 'per one': 40 km/h means 40 km in ONE hour, so 60 km takes 60÷40 = 1.5 h. Track units so km ÷ km/h leaves hours. For a unit price, cost goes on top so the result is £ per g (or per item), not g per £.
If the converter uses a single ×60 or ÷60, redo the chain as two labelled steps with units cancelling, and apply the magnitude check (36 km/h ≈ 10 m/s).
If best-buy is decided on total price or pack size, require both products as cost per 100 g (or per item) first; only same-basis figures are comparable.
When the prediction '50' differs from the computed 48, name the gap as the insight: equal distances covered at unequal speeds cannot be averaged by taking the mean of the speeds.
activities.rationale: Compound measures are procedural and comparative, so the learner should perform the rate calculation and get immediate feedback on best-buy, faster-of-two, and unit conversion, with a double number line that recomputes as they scale. Deriving the unit rate first and comparing on a common basis follows guidance to secure the meaning of 'per' and reason multiplicatively via the unit rate. A recomputing double number line, drag-onto-shared-line, a plotted distance-time graph, and on-screen unit cancelling are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory features.
sourceClaims: KS3 Ratio, proportion and rates of change requires pupils to 'use compound units such as speed, unit pricing and density to solve problems' and to 'change freely between related standard units'; KS4 adds 'convert between related compound units (speed, rates of pay, prices, density, pressure) in numerical and algebraic contexts'.

NCETM treats compound measures (speed = distance÷time, density = mass÷volume) as multiplicative comparisons and names as a common misconception that 'compound measures are different from other forms of proportional relationship' when they follow the same multiplicative rules; it stresses securing the meaning of 'per', recommends double number lines and ratio tables, and raises formula triangles as a practice to scrutinise for whether they promote understanding.
Reasoning about rate multiplicatively via unit rate (per one) rather than additively underpins best-buy and speed comparisons.
learnerActions: Best-buy station: compare two shelf tags (e.g. 400 g for £1.80 vs 250 g for £1.20). Put both onto a shared 'cost per 100 g' line and state which is cheaper.
Two-leg journey station: assemble a journey of 60 km at 60 km/h then 60 km at 40 km/h, and — before doing any arithmetic — predict the average speed for the whole journey.

Now compute it: write down the time each leg takes (60÷60 = 1 h and 60÷40 = 1.5 h), then total distance (120 km) and total time (2.5 h), then average speed (120 ÷ 2.5 = 48 km/h). Compare this with your prediction and explain the gap.
Converter station: turn a km/h figure into m/s as two visible steps — ×1000 (km→m), then ÷3600 (per hour→per second) — tracking units so they cancel on screen.
Sanity-check magnitude: 36 km/h should come out as about 10 m/s — a fast cycling/sprinting pace, well above a walk — not 0.6 or 600.
activities.intendedInsight: A rate is 'how much for exactly one', computed by dividing the right way round; average speed is total distance ÷ total time (not the mean of speeds) because more time spent at the slower speed pulls the average down; conversions are a tracked chain, not a single memorised factor; and fair comparisons need a common per-unit basis.

activities.title: Average-speed performance task: work the journey on paper
feedback: Correct answer: 48 km/h. First leg 60÷60 = 1 h; second leg 60÷40 = 1.5 h; total 120 km over 2.5 h gives 120÷2.5 = 48 km/h.
If the answer is 50 from (60+40)÷2, have them find each leg's time first and ask which speed was ridden longer; more time at 40 drags the average below 50.

For the equal-times variant (1 h at 60 then 1 h at 40): total 100 km over 2 h = 50 km/h — here the mean IS correct because equal times are spent at each speed. Use this as a contrasting counterexample, not the general rule.

Full response: produces 48 via leg times → total÷total, forms rates the right way round, converts km/h↔m/s as a correct two-step chain with sensible magnitude, compares best-buys on a common per-unit basis, and transfers to an unfamiliar rate.
Partial response: computes total÷total correctly but slips on a related procedure (inverts a division or botches the conversion) — method not yet secure across compound units.
activities.rationale: Asking the pupil to work the journey on paper discriminates between those computing average speed as total distance ÷ total time and those averaging the speeds, because the equal-distance, unequal-speed setup makes 48 and the naive 50 genuinely different numbers. The equal-times counterexample is mathematically precise: the mean equals the true average speed only when equal times are spent at each speed.
sourceClaims: Average speed is total distance ÷ total time, which equals the arithmetic mean of the two speeds ONLY when equal TIMES are spent at each; for equal DISTANCES the average is the harmonic mean 2uv/(u+v). The page proves the harmonic mean is ≤ the arithmetic mean (difference factorises to (u−v)²/[2(u+v)]), so averaging the two speeds overestimates the true average speed on equal-distance legs — the exact 48-vs-50 trap in this record.
learnerActions: Work out: a cyclist rides 60 km at a steady 60 km/h, then another 60 km at a steady 40 km/h. Find the average speed for the whole journey, showing every step on paper.
Find each leg's time first (60÷60 = 1 h; 60÷40 = 1.5 h), then total distance (120 km), total time (2.5 h), and average speed (120 ÷ 2.5 = 48 km/h).
Answer probes: which leg took more time, so should the average be nearer 60 or nearer 40 — does 50 fit? Then redo with equal TIMES (1 h at 60, 1 h at 40) and explain why the average is 50 this time.
Convert your 48 km/h into metres per second, talking through each step and the units.

Compare two products (e.g. 400 g for £1.80 vs 250 g for £1.20): put both on a cost-per-100 g basis (45p vs 48p), say which is the better buy, and explain what would go wrong if you just compared their prices.
activities.intendedInsight: Watching the pupil compute (rather than recite a rule) reveals whether they use total÷total or average the speeds; because equal distances are covered at unequal speeds, the correct 48 cannot be reached by the mean method, so the method is visible in the number produced. The equal-TIMES counterexample shows the mean is correct only when equal times are spent at each speed.

activities.title: Short check on rates, best-buy and conversion
feedback: If the mean-of-speeds option is chosen, route back to computing leg times and total÷total.
If the 'bigger pack is automatically cheaper' option is chosen, require both products on a common per-100 g basis before deciding.
For a wrong conversion, prompt the two-step ×1000 then ÷3600 chain and the magnitude check.

Use this check to confirm or challenge mastery; it records which answer was produced but does not by itself show the pupil can construct the full method independently — pair it with the paper performance task.
activities.rationale: Rate computation, best-buy choice, and conversion are cleanly checkable in short formats, and the characteristic errors make strong tempting wrong options. A recognition/short-answer format is efficient for surfacing specific slips but does not elicit the independent step-by-step construction that the performance task requires; it is a complement, not a replacement.
learnerActions: Work out and type the cost per 100 g for a product given its price and weight.
Choose the better buy between two differently sized packs where the smaller pack is actually cheaper per unit, so that 'the bigger pack must be cheaper per unit' is a tempting but wrong option.
Choose the average speed of a two-leg equal-distance journey, with the mean-of-the-two-speeds value (e.g. 50) offered as the key trap.
Give a km/h→m/s conversion as a typed value, then check its magnitude.
activities.intendedInsight: The mean-of-speeds error and wrong-way-round division make sharp, diagnostic wrong options, so a quick check can surface whether these specific slips persist after teaching.

activities.title: Consolidation reference card: 'per one' facts and the average-speed warning
feedback: Use the card to remind yourself what 'per one' means for each measure, then go and perform an actual calculation to check you can apply it.
Treat the revealed 'total distance ÷ total time' statement as a prompt to redo a worked journey, not as the whole lesson.
activities.rationale: A static labelled double number line or reference card with tap-to-reveal facts consolidates the idea and keeps the key warning visible. It cannot let the learner perform and check a calculation, which is the heart of this procedural topic, so it functions as a consolidation aid alongside the workshop and performance task rather than as the main teaching activity.
sourceClaims: NCETM treats compound measures (speed = distance÷time, density = mass÷volume) as multiplicative comparisons and names as a common misconception that 'compound measures are different from other forms of proportional relationship' when they follow the same multiplicative rules; it stresses securing the meaning of 'per', recommends double number lines and ratio tables, and raises formula triangles as a practice to scrutinise for whether they promote understanding.
learnerActions: Tap a shelf tag to reveal its unit price (e.g. cost per 100 g) and restate it in words: 'this much for one hundred grams'.
Tap 'average speed' to reveal 'total distance ÷ total time, NOT the average of the two speeds'.
Tap density, speed, and unit-price entries to reveal the 'per one' meaning behind each formula before using it in a calculation.
activities.intendedInsight: A labelled double number line and tap-to-reveal 'per one' facts consolidate the meaning of each compound unit and keep the average-speed warning salient.

constraints: Derive every compound measure as a unit rate first ('how much for exactly one?') using a double number line or ratio table before introducing any formula.
For best-buy, insist on a common basis (cost per 100 g, or per item for both products) rather than comparing raw price to raw size.

Teach average speed as total distance ÷ total time by working a two-leg journey where the naive mean-of-speeds answer is demonstrably wrong; include the equal-TIMES counterexample where the mean IS correct, so pupils learn the precise condition rather than a blanket 'never average speeds'.
Do km/h↔m/s as a deliberate two-step chain (×1000 m per km, ÷3600 s per hour) with units tracked, not a single memorised factor; include a magnitude sanity check (e.g. 36 km/h ≈ 10 m/s).
Prefer double number lines / ratio tables over the formula 'magic triangle', which can reduce proportional reasoning to symbol-shuffling; use the triangle only with care if at all.
The reference card is a consolidation scaffold: it holds facts but does not let the learner perform or check a calculation, so it must not be the sole activity for this procedural skill.

The short check records which answer was produced and surfaces specific slips, but recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction of the full method; pair it with the paper performance task.
Density and unit price follow the same multiplicative 'per one' structure as speed; comparisons and conversions should be modelled on that shared structure rather than treated as separate rules.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support teaching principles, not the tested effectiveness of these specific activities.

Self-audit (arithmetic): 60÷60 = 1 h; 60÷40 = 1.5 h; total 120 km over 2.5 h = 48 km/h — confirmed. Equal-times variant: 100 km over 2 h = 50 km/h — confirmed; the arithmetic mean is exact only for equal times, matching the harmonic-mean argument in the sources. Conversion: 36 km/h = 36000 m / 3600 s = 10 m/s — confirmed.

Self-audit note on framing: the equal-distance case gives the harmonic mean 2uv/(u+v) = 2·60·40/100 = 48, consistent with the computed answer; the activities state the correct method (total÷total) and present the mean only as the trap, so no erroneous instruction is taught.

The original row described 10 m/s as 'walking-fast'; this is inaccurate (10 m/s ≈ 36 km/h, a fast cycling/sprinting pace), so the activity now describes it as a fast cycling/sprinting pace while keeping the numeric magnitude check.

The original row contained non-preferred-format rationales asserting '3D adds nothing' and that an in-role dialogue 'cannot exercise' the required doing-and-checking. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the sources and have been softened or dropped; the short check and reference-card activities are retained with scoped affordances and stated limits rather than universal exclusions.

The original 'formula triangle blocks proportional reasoning' claim is retained as a cautious preference (prefer number lines/tables; use the triangle with care), consistent with the practitioner source scrutinising rather than universally banning it.

probeDeeper: Which leg did the cyclist spend more time on — the fast one or the slow one? So should the average be nearer 60 or nearer 40? Does 50 fit that?

Redo it with the two legs the same TIME instead of the same distance (1 hour at 60, then 1 hour at 40). Now what is the average speed — and why is it 50 this time? (counterexample: equal times DO give the mean.)
Show me how you'd turn 48 km/h into metres per second — talk me through each step and what the units are.
For the best buy, how did you make the two products comparable? What would go wrong if you just compared their prices?
assess.correctAnswer: 48 km/h. First leg takes 60÷60 = 1 hour; second leg takes 60÷40 = 1.5 hours. Total distance = 120 km, total time = 2.5 hours, so average speed = 120÷2.5 = 48 km/h.

errorPatterns.pattern: Averages the two speeds directly — (60+40)÷2 = 50 km/h — instead of total distance ÷ total time
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have them find the TIME for each leg first (1 h and 1.5 h). Ask 'which speed did the cyclist spend more time at?' — more time at 40 pulls the average below 50. Rebuild on a double number line, total over total.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes (60+40)÷2 or otherwise combines the speeds without ever computing the two times; answer is 50

errorPatterns.pattern: Divides the wrong way round when forming a rate (time÷distance for speed, or inverts a unit price)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor 'per one': speed is 'km for ONE hour', so distance goes on top. Track units through the division so km/h falls out, not h/km.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Computes 60÷60 correctly by luck but on a leg like 60 km at 40 km/h writes 40÷60, or forms cost-per-pound as size÷price

errorPatterns.pattern: Mishandles the km/h↔m/s conversion, using a single wrong factor (×60 or ÷60) instead of the ×1000 then ÷3600 chain
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do the chain as two labelled steps with units cancelling: km→m (×1000), then per hour → per second (÷3600). Check magnitude: 36 km/h should be a walking-fast 10 m/s, not 0.6 or 600.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a follow-up conversion, multiplies or divides by 60 once, or forgets one of the two steps, giving an answer out by a factor of 60 or 1000

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares best-buys on different bases — assumes the bigger pack or the lower total price is automatically better value
errorPatterns.nextMove: Insist both are expressed as cost per 100 g (or per item) before deciding; only same-basis figures are comparable.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On a best-buy task picks the cheaper total or the bigger pack without reducing both to a common per-unit basis

responseLevels.gap: Answers 50 by averaging the speeds; does not compute the leg times or total÷total, and cannot correctly form or convert a rate.
responseLevels.full: Produces 48 km/h via leg times → total distance ÷ total time, forms rates the right way round, converts km/h↔m/s as a correct two-step chain with sensible magnitude, and compares best-buys on a common per-unit basis — and can transfer to an unfamiliar rate.
responseLevels.partial: Computes total distance ÷ total time correctly for the average-speed task, but slips on a related procedure (inverts a division, or botches the km/h↔m/s chain), showing the method is not yet secure across compound units.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a journey to work out. A cyclist rides 60 km at a steady 60 km/h, then rides another 60 km at a steady 40 km/h. Find the cyclist's average speed for the whole journey. Work it out on paper — show your steps.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the pupil work (not asking them to explain the rule) separates those who compute average speed as total distance ÷ total time from those who average the two speeds to get 50. Because equal DISTANCES are covered at unequal speeds, the correct answer (48) differs from the naive mean (50) — a pupil cannot land on 48 by the mean method, so the procedure is visible in the number they produce.
