topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Proportion Graphs
topic.description: Represent proportional relationships using double number lines (two parallel number lines aligned at 0) and ratio tables; recognise that equivalent ratios generate straight lines through the origin when graphed
evidence: Plot pairs of proportional values on a coordinate grid and draw the straight line through the origin
Explain why a directly proportional relationship always passes through (0,0)
Read a proportion graph to find an unknown value — e.g. 'If 3 kg costs £6, how much does 5 kg cost?'
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is comparing the cost of buying different numbers of cinema tickets, can they sketch a proportion graph — a straight line through zero — and use it to read off the cost of any number of tickets without recalculating each time?

pedagogy.summary: Proportional relationships are represented with double number lines (two parallel scales aligned at 0), ratio tables, and coordinate graphs — and the defining graphical signature is a STRAIGHT LINE THROUGH THE ORIGIN. The representational skills are (1) plotting proportional pairs and drawing that line, (2) explaining WHY it must pass through (0,0) — because zero of one quantity means zero of the other — and (3) reading off an unknown value from the line or table (if 3 kg costs £6, find 5 kg). The key idea to build is that the three representations show the SAME constant multiplier: the gap between rungs on a double number line, the column multiplier in a ratio table, and the gradient of the line are one and the same. The persistent error is thinking any straight line (or any rising graph) shows proportion, ignoring the origin.
bestPractices: Connect the three representations explicitly — double number line, ratio table, and graph — as views of one constant multiplier, moving between them on the same example.
Foreground the origin: ask 'what does it cost for 0 kg?' so pupils reason that a proportional graph MUST pass through (0,0), and use that as a test.
Align double number lines at 0 and keep the scales consistent, so equivalent ratios sit at matching positions.
Read unknowns both by scaling on the table/number line and by reading off the graph, checking the two agree.
Contrast a proportional line (through origin) with a straight line that misses the origin (e.g. a fixed charge plus a rate) so 'straight' alone is not mistaken for 'proportional'.
keyRepresentations: Double number line (two parallel scales aligned at 0)
Ratio table with a constant column multiplier
Coordinate graph: straight line through the origin (gradient = the rate)
Overlay contrasting a through-origin line with a not-through-origin line
commonMisconceptions: Thinking any straight line — or any rising graph — shows direct proportion, ignoring whether it passes through the origin.
Not aligning the double number line at 0, so equivalent ratios don't correspond.
Reading a graph as isolated points and being unable to interpolate an unknown, or swapping the axes when reading off.
Believing the graph need not start at (0,0) — missing that zero of one quantity means zero of the other.

learn.summary: Pupils aged 11–14 learn to represent direct proportion across three linked views — a double number line (two parallel scales aligned at 0), a ratio table in which every kg entry is multiplied by the same constant to give its £ entry, and a coordinate graph whose signature is a STRAIGHT LINE THROUGH THE ORIGIN. The core insight is that the factor linking each pair of matching marks on the double number line (e.g. 1 kg ↔ £2, 3 kg ↔ £6), the kg-to-£ multiplier in each pair in the table, and the gradient of the line (£ per kg) are ONE AND THE SAME constant multiplier. Learners plot proportional pairs and draw the line, explain why it must pass through (0,0) (zero of one quantity means zero of the other), and read off unknowns (if 3 kg costs £6, find 5 kg → £10). The persistent error to confront is treating any straight or rising line as proportional while ignoring the origin.

activities.title: Linked board: one rate, three views that move together
feedback: If a drawn line misses (0,0), ask 'what does it cost for 0 kg?' — it must be £0, so the line has to start at the origin.
If the double number line is not aligned at 0, highlight that equivalent ratios then fail to sit at matching positions; realign at 0.
If axes are swapped when reading off, prompt: read UP from the weight on the x-axis to the line, then ACROSS to the cost on the y-axis.
When the fixed-charge toggle lifts the line off the origin, name it: still straight, but no longer proportional because 0 kg no longer costs £0.
activities.rationale: Plotting pairs, drawing the line, and reading off unknowns are direct-manipulation tasks; moving between the three views on one example is intended to make the shared multiplier concrete, and the fixed-charge contrast separates 'straight' from 'proportional'. Live linking and dragging are offered as examples of how to make the shared multiplier visible, not as the only possible medium.
sourceClaims: A directly proportional relationship graphs as a straight line through the origin; properties include that doubling one quantity doubles the other and that if one quantity is zero the other is zero.

Pupils should use double number lines and ratio tables, and recognise that proportional relationships are represented by straight-line graphs through the origin, relating the multiplicative relationship to linear functions.
learnerActions: Enter or accept a rate such as 3 kg → £6 and watch a ratio table, a double number line, and a coordinate graph populate for the SAME example.
Plot the proportional pairs on the graph and draw the line; confirm it passes through the origin.
Drag a point to 5 kg and read £10 simultaneously on the table, the number line, and the graph.

Point to where the constant '×2' appears in each view: the gradient of the line (£2 per kg), the multiplier from each kg entry to its £ entry in the table (3 → 6, 5 → 10), and the factor linking each pair of matching marks on the double number line (1 kg ↔ £2, 3 kg ↔ £6).
Flip a 'fixed charge' toggle (e.g. add a standing £2) and observe the whole line lift OFF the origin while staying perfectly straight; state whether it is still proportional and why not.
activities.intendedInsight: All three representations encode the SAME constant multiplier, and the origin — not mere straightness — is the test of proportionality.

activities.title: Annotated proportion graph: reveal the origin, the rate, and a read-off
feedback: If the learner calls the not-through-origin line proportional, return to the origin: at 0 kg the fixed-charge line already costs £2, so it fails the origin test.
If the rate is misread, trace one unit along x and read the matching rise on y to recover the constant multiplier.
activities.rationale: A proportion graph is largely a fixed object; annotating it with tap-to-reveal on origin, gradient, and read-off, plus a contrasting line, is intended to rehearse the recognition cues at low cost. A fixed image here cannot be freely manipulated but can still surface these cues for inspection; it complements rather than replaces the interactive board.
sourceClaims: A directly proportional relationship graphs as a straight line through the origin; properties include that doubling one quantity doubles the other and that if one quantity is zero the other is zero.
learnerActions: Examine a proportion graph and reveal, at the origin, that 'at 0 kg, cost is £0'.
Reveal along the line the constant multiplier (the rate, e.g. £2/kg).
Reveal at a chosen point its read-off (e.g. 5 kg → £10).
Compare a companion line that is straight but does NOT pass through the origin (a fixed £2 charge plus £2/kg) and decide, with reasons, that it is not proportional.
activities.intendedInsight: The recognition cues of a proportional graph are the origin crossing and a single constant rate; a straight line that misses the origin is a direct counterexample to 'straight means proportional'.

activities.title: Identify, read, and produce proportional lines
feedback: If a produced line misses (0,0), it is the key discriminator: recognition alone will not place the line; re-anchor using 'at 0 kg, cost £0'.
If an unknown is only found when the weight is an already-plotted point, stress that the line gives a value for EVERY weight, so interpolate between plotted points.
If axes are swapped during read-off, label both axes first, then read up-then-across.

If a £2/kg line is drawn as if it were separate from the given line, point out that equal rates give the SAME line through the origin; a genuinely different rate (e.g. £1/kg through (3,3)) gives a shallower distinct line.
activities.rationale: Identifying the proportional graph, reading off values, matching a table to a line, and drawing a new line are cleanly assessable, with 'any straight line' and axis-swap as sharp distractors. The draw step elicits independent construction, which recognition-only items do not.
sourceClaims: Pupils should use double number lines and ratio tables, and recognise that proportional relationships are represented by straight-line graphs through the origin, relating the multiplicative relationship to linear functions.
learnerActions: Choose which of several graphs shows direct proportion, where a straight not-through-origin line is a deliberate trap.
Given a ratio table, plot the points and draw the matching line through the origin.
Read an unknown off a line through (3,6) (e.g. find the cost of 5 kg → £10), stating which axis you read up from and which you read across to.

On the same axes, DRAW a line for a DIFFERENT fruit's price: note that a £2/kg fruit would COINCIDE with the given £2/kg line through (3,6), whereas a shallower £1/kg line passes through (3,3) — and check your line is anchored at the origin.
activities.intendedInsight: Interpreting a point, interpolating an unknown, and independently producing an origin-anchored line together show whether the learner sees the graph as a constant-multiplier relationship rather than a picture.

constraints: Multiple-choice identification and tap-to-reveal items assess or rehearse recognition of cues; they do not by themselves elicit the independent production of an origin-anchored line, so include a draw/plot task for full mastery.
An annotated fixed graph cannot be freely manipulated; pair it with a task where learners plot, drag, or draw so the constant multiplier is explored, not just viewed.
Always keep double number lines aligned at 0 and scales consistent, or equivalent ratios will not correspond.
When introducing the fixed-charge contrast, state the setup explicitly (e.g. £2 standing charge plus £2/kg) so learners attribute the lifted line to the non-zero start, not to a changed rate.

When asking learners to draw a 'different' line, ensure the chosen rate is genuinely different from any line already on the axes (£1/kg, not £2/kg, against a given £2/kg line), so the task is coherent.

In-role dialogue and 3D manipulation were judged poor fits here: the relationship is inherently 2D (two quantities, one plane), and drawing/reading a graph is a visual-spatial task; these are design judgements for this topic, not universal rules.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic and geometry: at £2/kg, 3 kg → £6 and 5 kg → £10 are consistent; a £1/kg line through the origin passes through (3,3); the fixed-charge example (£2 + £2/kg) correctly gives £2 at 0 kg and so misses the origin. The original's note that a £2/kg drawn line coincides with the given (3,6) line has been preserved and the 'different rate' wording kept coherent (£1/kg used as the genuinely different, shallower line).

The source claims support the mathematical signature (straight line through the origin; zero maps to zero; use of double number lines and ratio tables) but do not establish the comparative efficacy of any particular interface (linked board, tap-to-reveal, drag). Efficacy of specific media is not asserted; medium wording has been kept to proposed/intended.
The original judgement that conversation and 3D 'add nothing' has been softened to a scoped design decision for this 2D topic rather than a universal law.

probeDeeper: What would this fruit cost for 0 kg? Where must the line be at x = 0, and why?
How did you find the cost of 5 kg from the line — which way did you read, and how do you know it isn't, say, £, from the other axis?

Here is a line that is straight but does NOT go through the origin (a fixed £2 charge plus £2/kg) — is THAT one directly proportional? How can you tell? (counterexample separating 'straight' from 'proportional'.)
Show me this same relationship as a ratio table — where is the '×2' that the graph's steepness shows?
assess.correctAnswer: (a) 3 kg costs £6 (so this fruit is £2 per kg). (b) 5 kg costs £10 — read up from 5 on the x-axis to the line and across to £10. (c) A straight line through the origin passing through (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6)… — in fact the SAME line here, since £2/kg matches; if asked for, say £1/kg would be a shallower line through the origin, e.g. (3, 3).

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks any straight (or rising) line shows proportion; draws or accepts a line that misses the origin
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'what does this fruit cost for 0 kg?' — it must be £0, so the line has to start at the origin. Contrast with a fixed-charge line that misses it. Rehearse the origin test.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In (c) draws a line not through (0,0), or when shown a not-through-origin line calls it proportional

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the graph as isolated points and cannot interpolate an unknown, or swaps the axes
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model reading up from the x-value to the line and across to the y-axis; the line gives a value for EVERY weight, not just plotted ones. Label axes before reading.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 5 kg, only answers if 5 is a plotted point, or reads across-then-up the wrong way giving the wrong coordinate

errorPatterns.pattern: Does not connect the graph to the double number line / ratio table — treats them as unrelated
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put the three side by side for the same example; show the gradient, the column multiplier, and the number-line gap are the same number. Align the number line at 0.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Can read the graph but cannot say how the same relationship looks as a ratio table, or does not align the double number line at 0

responseLevels.gap: Misreads the axes or cannot interpolate; draws a line that misses the origin and treats any straight line as proportional.
responseLevels.full: Reads (3,6) as '3 kg for £6', interpolates 5 kg → £10 by reading the line, DRAWS a new proportional line through the origin, explains why it must pass through (0,0), and links the graph to the ratio table/double number line as the same constant multiplier.
responseLevels.partial: Interprets the given point and reads off 5 kg → £10 correctly, but draws a new line without anchoring it at the origin, or cannot translate the graph into a ratio table / double number line — recognition without full production or cross-representation.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a graph: a straight line through the origin passing through the point (3, 6), where the x-axis is weight in kg and the y-axis is cost in pounds. (a) What does the point (3, 6) tell you? (b) Use the line to find the cost of 5 kg. (c) Now, on the same axes, DRAW the line for a different fruit that costs £2 per kg.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Interpreting a point, reading off an unknown, and then PRODUCING a proportional line all test whether the child sees the graph as a constant-multiplier relationship, not a picture. A child who has it reads (3,6) as '3 kg for £6', interpolates 5 kg → £10, and draws a new line THROUGH THE ORIGIN. A child who hasn't reads the axes the wrong way, cannot interpolate, or draws a line that misses (0,0). The 'now draw one' step is the discriminator — recognition alone won't produce a correct origin-anchored line.

Convert volume units such as cm³ to litres and explain the relationship
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} convert between units confidently — for example, changing kilometres to metres, kilograms to grams, or hours and minutes to just minutes — including multi-step problems?

pedagogy.summary: Converting between related standard units means multiplying or dividing by the right power of the conversion factor, going the correct way (to a SMALLER unit the NUMBER gets bigger). The distinctive KS3 demands are (1) AREA and VOLUME conversions, where the factor is the SQUARE or CUBE of the linear factor — 1 m² = 100² = 10 000 cm², 1 m³ = 100³ = 1 000 000 cm³, NOT 100 — and (2) multi-step conversions like hours→minutes→seconds, done as a chain. The dominant error is applying the LINEAR factor to area/volume; the antidote is to derive the squared/cubed factor from a picture (a 1 m square tiled by cm squares) rather than memorise it. Decimal place value underpins the arithmetic (5 cm = 0.05 m).
bestPractices: Fix the direction with a sense-check: converting to a smaller unit gives a bigger number; estimate the size of the answer before calculating.
Derive area/volume factors from the linear one on a diagram — a 1 m square holds 100×100 = 10 000 cm squares — so pupils SEE why it is k² (or k³), not k.
Do multi-step conversions as an explicit chain with the factor at each step (2.5 h ×60 = 150 min ×60 = 9000 s), tracking units.
Anchor key equivalences that pupils reason from: 1000 cm³ = 1 litre, 1 m² = 10 000 cm², 1 km = 1000 m.
Use decimal notation carefully to 3 d.p. and check by converting back.
keyRepresentations: Tiled-square / stacked-cube diagram showing k² and k³ (1 m² = 10 000 cm²)
Conversion chain with the factor written on each arrow (h → min → s)
Place-value / decimal grid for cm↔m
Double number line pairing the two units
commonMisconceptions: Converting area/volume with the LINEAR factor — 1 m² = 100 cm² (should be 10 000), 1 m³ = 100 cm³ (should be 1 000 000).
Going the wrong direction — multiplying when converting to a bigger unit, so the number grows when it should shrink.
Stopping a multi-step conversion partway (hours to minutes but not on to seconds), or using a wrong intermediate factor (e.g. treating an hour as 100 minutes).
Decimal place-value slips when moving between units (5 cm → 0.5 m instead of 0.05 m).

learn.summary: Pupils convert freely between related standard units (time, length, area, volume/capacity, mass) using decimal notation to up to three decimal places where appropriate. The KS3-distinctive demands are (1) area and volume conversions, where the factor is the SQUARE or CUBE of the linear factor (1 m² = 100² = 10 000 cm²; 1 m³ = 100³ = 1 000 000 cm³, NOT 100), and (2) multi-step conversions done as an explicit chain (hours → minutes → seconds). The dominant misconception is applying the linear factor to area/volume; the antidote is to derive the squared/cubed factor from a tiled-square or stacked-cube picture rather than memorise it. Decimal place value underpins the arithmetic (5 cm = 0.05 m), and a direction sense-check (to a smaller unit the number gets bigger) guards against inverted conversions.

activities.title: Tile the square metre: deriving the k² (and k³) factor
feedback: If a pupil writes 3 × 100 = 300 cm², tile the 1 m square on a grid: 100 squares along each side gives 10 000 inside, not 100. Make them count a strip then the whole.
If the squared factor never appears, ask: 'How many cm squares fit along one side? So how many fill the whole square — why square the 100?'
For volume, confirm the chain of reasoning: one edge holds 100, so the cube holds 100 × 100 × 100 = 1 000 000 — not 100 and not 10 000.
Reinforce the correct result: 3 m² = 30 000 cm² because 1 m² = 10 000 cm².
activities.rationale: Deriving the factor from a picture targets the documented persistent error of applying the linear factor to area and volume, replacing a memorised rule with a visible reason.
sourceClaims: Length scale factor k means area scales by k² and volume by k³ — the same relationship that makes 1 m² = 100² cm² and 1 m³ = 100³ cm³; applying the linear factor to area/volume is a documented persistent error.

Pupils should change freely between related standard units (e.g. time, length, area, volume/capacity, mass) and use decimal notation up to three decimal places; convert between standard units including area and volume units.
learnerActions: On a 1 m square, mark how many cm fit along ONE side (100), then work out how many cm squares tile the whole square (100 × 100 = 10 000). State the equivalence 1 m² = 10 000 cm².
Convert 3 m² to cm², showing working: 1 m² = 100² = 10 000 cm², so 3 × 10 000 = 30 000 cm².

Extend to volume: picture a 1 m cube filled with cm cubes along each edge (100), so the whole cube holds 100³ = 1 000 000 cm³. Decide whether 1 m³ equals 100, 10 000, or 1 000 000 cm³ and justify your choice — the correct answer is 1 000 000; 100 is the trap of applying the linear factor and 10 000 the trap of applying the area factor.

If using an interactive bench, enter the value and units and watch a 1 m square flood with a 100×100 grid as the counter climbs to 10 000; optionally switch to a 3D mode that stacks cm cubes in a 1 m cube up to a million — these visuals are optional illustrations of why the factor is squared/cubed, not required mechanisms. A printed grid may be used the same way; treat it as a thin physical approximation of the ideal square metre.
activities.intendedInsight: When a length scales by factor k, area scales by k² and volume by k³, so converting area/volume uses the square/cube of the linear conversion factor, not the linear factor itself.

activities.title: Multi-step conversion as a tracked chain
feedback: If a pupil gives 2.5 h = 150, point out that is minutes, not seconds, and prompt the second step: 'how many seconds in a minute?'
If an hour is treated as 100 minutes, correct the factor explicitly (60) and redo the step.
Confirm the full result: 2.5 hours = 150 minutes = 9000 seconds.
Encourage a convert-back check: convert 9000 s back to hours (9000 ÷ 60 = 150 min, 150 ÷ 60 = 2.5 h) to confirm 2.5.
activities.rationale: Writing the factor on each arrow and tracking units is intended to make the stopping-partway and wrong-intermediate-factor errors visible and correctable; this technique is a proposal not established by the cited sources.
learnerActions: Convert 2.5 hours to seconds as an explicit chain, writing the factor on each step: 2.5 h × 60 = 150 min, then 150 × 60 = 9000 s. Track the unit at every stage.
Check you have not stopped partway: after reaching minutes, ask 'how many seconds in a minute?' and complete the second step.
Verify no wrong intermediate factor is used (an hour is 60 minutes, not 100).
Build at least one more chain of your own (e.g. a length or capacity conversion needing two steps) and label the factor on each arrow.
activities.intendedInsight: A multi-step conversion is a chain of single conversions, each with its own factor and unit; the answer is only complete when every required step has been carried through.

activities.title: Direction sense-check and decimal place value
feedback: If 3 m² converts to a number smaller than 3, flag the direction: cm² are smaller, so the number must grow.
If cm→m makes the number bigger, the direction is reversed; re-state that a bigger unit gives a smaller number.
If a pupil writes 5 cm = 0.5 m, use a place-value chart: 100 cm in 1 m, so 5 cm = 5 ÷ 100 = 0.05 m (0.5 m would be 50 cm). Confirm by converting back.
Praise an estimate-then-check approach as the habit that prevents these slips.
activities.rationale: A magnitude sense-check and careful decimal placement address the wrong-direction and place-value errors; the decimal-notation precision requirement is directly stated in the curriculum claim.
sourceClaims: Pupils should change freely between related standard units (e.g. time, length, area, volume/capacity, mass) and use decimal notation up to three decimal places; convert between standard units including area and volume units.
learnerActions: Before calculating, decide whether the answer should be bigger or smaller: converting to a SMALLER unit gives a BIGGER number (cm² are tiny, so there are many in a m²). Estimate the answer's size first.
Optionally pair the two units on a double number line (e.g. cm on one line, m on the other) to see the direction and relative scale of the conversion at a glance.
Convert a length with decimals carefully, e.g. 5 cm = 0.05 m (not 0.5 m), using a place-value chart to place the decimal.
Check each conversion by converting back to the original unit.
For 3 m² → cm², confirm the answer (30 000) is larger than 3, as expected when moving to a smaller unit.
activities.intendedInsight: Checking the direction of a conversion against the relative size of the units, and placing decimals precisely, catches inverted conversions and place-value slips before they become final errors.

activities.title: Capacity and volume equivalences: cm³ and litres
feedback: If the conversion goes the wrong way, apply the direction sense-check: litres are larger, so fewer of them.
Confirm 1000 cm³ = 1 litre and have the pupil state the factor used.
If an equivalence is misremembered, rebuild it from the metric structure rather than re-memorising.
activities.rationale: Anchoring and reasoning from key equivalences supports the curriculum requirement to convert volume/capacity units and explain the relationship.
sourceClaims: Pupils should change freely between related standard units (e.g. time, length, area, volume/capacity, mass) and use decimal notation up to three decimal places; convert between standard units including area and volume units.
learnerActions: State and use the equivalence 1000 cm³ = 1 litre, and explain why it links volume and capacity.
Convert a given volume in cm³ to litres and back, checking the direction (cm³ to litres gives a smaller number because a litre is the larger unit).
Anchor the key equivalences you reason from: 1000 cm³ = 1 litre, 1 m² = 10 000 cm², 1 km = 1000 m.
Explain the relationship in words, e.g. why a 1 litre container holds 1000 cm³.
activities.intendedInsight: Capacity and volume units are related through fixed equivalences that can be reasoned from and checked for direction, not just recalled.

activities.title: Short conversion practice with diagnostic distractors
feedback: An answer of 300 for 3 m² signals the linear-factor misconception — return to tiling the square metre.
An answer of 150 for 2.5 h signals stopping after one step — complete the chain to seconds.
Always ask to see working: whether the pupil used 100 or 100² reveals understanding that a bare answer hides.
For recognition-style items, follow up with a constructed conversion so the pupil produces the method independently; recognition alone checks selection but does not elicit independent production.
activities.rationale: Sharp distractors tied to the two dominant errors make practice diagnostic; requiring shown working guards against a correct answer that masks a wrong method.
sourceClaims: Length scale factor k means area scales by k² and volume by k³ — the same relationship that makes 1 m² = 100² cm² and 1 m³ = 100³ cm³; applying the linear factor to area/volume is a documented persistent error.
learnerActions: Complete: 3 m² = ___ cm² (correct 30 000; the linear-factor trap gives 300).
Complete: 2.5 h = ___ s (correct 9000; the one-step-only trap gives 150).
Answer a multiple-choice item on cm³ ↔ litres.
Do a length conversion with decimals and an area conversion, showing your working so the method (factor 100 for cm↔m length, 100² for cm²↔m² area) is visible, not just the answer.
activities.intendedInsight: A correct answer supported by shown working that uses the squared factor and a complete chain is evidence of secure understanding; the common trap answers (300, 150) come from the linear-factor and stopping-partway errors, so they signal which step went wrong.

constraints: The target objective requires pupils to construct and show conversion working (especially the squared/cubed factor and each chain step), not merely select correct answers; recognition-only items assess classification/selection but do not elicit independent construction, so pair them with a produced conversion.

Interactive visuals (flooding a 1 m square with a 100×100 grid, stacking cm cubes in a 1 m cube, factor-on-each-arrow chains that refuse skipped steps) are optional illustrations of the mechanism; they are not the only way to teach the k² / k³ idea. A static tiled-square diagram with reveal of '10 000 cm² in 1 m² because 100²' can consolidate the fact but does not itself let a pupil run and check their own conversion.

A paper/card cm-square cutout or printed grid has slight thickness and is a physical approximation of the ideal (zero-thickness) area model; use it to count tiles but keep the represented square metre distinct from the cutout.
The 3D cube-fill is a volume-focused extension; most of the topic is handled well with 2D grids and chains.
Decimal place-value accuracy (to three decimal places) is a precision requirement; a place-value chart and convert-back check are prompts for accuracy, not a conceptual reteach.
Direction must be sense-checked against relative unit size: converting to a smaller unit increases the number, to a larger unit decreases it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support teaching principles/content rather than proving any specific activity was tested.

The curriculum claim names time-unit conversion and other standard-unit conversion, i.e. the content/objective of the multi-step-chain activity, but does NOT support the specific chaining technique (factor-on-each-arrow, unit-tracking). Its sourceClaims were therefore set to []; the technique's effectiveness remains an unvalidated proposal.

The original source rated in-role dialogue as adding nothing to a conversion procedure; this categorical claim was dropped rather than reproduced — the conversation format is simply not the focus here, without asserting a universal law.

Claims that the quiz 'cannot let the pupil run and check a conversion' and that a static image 'cannot' teach the running-check have been scoped to narrow affordance/limit statements rather than universal impossibility claims.

Arithmetic self-audit: 100² = 10 000 and 3 × 10 000 = 30 000 (not 300); 100³ = 1 000 000 (not 100 or 10 000); 2.5 × 60 = 150 and 150 × 60 = 9000 (not stopping at 150); 5 cm = 0.05 m (since 100 cm = 1 m). All verified consistent across the guidance.
The source links two distinct comparisons clearly: area uses k² and volume uses k³ from the same linear factor k; both are preserved without conflation.
The double number line representation from the original keyRepresentations was missing from the candidate and has been restored as an optional representation in the direction/place-value activity.

In the 1 m³ discrimination task the trap values 100 and 10 000 appear only as explicitly labelled wrong options with the correct answer (1 000 000) and the reason each is wrong stated; they are never presented as legitimate alternatives.

probeDeeper: How many cm squares fit along ONE side of a 1 m square? So how many fit inside the whole square — why square the 100?
Is your answer bigger or smaller than 3 — should it be, going from m² to cm²? Why?
Now convert 1 m³ to cm³ — is it 100, 10 000, or 1 000 000? (counterexample extending the idea to k³.)
For 2.5 hours to seconds, what were the two steps and the factor at each one?

errorPatterns.pattern: Converts area (or volume) using the LINEAR factor — 1 m² = 100 cm² instead of 100² = 10 000
errorPatterns.nextMove: Tile a 1 m square with cm squares on a grid — 100 along each side, 10 000 in total. Establish area → k², volume → k³ from the picture. Reteach the underlying metric conversion.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 3 × 100 = 300 cm² (or for volume ×100 instead of ×100³); the squared/cubed factor never appears

errorPatterns.pattern: Goes the wrong direction — multiplies when converting to a bigger unit (or divides to a smaller one), so the number moves the wrong way
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sense-check first: cm² are tiny, so there are MANY in a m² — the number must grow. Estimate the answer's size before computing. Reteach direction of conversion.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Converts 3 m² to a number SMALLER than 3, or on cm→m makes the number bigger; no sense-check on magnitude

errorPatterns.pattern: Stops a multi-step conversion partway, or uses a wrong intermediate factor
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold: 'that's minutes — how many seconds in a minute?' Lay the chain out with the factor on each arrow and complete the second step. Add-back check.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives 2.5 h = 150 (minutes, not seconds), or treats an hour as 100 minutes

errorPatterns.pattern: Decimal place-value slip when moving between units
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold: use a place-value chart and check by converting back. Not a conceptual reteach — a precision prompt.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 5 cm = 0.5 m instead of 0.05 m, or misplaces a decimal in the ×/÷

responseLevels.gap: Applies the linear factor to area (300), or converts the wrong direction; cannot reach a correct area or multi-step conversion.
responseLevels.full: Converts 3 m² to 30 000 cm² using 100², explains it via the tiled square, carries the 2.5 h → 9000 s chain through both steps with a magnitude sense-check, and extends correctly to volume (k³).
responseLevels.partial: Converts lengths and simple units correctly and may do the time chain, but applies the linear factor to area/volume (or vice versa) — the squared/cubed idea is not yet secure.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Convert 3 m² into cm². Show your working. Then, separately: convert 2.5 hours into seconds.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A pupil who understands area conversion uses the SQUARE of the linear factor and reaches 30 000; a pupil applying the linear factor gets 300. Watching the working shows whether they used 100 or 100². The time conversion separately reveals whether they carry a multi-step chain through both stages (9000) or stop after one (150). Neither correct answer is reachable by the mistaken method.
